Dunaway seeking retail re-entry 


ATLANTA — Chain drug veteran Bill - 
Dunaway is working to put together financing _ 
for a new retail venture in suburban Gwinnett 
County, one of the nation’s fastest-growing [Ry ‘ 
metropolitan areas and site of two former © 
Dunaway drug stores. Dunaway sold the 16- 
store, family-owned chain to Jack Eckerd 
Corp. in May 1989. 

Plans are to open a “fresh market” retailcon- ~~ 
cept on a site of more than 80,000 square feet. The store would 
anchor itself with high-quality, fresh produce, high-quality 
meats and fresh seafood, dairy, beer and wine, a scratch bakery, 
ethnic H&BAs and dry groceries. The store will not feature a 
pharmacy or mainline H&BAs, Dunaway said. 

“I have the management team and the location in place,” 
Dunaway said. “This will be a destination-type store for an up- 
scale market, with a lot of knowledgeable service on the floor 
and alot of sampling, along the lines of a Stew Leonard. The idea 
is to open more than one. 2 

Dunaway signed a three-year non-compete clause with Eck- 
erd last year, barring him from drug retailing until 1992. Since 
then, he has taught college courses, run for mayor of Marietta, 
Ga., and overseen other business interests, including partial 
ownership of Atlanta’s well-known Abbey Restaurant.

DRUG STORE NEWS, November 5, 1990 


Walgreen’s fiscal 1990 
sees sales top $6B mark 


DEERFIELD, Ill. 
Lending credence to the old 
maxim that nothing succeeds 
like success, Walgreen Co. 
racked up strong gains in 
sales, earnings and store 
count in fiscal 1990, smashing 
through the $6 billion sales 
mark and opening 104 new 
stores in the past year. 


The nation’s top drug chain 
produced a 12.4-percent gain 
in sales for the year ended 
Aug. 31, to $6.05 billion. Net 
earnings advanced 13.2 per- 
cent, to $174.6 million. 


In the fourth quarter, sales 
advanced 11.3 percent to 
$1.49 billion, with net hitting 
$40.4 million, compared with 
$33.7 million the previous 
year. Walgreens’ board of di- 
rectors announced a 15-per- 
cent hike in the dividend, to 92 


cents a year. 

Walgreens’ expansion pace 
continued at a 7 clip for 
the year, as well. The chain’s 
104 new drug stores and two 
RxPress retail pharmacies 
brought store count near the 
1,600-unit level. The chain 
also remodeled 165 stores dur- 
ing the year, and will step up 
remodeling efforts this year. 

In October, Walgreens also 
completed its takeover of Lee 
Drug, a nine-store chain oper- 
ating in New Hampshire and 
Massachusetts. The Lee 
stores will be converted early 
next year, according to the 
company, strengthening the 
chain’s relatively new market 
presence in New England. 

“Since 1983, we’ve im- 
proved market share in each of 
our top 10 markets,” noted

By David Vaczek 

GOUVERNEUR, N.Y. 
— Kinne has joined a 
distinct. chai minority, 
with its recently completed 
chainwide instailation of an 
advanced POS scanning sys- 
tem in all 32 stores. 

The upstate chain (with 
six stores in Vermont) 
made the leap from a 
hodgepodge of mechanical 
non-computerized cash 
registers to an IBM system 
after trying out various al- 
ternatives for five years, 
Steve Hayden, vp-MIS, 
told Drug Store News. 

After a two-store pilot 
that began last fall, the rest 
of the stores were equipped 
with IBM 4688 registers 
and IBM drug chain POS 
software this summer, said 
Hayden. 

he typical setup in 
stores averaging 7,500 
square feet is one IBM PS/2 
controller, five registers, 
and a combination of verti- 
cal and horizontal slot scan- 
ners. Each store also has a 
Telxon portable, for cycle 
inventory, and price audit 
via radio frequency. 

F&M Distributors, the 
deep discounter, has been 
the only large retailer with a 
full chainwide a hae Seg 
out. Many smaller chains, 


RAY 


and some larger ones, have 
wrestled with cost justification 
of scanning systems. 

Hayden said elimination of 
item stickers won’t be among 
initial savings since chain ex- 
ecutives feel that consumers 
want sticker pricing: “Our 
customers are not used to 
[UPC codes]. I think they ex- 
pect price tags.” 

Kinney expects to pay for 
the $40,000-per-store system 


in about one-and-a-half years. 
A key area of savings, Ha den 
believes, will be in refined 
merchandising from the 
store’s sales reports. Other 
cost savings will be in auto- 
mating store’s bookkeeping, 
greater pricing accuracy, fast- 
er implementation of price 
changes, faster customer 
checkout, and consistent 
training for associates. 
Kinney sent three people— 
two from MIS and one from 
fo ae it a week-long 
IBM training session on how 
to use the system and how to 


ered installation, operation 
and trainin e: 

With POS installed, Hay- 
den is now focusing on inte- 
grating the front-of-store 
system with a new pharma- 
cy system. Last year, Kin- 
ney put in a General Com- 
pee Corp. system with 

EC Astra hardware. 

Working with IBM, GCC 
and Telxon, MIS is now 
uaa | an interface be- 
tween the two systems to al- 
low creation and use of a sin- 
gle file of sales information, 
allowing access to pharmacy 
pricing from any register. 

MIS is also writing a pro- 

am for breaking up the 

ay’s-end sales information 
from the stores so it can be 
meaningfully used by buy- 
ers and operations. 

The next major project 
will be creation of a perpet- 
ual inventory system that 
will employ IBM’s in-store 
inventory management 
software to allow automatic 
updating of the inventory 
and creation of orders. 

Kinney’s MIS staff now 
numbers 10, as the chain 
prepares to open its 33rd 
store in Manlius, N.Y.

By James Frederick 

HOUSTON — More than 
200 supermarket retailers 
came here last month with a 
mission: to become better mer- 
chants of health and beauty 
aids and general merchandise. 

They left armed with a 
wealth of facts to support 
what they already suspected: 


that their strongest weapon in 
the battle for non-foods sales 
against drug and discount 
store retailers was their built- 
in strength as convenient, 
one-stop shopping outlets. 
But they also came away 
with new research findings 
which confirm that consumers 
continue to shun food stores 


when it comes to many of their 
non-foods needs, in spite of the 
one-stop convenience factor. 
The reason: lingering percep- 
tions among shoppers that su- 
permarkets remain high- 
priced outlets for many CM 
and H&BA categories.

DRUG STORE NEWS, November 5, 1990 


OPINION 


4 


Finally, real numbers on product intros 


It costs a bundle to introduce a new product. It also 
costs plenty to get rid of a flop. No one argues against 
those propositions. But who should pay for the retail- 
er’s portion of the costs? The manufacturer? That’s 
what many retailers believe. After all, their argument 

goes, manufacturers have exacerbated 


the problem. In clawing for shelf space, 
they’ve created a torrent of product in- 
troductions, most of them unnecessary 
line extensions that do virtually nothing 
to build real category growth. One 
study, for example, shows the number 
of upfront intros tripling in the past de- 
cade. I don’t have to tell you how many 
items in this growing stream become 
~ lasting winners. Damn few. 


an , Then there’s the other side of the ar- 
IN THE MARKET gument. Isn’t the manufacturer already 
BRUCE BUCKLEY shouldering a disproportionate share of 


(at least) the introductory costs through 
research and development and consum- 
er advertising? Shouldn’t a retailer assume part of the 
burden as a cost of doing business? And, whoever said 
retailing should be risk-free, anyway? Failures and 
markdowns have always been part of the business. No 
pain, no gain. 

Besides, the argument goes on, manufacturers can 
only give up so much margin. If a retailer wants a 
neatly wrapped guarantee, he’d better be prepared to 
give up other perks that have more potential for build- 
ing the business—like some of his co-op allowances. 
There’s no free lunch, is another way of putting it. 

These arguments and counter-arguments have 
grown in intensity as supermarkets, and later (and to 
a much lesser extent) drug chains, have tried to exact 
up-front money from manufacturers seeking to intro- 
duce new products. The controversy over these so- 
called slotting allowances (and their grimmer cousins, 
failure fees) has generated lots of heat, of course, but 
not much light. 


Now comes a study that, for the first time, puts 
some real numbers on the cost of introductions—from 
research and development at the manufacturing end 
to wholesalers’ and retailers’ actual, real-time costs of 
putting these products into distribution—and of tak- 
ing them out if they fall flat. This new study is the 
product of more than a year of research under the ae- 
gis of six food and drug associations, including 
NACDS, the Food Marketing Institute and the Gro- 
cery Manufacturers Association. The consultants who 
carried out the study are from the highly respected ac- 
counting firm Deloitte & Touche. ~— 

Their report covers a number of actual product intro- 
ductions and deletions over a range of categories, and 
apportions and totals up the true costs incurred by man- 
ufacturers, wholesalers, retailers and, in the case of food 
product intros, food brokers. Although the costs are not 
meant to be projectable, the process through which they 
were attained can serve as a valuable template for drug 
retailers who want to do cost measurements based on 
their own actual experience. That will be the ongoing 
legacy of this pathfinding study. 

Perhaps it will help move retailers away from the 
“protection money” game and into sharing with manu- 
facturers the investment and risks of total marketing 
programs. That process has been practiced more suc- 
cessfully in the chain drug industry, where retailers 
and manufacturers have developed some cohesive re- 
lationships under the umbrella of NACDS, than 
among supermarkets, where conflicts have been 
fierce and long-lasting. 

The downside may be that, because the study con- 
firms the heavy costs of introductions and deletions, it 
will be used by some retailers to justify a stepped up 
demand for slotting allowances and failure fees. That 
would be a mistake, in my opinion. 

(Copies of the study by the Joint Industry Task 
Force on Product Introductions and Deletions may be 
purchased at $10 each from NACDS, 413 N. Lee St., 
Alexandria, VA 22314.) 


can never have too much good will 


One of this industry’s strengths has always been the 
brazen willingness of drug chains to steal ideas from 
each other. 

One chain shows some success with in-store optical 
centers and half a dozen others start testing the same 

waters. 


Somebody else merges a drug store 
with asupermarket, and suddenly we’re 
up to our ears in combo stores. 

Another chain offers prescription dis- 
counts to senior citizens and... well, 
you get the picture. 

At the same time, I’ve always felt that 
a key weakness of the industry was the 
failure of both chains and independents 
to seize opportunities to project a posi- 
tive image of drug store retailing. 


WASHINGTON Now, don’t get me wrong. . . I’m not 
PERSPECTIVE saying that the industry has a negative 
KEN RANKIN image. But I am saying that the nation’s 


drug stores are the Good Guys, and it 
sure would be nice if everyone recognized that fact. 

Here’s a two-step plan to capitalize on one of the in- 
dustry’s main strengths in order to bolster the public’s 
appreciation of drug store retailers. 

Step One: Copy Jack Eckerd’s new policy support- 
ing U.S. military reservists stationed in the Middle 
East. (See Drug Store News, Oct. 8, 1990, p. 1.) 

Back on the same day that President Bush activated 
the military reserves in response to the Iraqi invasion 
of Kuwait, Eckerd CEO Stew Turley announced that 
reservists employed by the chain who are called to ac- 
tive duty will not be subjected to economic hardship. 


Under the new Jack Eckerd policy the company will 
make up the difference between any affected employ- 
ee’s military pay and his or her civilian salary while on 
active duty. ‘i 

While it’s not yet clear whether this new policy will 
earn Turley a place in Heaven, it has earned Jack Eck- 
erd immeasurable good will here in Washington. 

Indeed, in a speech to the U.S. Senate recently, 
Sen. Bob Graham (D-Fla.) called attention to the 
chain’s pay program for employee reservists while 
outlining “the sacrifices of corporate America in sup- 
port of American reservists” in the Persian Gulf. 

“For many families, it means peace of mind for the 
brave reservists sent halfway around the world to 
augment our military mission,” he said. “At home, it 
means mortgages and tuition will be paid” and “fam- 
ilies can put food on the table when breadwinners are 

one.” 
: Significantly, however, Graham didn’t hear of Eck- 
erd’s program from the chain. Rather, he learned of it 
by pure chance while working with other volunteers 
to clean up Tampa Bay earlier this fall. 

One of those volunteers, a Marine Reserve officer 
named Moises Suarez who works for Eckerd, just hap- 
pened to tell Graham “how much it meant for him that 
his company offered to maintain his salary if he was 
called up for duty.” 

Step Two: Don’t imitate Jack Eckerd’s modesty. 
When you take action that reflects positively on your 
company or on the drug store industry as a whole, let 
everyone know about it! 

Remember, you'll never have too much good will— 
not even here in Washington.

High-price 
image haunts 
supermarkets 
in non-foods 


HOUSTON — Consumers 
still think of supermarkets as 
being higher-priced than their 
competition in many general 
merchandise and health and 
beauty aids categories, ac- 
cording to new research from 
the Food Marketing Institute 
and the Grocery Manufactur- 
ers of America. 

The GM/HBC Consumer 
Shopping Preferences 1990 
report points up wide dispari- 
ties in where consumers 
choose to shop for their non- 
foods. The report, 
based on a survey of 2,000 con- 
sumer households by Market 
Facts, Inc., was released Oct. 
16 at the GM/HBC Conference 
and Educational Exposition. 

The study underscores 
what the food industry has 
long suspected: that the per- 
ception—if not the reality—of 
higher prices cuts into sales of 
many non-foods categories of- 
fered by food stores, despite 
the powerful advantage of 
convenient, one-stop shop- 
ping supermarkets have in 
their arsenal. 

Supermarkets were named 
as the primary outlet for oral 
care products, deodorants and 
shampoo by consumers in the 
survey. But in many of the 
other 16 key categories sur- 
veyed—including video cas- 
settes, kitchen gadgets, 
school supplies and hosiery— 
food retaiels are still losing 
out to drug and discount 
stores. Perceived higher 
prices were the culprit. 

“By a wide margin, the ma- 
jor deterrent to supermarket 
purchase of non-food items is 
price—a loud and clear hin- 
drance regardless of market 
area or shopper subgroup,” 
the report concludes. “To en- 
courage more purchase of 
such items in grocery stores, 
shoppers want lower every- 
day prices.” 

By the same token, the re- 
ort notes, “the major reason 
y far for purchasing non-food 

items in a supermarket is con- 
venience,” and “the major 
draw for discount or mass 
merchandisers and discount 
drug stores is everyday low 
prices.” 

The study also found a 
strong unmet demand for such 
in-store services as pharma- 
cies, postal stations and pack- 
ing/shipping centers in food 
stores. 

The survey prompted a 
strong reaction from a panel of 
11 supermarket and supplier 
executives convened to dis- 
cuss its findings. Several of 
the participants acknowl- 
rin pe the pricing problem, 
and said the supermarket in- 
dustry could no longer rest on 
its advantages as a natural 
customer traffic center. They 
also agreed the industry faces 
big hurdles in overcoming the 
high-price image in non-foods, 
and several hinted at the pos- 
sibility of a major shift in pric-

“We have to build a better 
‘ie perception,” said Jeff

Phoenix. “In the short term, 
it’s nice to sit back and collect

Tim Snee of Ralphs Grocery

rice perception that keeps 
customers] from shopping 
from us [for non-foods]. We 
need to face this issue head-on; 
we can’t keep wrapping our-

flag.”

of the non-foods business, we 
win the game, but in the price 
aspect, we have a problem,” 
Brian Joyce of Dominick’s

fully capitalize on their pres- 
ence in non-foods—despite 
the fact that they already have 
those consumers in their

approaches to non-foods mer- 
chandising.

ers getting value for their 
money,” noted Bill Harris of 
Randall’s Food and Drug. 
“Service, selection and quality 
are what we have going for us 
against the low-price angle of 
our competitors.” 


DRUG STORE NEWS, November 5, 1990 


Supermarket retailers 
seek non-foods savvy at 
1st GM/HBC Conference 


Continued from A 3 
annual GM/HBC (health and 


beauty care) Conference spon- 
sored by the Food Marketing 
Institute and the Grocery 
Manufacturers of America. 
The three-day event in mid- 
October drew a total of nearly 
1,500 retailers, wholesalers, 
suppliers and brokers, and in- 
cluded both educational semi- 
nars and trade-floor dealmak- 
ing between buyers and 
vendors. 

“I’m excited about this con- 
vention,” FMI president Rob- 
ert Aders told the gathering 
on opening day. “It marks a 
new direction in education at 
FMI, applying the magic of a 
convention to two of the most 
powerful categories in modern 
supermarketing.” 

Indeed, the creation of a 
separate event among food re- 
tailers to support non-foods 
merchandising and marketing 
signals the growing impor- 
tance of GM and H&BA cate- 
gories to the supermarket in- 
dustry—and the growing 
determination among food 
chains to challenge drug 
stores on their own turf. 

In that sense, the show was 
a pivotal event in the ongoing 
competition among trade 
classes and the blurring of 
lines between food, drug and 
discount stores. The confer- 
ence marked the willingness 
of many food retailers to-shift 
their strategies in the battle 
for GM and H&BA sales— 
even regarding long-held pric- 
ing policies. It underscored 
the growing status of non- 
foods managers. And it for- 
maily signaled the arrival of 
non-foods as an integral com- 
ponent of supermarket retail- 
ing; indeed, food and non- 
foods are rapidly approaching 
parity at some leading food 
chains. 


‘In the beginning. . .’ 


“In the beginning, the first 
grocers and supermarket op- 
erators were very much in the 
non-food business,” Aders 
said. “The movement into 
GM/HBC products today is 
less a new direction than an ef- 
fort to rediscover markets 
that were lost or never fully 
developed.” 

Echoing that theme was a 
conference participant from 
Schwegmann’s in New Or- 
leans. “Our goal is to allocate 
40 percent of our space to non- 
foods,” he said. 

He was not alone. Confer- 
ence speakers and partici- 
pants from all sides of the food 
industry expressed a determi- 
nation to capitalize on the in- 
herent strengths of supermar- 
kets to boost their $21 billion 
in non-foods sales. Said outgo- 
ing FMI chairman Dean Wer- 
ries of Fleming Companies, 
“The competition is formida- 
ble—but we, too, bring to the 
marketplace numerous 
strengths: consumer aware- 
ness, technology, conve- 


nience, selection, one-stop 
shopping, and seeing our cus- 
tomers at least once a week.” 

Werries and other speakers 
urged non-foods managers to 
push for the opening of more 
pharmacies at their respective 
chains. “The single most effec- 
tive step many grocers can 
take is to extend the health- 
care category and—where the 
demographics and competi- 
tion are right—open a phar- 
macy,” said the FMI chair- 
man. “A Paci adds a new 
source of high-margin income, 
and it improves the sales of the 
entire HBC category—by as 
much as 40 percent in some 
cases.” 


Pharmacies urged 


In a separate address, in- 
dustry consultant Murray Ra- 
phel noted that only about 
4,000 out of a possible 30,000 
supermarkets have pharma- 
cies. He urged non-foods man- 
agers to spur their companies 
to add more pharmacies and 
other key non-foods catego- 
ries to build a complete busi- 
ness, including video depart- 
ments, greeting cards, photo 
and books and magazines. 

“The secret is not to be the 
best supermarket, but to have 
the best selection in targeted 
areas,” Raphel said. 

Speaker and consultant 
Harold Lloyd told his audi- 
ence to put more spark in their 
GM aa H&BA sales with a 
multi-pronged strategy. Call- 
ing non-foods “a very, very 
important part of [the store’s] 
profitability,” Lloyd urged 
non-foods managers to “mer- 
chandise the merchandise. . . 
and give your GM/HBC peo- 

le a chance to be creative.” 

etailers and industry ex- 
perts at the conference made 
no bones about the obvious 
lures offered by GM and 
H&BA categories: high mar- 
gins, incremental revenues, 
and the ability to turn super- 
markets into one-stop power 
centers. 

The challenge to nonfood 
execs: winning more space 
and commitment for GM and 
H&BA from their bosses; 
overcoming high-price per- 
ceptions among consumers in 
the face of growing competi- 
tion from deep-discounters 
like Phar-Mor; battling “cate- 
gory killers” like Wal-Mart 
and Toys “R” Us; coping with 
a flood of new-product intro- 
ductions—nearly 12,000 last 
year alone; coping with the in- 
creasing fragmentation of the 
consumer base; and watching 
overall net margins in super- 
markets shrink to a low of 0.71 
percent in 1988-89. 

Meanwhile, said Werries, 
the food industry is enterin 
“a time of transition” od 
slowing growth. Store size is 
also growing at a slower 
space, he said. 

“Maybe in the ’90s,” We.- 
ries said, “we will enter the 
one-stop shopping business.”

Safeway’s 3rd gtr. 
net income is up 


OAKLAND, Calif. 
Safeway’s investment in the 
Vons supermarket chain 
helped third-quarter net in- 
come climb from last year’s $7.1 
million to $20.8 million for the 
period ended Sept. 8, the com- 
pany reported, even though 
sales were essentially flat. 

Sales for the quarter in- 
creased 4.6 percent to $3.5 bil- 
lion. For the 36-week period, 
income climbed from $23.5 
million to $59.4 million, on 
$10.2 billion in sales, a 4.4-per- 
cent increase. Same-store 
sales increased 3.9 percent for 
the quarter and 3.4 percent for 
the 36-week period, and gains 
were also noted for gross prof- 
it, operating profit, and oper- 
ating cash flow. 

The 35-percent equity in- 
vestment in Vons was a prime 
factor for other income in- 
creasing from $1.1 million for 
the quarter to $12.0 million. 

Interest expense for the 
quarter increased from $88.4 
million to $91.2 million, and 
declined for the 36 weeks from 
$267.8 million to $261.4 million 
for the 86 weeks. The compa- 
ny attributed the 36-week 
performance to lower borrow- 
ings in the wake of its initial 
public offering of 11.5 million 
shares of cortimorr stock last 
April.

Nichols reports 
$21.5M net loss 


NEW YORK — S.E. Nich- 
ols reported a net loss of $21.5 
million for the three months 
ended August 4, on sales of 
$11.5 million. 

The loss includes a $15.5 
million provision for reorgani- 
zation costs connected with 
the company’s filing for Chap- 
ter 11 protection this past Au- 
gust. This quarter’s figure 
compares with last year’s net 
gain of $1.8 million, which in- 
cluded a $4.3 million gain from 
the discontinuance and sale of 
the company’s F.R. Schreiber 
wholesale division. 

The quarter’s sales figure 
solely reflects activity from 
the company’s new Pharm- 
house deep discount super 
drug stores, a format which 
bowed last April. As such, the 
company noted, the figure is 
not comparable with last 
year’s $51.4 million that the 
company’s 34 discount depart- 
ment stores, no longer in oper- 
ation, tallied. 

S.E. Nichols’ strate has 
been to liquidate and close its 
discount department store 
base, and reopen the units as 
Pharmhouses. Currently, 19 
Pharmhouse units operate in 
the mid-Atlantic region.

Drug Emporium buys 
St. Louis franchise rights 


ST LOUIS — Drug Emporium has repurchased the franchise 
rights for the St. Louis area from Alpha , Inc., which since 
the mid-1980s has operated four stores in the city and suburbs. 

It advances a strategy of buying certain franchises and fol- 
lows franchise buyouts in Minneapolis, Indianoplis, Augusta, 
Ga., and Charleston and Columbia, S.C. 

Indicating that under corporate ownership the St. Louis 
stores will continue to do business as before, ceo Gary Wilber 
pointed out that corporate-owned stores will receive the compa- 
ny’s major emphasis as the key to growth in today’s competitive 
environment. “Nearly all” of the stores planned for opening in 
the early 1990s will be company-owned, Wilber said. 


Wal-Mart buys Wholesale Club 


BENTONVILLE, Ark. — Wal-Mart has ~~ a definitive 
agreement to buy The Wholesale Club chain for an estimated 
$163.8 million in cash and Wal-Mart common stock. The pact re- 
affirms Wal-Mart’s commitment to this format, which it has 
stressed by operating 141 Sam’s Wholesale Clubs. 

The 27 Wholesale Clubs in six Midwestern states will probably 
be converted to the Sam’s name, since Wal-Mart has said the clubs 
will not be operated as a separate division, Thomas Geisse, senior 
vp-marketing at The Wholesale Club, told Drug Store News. 


FoxMeyer selis compufer subsidiary 


ARLINGTON, Texas -— FoxMeyer Corp. has sold its Fox 
Computers subsidiary to Reynadyne Corp., an investor group 
headed by Daniel G. Williams. Fox Computers has relocated 
here, and changed its name to Reynadyne Data Systems, Inc. 


Nichols financing in effect 


NEW YORK —S.E. Nichols; operating as debtor-in-posses- 
sion, said all technical requirements have been fulfilled relating 
to its DIP-secured financing facility for up to $10 million with 
Serums National Bank & Trust Co. of New York. The financing 
is in effect, the company stated. S.E. Nichols operates 19 deep- 
discount super drug stores under the name Pharmhouse. 


Child IDs mark Happy Harry’s openings 


NEWARK, Del. — wf. Harry’s offered its award-winning 
Child ID Program as part of the ee ee festivities in No- 
vember of two new stores, in Pike Creek Valley and Hockessin, 
respectively. 

per of the Child ID Program, which won a 1989 Gold Link

ty service, each child is weighed, measured, fingerprinted and 
photographed. A laminated identification card containing this 
information is then given to parents to carry, so they can pro- 
vide authorities with vital formation quickly, should their 


child ever disappear.

New Mexico stores proved too remote: Thrifty 


LOS ANGELES — Thrifty Corp. decided 
tc vacate New Mexico because it was too cost- 
ly to continue trucking from distribution cen- 
ters in California, vp Chris Bement told Drug 
Store News. The drug chain closed 11 stores, 
but offered management and pharmacy em- 
ployees other jobs in California, he said. 

He attributed Thrifty’s closing of five 
stores in Tucson, Ariz., to an economic slump 


in that market. Thrifty also closed seven 
stores around Phoenix due to duplication of 
market areas, Bement said. Yet, the chain 
feels the Arizona market is still profitable 
enough to support its other 23 stores in the 
state, so no other closings are planned, he 
said. In addition, the company has opened 27 
stores in California over the course of the cur- 
rent fiscal year, which ends December 1.

A ne 


Company success always on the line 


Fall is a good time for me: I like the colors, the smell of 
wood smoke and, perhaps most of all, football. But foot- 
ball gets boring sometimes. Then, even the spectacular 
pass or the slashing run seem to blend with all the others 
witnessed over the years. When that mood settles in, I 

eweuld turn off the set and go out for a 


IN THE MARKET 


waik. But I don’t, couch potato that I am 
in the fall. I watch the line play. 

Try it sometime. It’s not easy. The 
ball draws the eye like a magnet. But 
hold your focus on the line, and you'll see 
where the game outcome is really decid- 
ed. Strength, speed and agility are im- 
portant, but gut determination and 
pride are what count in the end. 

If there’s a parallel for retailing here 
it’s that winning depends not so much on 
the top execs—the quarterbacks, etce.— 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


as on the unsung people in the stores, 
headquarters and distribution centers. 


Competing effectively depends on the 
accumulation of all the dozens of little things they do 
every day, most of which go unnoticed by their bosses. 

Then why do they do it? Well, a cynic would say 
money and job security. But that’s bull. Mostly it’s 
pride and involvement—that special feeling of making 
a difference, even in a small way, in a successful enter- 
prise. | 

The parallel between line play on the football field 
and line play in the retail drug industry is particularly 


apt for this current issue, which reveals the winners of 
the 1990 Drug Store News REX Awards. It is six 
years since we presented our first awards for retail ex- 
cellence in the crowded ballroom of the Omni Park 
Central Hotel in New York. 

From the winner of that first REX chain award— 
Walgreens—to the 1990 chain honorees, Phar-Mor 
and Kerr Drug, the not-so-secret success ingredient 
has been the largely invisible people on the line. 

So, in this column, rather than laud Banks and John- 
ny Kerr or Mickey Monus for their companies’ well- 
deserved awards. . . I’d like to toast their players in 
the trenches. And if it doesn’t sound too much like a 
beer commercial, here’s to them.

solidation or retrenchment and are trying tc line up

Chain drug stationery story: 


Neon a hot s 


everal drug chains that 

mainly stuck to the ba- 

sics reported good, if not 
spectacular, results this back- 
to-school season, with neon, 
as buyers had bet, providing 
an especially brignt spot. 

Heavily promoted commod- 
ity items were tremendous for 
K&B, said buyer Chris Mi- 
chel. And while the chain held 
to a limited fashion selection, 
neons were hot throughout. 

“We were generally pleased 
with back-to-school,” Michel 
said, adding that “where we 
strayed from the basics much, 
sales were slower.” 

Although schools in K&B’s 
markets generally open about 
Aug. 20, the chain started 
BTS advertising in July, rath- 
er than August, this year. The 
strategy worked in pulling 
customers in\to pick up com- 
modity school supplies before 
other school-related spend- 
ing, for clothes, tuition and the 
like, depleted their disposable 
income, he maintained. 

In contrast, Rite Aid’s BTS 
season gathered steam later 
than usual this year, said buy- 
er Mark Blandford, but sales 
ended up 12 percent-15 per- 
cent higher than last season. 

It was a good year for li- 
censes at the chain, with New 
Kids on the Block and Teenage 
Mutant Ninja Turtles the 
standouts, and The Simpsons 
also strong. Thanks partly to 
the strong licenses, Rite Aid 
had its best year ever with 
lunchboxes. 

Lisa Frank fashion portfo- 
lios continued to produce 
strong sales, and Pentech fab- 
ric-covered stick pens were 
—— with kids into the 

riendship-bracelet look. 


Changed planogram 


Rite Aid redid its stationery 
department planogram this 
i expanding mainly in the 

ome office supplies area, but 
also adding more college/nar- 
row-rule items, another SKU 
of scientific calculators, and 
more microperforated-edge 
notebooks, in response to stu- 
dent needs. Scme older, pat- 
terned fashion goods and book 
covers were culled. In addi- 


tion, Trapper Keeper and oth- 
er specialty notebooks were 
thinned, Blandford explained, 
because “we didn’t think we 
needed as broad an offering 
and couldn’t make much mon- 
ey on them. We found a trend 
of having a residue of that in 
the past.” 

Rite Aid doesn’t promote 
BTS as heavily as some 
chains, instead building up 
and concentrating on basic 
BTS merchandise, where the 
bulk of its sales are, augment- 
ed by some fashion and promo- 
tional goods. But the chain 
stepped up in-store signs and 
programs and sharpened pric- 
ing of in-and-out merchandise, 
which reduced carryovers and 
spurred incremental sales. 

Genovese was “really satis- 
fied” with its BTS season, said 
buyer Cynthia Stahley-Zun- 
iga. Anything neon was hot, 
especially Mead’s neon mar- 
bled composition books. 

Drug Emporium’s BTS 
sales increased in the double 
digits, reported director of 
merchandising Bill Brock, 
who said the chain bought 
more and sold more. “We had 
good cleanup sales.” 

The chain did more fashion 
and color business, for plus 
and profitable sales, while fill- 
er paper and some other com- 
modities were down. 

Reliable Drugs, itself a rela- 
tively new kid on the block, 
did a major revamp of its sta- 
tionery-home office depart- 
ment. Its aim was achieving a 
consistent merchandising 
look, rather than the rainbow, 

rice/item approach inherited 

rom Peoples, from which Re- 
liable acquired its first 100- 
plus stores last year. 

Reliable went from dealing 
with some 58 vendors in the de- 
partment to about 12, said 
Tony Montini, senior vp-pur- 
chasing and merchandising, 
with Stuart Hall and Empire 
providing most of the paper 
goods and writing instruments/ 

egged items, respectively. 

e consolidation not only cre- 
ates continuity and packaging 
consistency, but improves Re- 
liable’s ability to meet vendor 
minimums, Montini said.

Imasco reports drop 
in third-qtr. earnings 


MONTREAL — Imasco re- 
ported a 5-percent decrease in net 
earnings for the nine months and 
a 25-percent drop in net earnings 
for the third quarter ended Sept. 
30. 

For the nine months, net earn- 
ings were $236.1 million (Canadi- 
an), down from $24,.9 million in 
the 1989 period. For the third 
quarter, net earnings were $77.5 
million, compared with $103.5 
million for the same period a year 
ago. 

Net earnings include a contri- 
bution from Peoples Drug Stores, 
classified as discontinued opera- 
tions. Earnings from continuing 
operations were $232.4 million for 
the nine months, a 6 percent de- 
crease from last year’s $246.7 mil- 
lion, and $77.3 million for the 
third quarter, down from $103.4 
million. 

Purdy Crawford, Imasco chair- 
man, president and ceo, said of 
the results, “Hardee’s Food Sys- 
tems and Canada Trust are feel- 
ing effects of the weak economy, 
while Imperial Tobacco and Shop- 
pers Drug Mart have continued to 
register strong earnings gains.” 

Crawford said Imperial’s and 
Shoppers’ “excellent results” 
should be sustained.

DRUG STORE NEWS, December 10, 1990 


RNA EE ERE ORT EET, AIIM: 


The industry’s 10 best stories of ’90 


It’s that time of year: The time when newspaper and 
magazine writers, columnists, critics, etc., look back 
and compile their Ten Best (or Worst) lists. I won’t de- 
part from that tradition, as hackneyed as it may be. 
So, herewith is my 1990 Ten Best list. 

Eve Rich becomes president of 


IN THE MARKET 


Thrifty Drug. For me this story tops 
the list — a huge surprise. There were 
no doubt any number of possible retail 
drug suitors for this challenging, high- 
visibility job. Thrifty Corp. took a dif- 
ferent route and picked a top executive 
from apparel retailing. A sense of fash- 
ion, a woman’s point of view, a proven 
track record in guiding company growth 
— these should be considerable 
strengths for a.chain that badly needs to 
lure more women shoppers back into its 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 


stores. Thrifty’s to be commended for 


its intriguing choice. 

The return of familiar names to the 
chain drug scene. This involves not one but several 
stories that broke during during the year. Among the 
well known returning veterans: Bob Begley, Al Towle 
and Bill Edwards. 

Raisa Gorbachev’s impromptu visit to a Snyder’s 
drug store. Not a blockbuster news event, but for me 
symbolic, at the most basic, grassroots level, of how 
far we’ve come in reducing East-West tensions. 

Martin Grass and Rite Aid cleared in bribery 
case. This was a case that never should have been 
brought, as the trial judge quickly determined. That 
Rite Aid and its president were able to maintain the 
company’s momentum in the face of extraordinary 
pressures was a tribute to their toughness. 

Expansion of advanced computer technology. 
Again, not one story, but many. Drug chains such as 
Walgreens, Eckerd, Thrifty, Rite Aid, Pay Less and 
others committed their investment resources to auto- 
mation advances. Their health depended on it. 


Dan Jorndt becomes Walgreens’ president. With 
all the highly publicized management turmoil at other 
chains, it was refreshing to report on the well planned 
transition of leadership from Fred Canning to Dan 
Jorndt. 

Growing strength of pharmacy departments. 
Yes, supermarkets and discount department stores 
are installing pharmacies as fast as they can. But drug 
stores, with their neighborhood convenience and 
pharmacy tradition, retain the edge. In the end, there 
will be more than enough for everyone as America’s 
population ages, and new drugs are found for an as- 
sortment of ills. 

New drug store formats create excitement. Pe- 
riodic store remodels have always been a part of 
drug retailing. But within the past couple of years, 
there’s been an acceleration of new designs featur- 
ing exciting, easy-to-shop front ends coupled with 
warmer, ‘nore accessible pharmacy departments. 
It’s hard to single anyone out, but Drug Store News 
honored two of the best with REX awards: Eckerd 
and Pay Less. 

Peoples’ purchase by CVS. The good news was 
that a proud chain with a long history will continue and 
prosper under CVS’s management. The bittersweet 
part: the top-level management that got the chain 
turned around will be leaving. 

Chains respond to reserve call-up in Mideast cri- 
sis. Eckerd, Osco and others went far beyond what 
the law required in protecting the jobs and status of 
reservists called up during the crisis. It was the finest 
example of companies operating for the good of their 
communities, and thereby doing themselves good. 

If I were to compile a “worst list,” it would have to 
include the demise of Dart, the prosecution of Rite Aid 
and Martin Grass, the continuing erosion of drug 
stores’ H&BA market share, the bankrupcy turmoil 
at Revco and the failure of SupeRx Corp. of Arizona, a 
promising newcomer to the chain drug field. 

In any event, here’s to a more prosperous 1991. 


H.O plus Ulta® equals 


How much is H.O PLUS Ulta*? Chicago-area mer- 
chants know this really isn’t a math problem; rather, 
it’s a lesson in building loyal patronage, repeat visits 
and incremental sales and profits. 

In recent months, these two totally dissimilar special- 


ty chains — H,0 PLUS and Ulta® — have 


brought shoppers some fresh, feel-good 


approaches to some well-off, fast-grow- 
ing suburbs of the Windy City. Both ap- 
peal to sophisticated, value-oriented con- 
sumers who respond to service. 

Ulta? just opened its third, 6,000- 
square-foot, off-price cosmetics-fra- 
grances-costume jewelry-fashion store 
in Morton Grove around Thanksgiving 
and plans for two more to follow shortly. 
Ulta’, billed as the “ultimate beauty 


THE HUMAN SIDE store,” was developed by ex-Osco exec- 


AL HELLER 


utives Dick George and Terry Hanson, 


who know this local market. 

Their premise is direct: be first with 
new products; be 100-percent in-stock or sell it next time 
to a customer for half-price;'no display hassles, such as 
locked showcases; easy returns and exchanges; 20 per- 
cent to 30 percent discounts on most items. 

Cook that with a pamper premise: Color Me Beautiful 
makeovers available for $30; a three-seat hair salon an- 
chors the store’s rear corner; a calming gray, mauve and 
black decor. It could be a recipe for loyalty. The format’s 
development, an obvious stretch from their drug store 
roots, followed extensive consumer research. 

H.O PLUS operates 23 bath and skin care specialty 
shops — it’s aiming for 27 by year’s end — from San 


Francisco to Palm Beach, Fla., to West Hartford, 
Conn., with Chicago a prime market. Its dazzling pre- 
sentation befits a department store, whose shoppers the 
chain is attempting to pick off with unintimidating ser- 
vice, a sense of in-store fun and aggressive follow-up 
with those on their mailing list. 

Claims aside that H20 PLUS might aim too high and 
miss mass traffic, or has copied ideas from the better 
established Body Shops, the chain makes customers 
feel good. As Jonathan, an Oak Brook sales associate, 
said, “In department stores, you face pushy women, 
then leave the store with a little bag and a big receipt.” 

At H.O PLUS, yellow rubber ducks fill stainless 
steel sinks as part of the decor; signs urge customers 
to “indulge, pamper, caress” and more; gifts are 
wrapped; glass shelves are curved to resemble waves. 
People lighten up in here and are more receptive to 
buy. The result: $35 average transactions on a $12 av- 
erage SKU of concentrated skin care product. 

Cash register receipts include the store phone num- 
ber and salesperson’s name. Every salesperson attends 
intensive three-day seminars twice a year. Salespersons 
aren’t licensed to apply creams to the face, but liberally 
sample products on customers’ hands. And, in a matter 
of minutes, a shopper and salesperson can complete a 
detailed skin care profile form — with copies going to the 
customer, who feels pampered; the salesperson and the 
store file for subsequent visits, and the corporate office 
for follow-up mailings. 

The Oak Brook store alone maintains profiles on 500 
customers — an enviable corps of repeat shoppers for 
any store selling toiletries. That’s the power of personal- 
ization.

Polish has not found it as

Nevertheless, no retailer in 
their right mind would risk of- 
fending the 44 percent of 
his/her customers who want 
and love nail polish. 

What makes the most sense 
is to fine-tune inventories so 


only the most popular brands 
are carried, and in this catego- 
ry, popular means Revlon, 
Cover Girl, L’Oréal, Maybel- 
line, Cutex, Wet & Wild and 


Sally Hansen.

counted for ail but one position

brands.

ucts, a line sold primarily 
door-to-door. 


Harmless mistake 


Unlike eye and face prod- 
ucts, where women can hurt 
their eyes or skin if they make 
a mistake, nail color is rela- 
tively harmless. The worse 
thing a women risks if she 
makes a mistake is hating the 
color which she can change in 
five minutes. 

That’s probably why wom- 
en are much more likely to buy 
a nail product when it’s on sale 
than they are to buy an eye 
color or face makeup product. 
Three out of 10 nail color users 
said they made their last pur- 
chase when it was on sale.

In the highly-competitive shampoo and conditioner category it is crucial that drug stores offer compet- 


itive pricing and the broadest assortment of mass and professional brands. 


Except for hair color users, 
women like to switch around in 
the hair care category in order 
to give their hair a “rest” from 
one formula or Rectang’ they 
want to try a uct they’ve 
seen sventaed. in hopes it will 
deliver what the ads promise. 
The array they have to choose 
from is nuge, and the fragment- 
ed brand loyalty to a sapere 
conditioner or spray is evident 
in the relatively low percent- 
ages for the top five preferred 
brands in these segments. 


Advertising campaigns 


Manufacturers’ advertising 
campaigns play a pivotal role in 
p: >-Sse i consumers on hair 
care ucts, and new prod- 
ucts t the category. For 
example, all-in-one sh 
/eonditioners, such as P&G’s 


Pert Plus, are opening up what ~ } 


appears to be a new segment, 
with the launches of Vidal Sas- 
soon’s Ultra Care and Revlon’s 
Flex & Go expected to create 
added excitement. 

In this kind of highly compet- 


itive category, being in stock 
and pricing competitively are 
crucial for drug store opera- 
tors; so is offering the broadest 
possible assortment of mass 
and professional brands. 

But the sheer breadth of se- 
lection in shampoos, condition- 
ers and sprays poses another 
challenge drug store retailers 
are trying tc meet: how to sim- 
plify hair-care shopping for 
their customers, the majority 
of whom are busy, working 
women. That’s where each re- 


tail operator can make a differ- 
ence. They weigh planogram- 
ming by family or by category, 
or a combination of the two a 
proaches. They use colorful 
point-of-purchase displays and 
special fixtures, call attention 
to new products with ceiling 
Si e and offer free samples. 
And they constantly advertise 
and promote this category, 
sometimes devoting -page 
ads to new products and includ- 
ing hair-care advice in circulars 
and other vehicles. 


| Fragrance users welcome variety, creative sales pitches 


omen are eclectic in 
their choice of fra- 
grances. Unlike sun 


care or facial moisturizer, 
where only one or two brands 
dominate, fragrance is a high- 
ly fragmented category, indi- 
cating that women are willing 
to buy more than one brand of 
fragrance and that they will 
try new fragrances as they 
come to market. 

In the Second Annuai Con- 
sumer Brands Preference 
Study, no fragrance com- 
manded more than a 9 percent 
preference among all women 
respondents. 

ut in considering women 
who actually purchased a fra- 
grance during the past 12 
months, Avon — an accessible 
f ce sold by helpful door- 

oor salespersons — had 
the highest brand preference 
share at 12 percent. 


Estée Lauder, a popular de- 
partment store line, was sec- 
ond with 9 percent. After that 
share preference breaks into 3 
percent shares and less. 

Cosmair’s Vanderbilt was 
the most popular mass fra- 
grance with a preference 
share of 2.8 percent. It ranked 
fourth on a list that included 
Poison as well as Estée Lau- 
der and Avon. 

Prince Matchabelli’s Wind 
Song, Revlon’s Charlie, Co- 
ty’s Emeraude, Lady Stetson, 
and Sand & Sable were the 
only other class mass fra- 
gees to make it into the top 

0 fe pee brands. 

ll the fragrances on the list 
were heavily advertised 
brands, indicating that wom- 
en are responsive to creative 
sales pitches, and that once 
again, good advertising con- 
tributes substantially to a 


product’s success in competi- 
tive categories. 

As a category, fragrance is 
in the moderate consumption 
range. Fifty-nine percent of 
all consumers, men and wom- 
en, had made a purchase of ei- 
ther a woman’s or a man’s fra- 
grance in the past 12 months, 
according to the survey done 
by Leo J. Shapiro and Asso- 
clates. 

That compares, on one end 
of the usage spectrum, to 
some 96 percent who had 
made a toothpaste purchase in 
the past 12 months, and on the 
other end to the 15 percent of 
consumers who had made a 
contact lens solution pur- 
chase. 

Another good thing about 
fragrance purchasers is they 
aren’t inclined to wait until a 
fragrance goes on sale before 
buying. Seventy-one percent 


of all fragrances are bought 
when they are not on sale. 
However, drug stores and 
other mass market outlets 
aren’t taking as much advan- 
tage of this trend as they 
could. The class mass lines, in- 
eluding Vanderbilt, Charlie 
and Lady Stetson, were pur- 
chased much more frequently 
when on sale. as opposed to 
ninety percent of all Estée 
Lauder purchases which were 


made at the regular price and 
this was true for most of the 
department store lines. 

is could indicate that if 
drug stores were to “dress up” 
their fashion counters more or 
provide more service, like de- 
partment stores, they could 
generate more full margin fra- 
grance purchases, and that 
could significantl enhance 
the bottom line profitability of 
mass market fragrance.

The most dramatic shifts in dollar 
sales shares, however, are still occur-

pe in in dollar sales volume

the H&BA categories tracked by Niel-

years now, drug stores = lost share 
on H&BA dollar sales. This year, they 
dropped 0.2 of a point to a 38. 1-percent 
share. In 1984, they had a 40. 1-percent 
share of H&BA dollar sales.

try’s share of H&BA sales is partly the 
result of mass merchandisers expand- 
ing and building up H&BA categories 
in their stores, and partly the result of 
everyday low-pricing strategies.

Category share shifts 


When you look at H&BA sales in 
drug stores on a category-by-category 
basis, you can see that drug stores are 
not getting strong dollar growth out of 
many categories these days. In 


H&BAs, the greatest growth in dollar — 


sales is coming from mass merchandise 
outlets. 


One indicator of the softenin in | 


drug store H&BA sales is the “What’s 
Hot In Drug Stores” chart based on 
the 66 Nielsen index categories. 

Two years ago, there were 25 
H&BA categories in the What’s Hot 
chart with sales growth in drug stores 
of 10 percent or better. Last year, 
there were only 10 showing strong 
growth. This year, there are only five, 
and only one generating dollars sales 
increases in excess of 15 percent: ex- 
ternal analgesics. 

But it would be misleading to think 
that this category only showed such 
strong growth vag Bon stores. This has 
been a year for external analge- 
sics in all mass outlets. 

Food stores generated a dollar sales 
increase almost as strong as the in- 
crease in drug stores, and mass mer- 
chandisers had an increase that was 12 
percentage points higher than drug 
stores for analgesics. 

Mass merchandisers and food stores 
also have more H&BA categories 
showing strong wth than drug 
stores do. Out of the 23 remedial cate- 
gories tracked by Nielsen, there were 
nine that, in mass merchandise stores, 
had dollar sales increases of 15 percent 
or better, and 16 with increases of 10 
percent or better. 

There were two remedial categories 
that had increases of 15 percent or bet- 
ter in food stores, and six with in- 
creases of wih gage or better.

Out of the 23 remedial categories

had a dollar sales share of 00 percent or 
better in nine segments. Their share of 
sales in the past two years had eroded 
on 19 of the 23 segments. 

The share shifts and the loss of “hot 
growth” categories clearly identify a 
continuing erosion of sales in catego- 
ries that have traditionally belonged to 
the drug store industry. So far, drug 
stores have depended on their conve- 
nient locations to offset the price ad- 
vantage that mass merchandisers 
hold, but that strategy, by itself, can- 
not contain erosion. 

Drug stores need to find ways to 
give their customers added values, and 
the solution may be in providing more 
and better custoiner service, a greater 
variety of product assortment, a bet- 
ter price/value relationship, or findin 
new departments like video, fast food, 
or convenience groceries to help gen- 
erate needed traffic.

almost as much space as drug chains. 

In 1990, mass merchandisers devot- 
ed an average of 2,050 linear feet per 
store to H&BAs, compared to the 
2,398 linear feet that drug chains gave 
the category. 

The mass merchandisers also have 
made a much stronger space commit- 
ment to toiletries than they did to re- 
medial products. 

Out of the 12 beauty aid segments 
Nielsen surveyed, mass merchandis- 
ers gave eight of them more space than 
drug chains did. In only three seg- 
ments — men’s toiletries, face creams 
and lotions and hair coloring — did 
drug chains have more space allocated 
than the mass merchandisers. 

In the remedial department, howev- 
er, drug chains gave more shelf space 
to 11 out of the 12 segments tracked. 
The only segment given more space by 
mass merchandise chains was contact 
lens solutions. 

Drug chains, which gave this catego- 
ry 31 linear feet on average, only gen- 
erated average sales of $53 per store 
per month. 

This year, ~~ chains do not seem to 
be getting the dollar sales increases the 
need to justify space expansion. Al- 
though drug chains gave face creams 
and lotions another 7.8 linear feet in 
1990, average sales per linear foot/per 
store/per month declined $4, to $47. 

Linear foot sales were either flat or 
down for 10 of the 12 toiletry catego- 
ries measured by Nielsen. 

Large independents and food 
chains, which i increased space for 
most toiletries, felt the same effect. 


Merchandising 
characteristics 


Drug chains spend a lot of money 
trying to persuade customers that, like 
traditional neighborhood drug stores, 
they care about their customers and 
will go out of their way to provide per- 
sonalized and courteous service. 

_In terms of some shopping conve- 
nience, vag 4 are actually more accom- 
modating than independents. For ex- 
ample, 96 percent of all chain dru 
stores are open on Sundays, compare 
to Just 54 percent of all independents. 
And 8 percent are open 24 hours a day, 
seven days a week compared to less 
than 1 percent of all independents who 
offer those hours. 

About 90 percent of both drug chains 
and independents are willing to take 
credit card purchases, and nine in 10 of 
both chains and independents still take 
the time to price every item in their 
stores. More drug chains than indepen- 
dents, however, give shoppers price 
comparisons so consumers can get a bet- 


ter sense of how they may be saving 
money by shopping these stores. 

However, chains are nowhere close 
to rivaling independents when it comes 
to home deliveries. Seventy-seven 
percent of all independents provide 
that service and only 21 percent charge 
for it. Just 6 percent of all chains do 
home deliveries and 3 percent charge 
for it. 

More drug chains than independents 
also offer special departments. For ex- 
ample, 93 percent of chains have a film 
developing department, compared to 
74 percent of all high-volume indepen- 
dents. Seventy percent of all chains 
stores are also in‘high traffic shopping 
center locations, corapared to just 34 
—" of all high-volume indepen- 

ents. 


scanning 


Chain drug stores are also far ahead 
of high-volume independents in scan- 
ning installations. By the end of this 
year, Nielsen estimates that 25 per- 
cent of all chain drug stores and 21 per- 
cent of all deep discount chain drug 
stores will have scanners at the front 
end, making it even easier for custom- 
ers to get in and out fast. In contrast, 
by year’s end, Nielsen is estimating 
that just 4 percent of all large indepen- 
dents will have scanners. 

By the end of 1998, Nielsen is pro- 
jecting that 63 percent of all chain drug 
stores and 55 percent of all deep dis- 
count chain drug stores will have scan- 
ners, compared to just 20 percent of all 
aa independents. 

t the end of this year, chain drug 
stores will have narrowed the gap be- 
tween themselves and food and mass 
merchandise stores, which are much 
re heavily into scanning at the front 
end. 


Display strategies 


Mass merchandise chains give 
H&BAs more displays per stores than 
drug chains do, but as you’d expect, 
the department’s share of display 
space relative to other categories is 
much higher in drug stores than it is, or 
ever could be, in mass merchandise 
stores. 

Drug chains and high-volume inde- 
pendents give one third of their off- 
shelf display space to H&BAs, making 
it the most visibly merchandised de- 
partment in their stores. Chain dru 
stores have an average of eight H&B 
displays per store, while high-volume 
independents have an average of 
three. 

Chain drug stores and high volume 
independents also give general mer- 
chandise products a high proportion of

Retail pharmacy 
is a whole new 
ballgame 


By James Frederick 

ess than a generation ago, a pharmacy school gradu- 

g ate had a pretty simple choice about where to launch 

his or her professional career. Practice settings were 

easy to distinguish: drug stores — both chain and indepen- 

dent — as well as hospitals, professional pharmacies or 
mail-order houses. 

Supermarket chains with in-store pharmacies were op- 

tions for a brave few. Often, that meant staffing a low-key 

operation that snagged 


: . | a few prescription cus- 
Inside Pharmacy tomers from the gro- 


cery aisles. 
Oh, how times have 
LY SPECIAL LY changed. 
For their part, most 
‘7 REPORT <7 shoppers 15 or 20 years 
ago refused to consider 
a supermarket or a dis- 
count store for something as specialized and professional as 
pharmacy services. Independent drug store operators fret- 
ted about the growing power of the drug chains, but neither 
side focused too much on the massive societal shifts and com- 
petitive forces that were building inexorably outside their 
own industry. They felt, as did most consumers at the time, 
that supermarkets and other upstarts in retail pharmacy 
could never duplicate the professionalism and level of 
trust that accrued to drug stores. It was, most industry 
experts said, an inviolable franchise. 

Fast-forward to 1990, and the whole landscape has 
shifted. Entire new trade classes have emerged as power- 
ful retail forces — witness deep discount drug stores and

Brand loyalty doesn’t 
mean store loyalty: study 


By Harold Cohen, R.Ph. 

onsumers continue to shop traditional drug stores for most 
of their over-the-counter product needs, but the growing 
attention being given to those products by nontraditional 
outlets is giving drug stores a run for consumers’ money. 

According to Drug Store News’ Second Annual Consumer Brand 
Preference Study, conducted by Leo J. Shapiro and Associates, 
shoppers are very brand loyal when it comes to OTC products (82 to 
99 percent prefer a brand, depending on category). But that loyalty 
doesn’t extend to where they purchase those brands. The product 
categories studied were: cough and cold, eye and lens care, analge- 
sics, dental and laxatives.

Food units give oral care squeeze 


ood stores continue to put the squeeze on drug stores in the 
toothpaste and mouthwash peg tala according to Drug 
Store News’s latest Consumer Brands Preference Study. 
Forty-four percent of consumers buy their toothaste and 35 per- 
cent their mouthwash products from food stores, the study found. 

That compares to drug stores’ 25-percent share of consumer 
purchases in toothpaste and 27 percent in mouthwashes. Drug 
stores, in fact, have about the same share as discount department 
stores when it comes to purchases in these two dental categories. 

The reason for this disparity between food stores and drug 
stores is, of course, the one-stop shopping convenience offered by 
ne peli: Toothpastes and rinses are products automatically 

ded to weekly shopping lists. Consumers perceive them as com- 
modities for the home cabinet, like flour, sugar or milk. 

Although consumers have strong brand preferences in this cate- 
gory, they are not brand loyal when it comes to toothpaste. They 

uy to fill the need. Should the retailer not have their preferred 
brand, most will switch. 

Seventy-seven percent said they would buy an alternative if 
their preferred brand was out of stock, and this often means that 
the switch brand becomes their first choice at the time of their next 
purchase. Nor are they particularly brand-loyal towards mouth- 
washes. Seventy-three percent said they would switch if their fa- 
vorite brand were not available. 

In addition, ey ee and mouthwashes are among the most 
price-sensitive of all H&BA categories. Thirty-nine percent of 
consumers said they made their fast purchase of toothpaste on 
sale, and 40 ogy said their purchase of mouthwash was on sale. 
Among all the 28 categories tracked in Shapiro’s consumer re- 
search, only batteries, shaving cream, deodorants, pantyhouse, 
deodorants and several hair care categories scored higher in the 
price-sensitivity area — and then ay much. 

Crest (42.7 percent) and Colgate (25.5 percent) completely dom- 
inate the market in consumer preference, while other Ste such 
as Aqua Fresh, Aim and Close-Up, reported in with single-digit 
percentage preferences. Among mouthwash preferences, Scope 
(26 percent) and Listerine (25 percent) were virtually even. Plax, 
the brand that helped establish the anti-plaque subcategory 
among mouthwashes, was third with 7 percent. 

Rinses, enjoying little growth the past few years, has steady 
sales due to its standing customer base. Its use is more of a person- 
al decision, rather than a necessity, like toothpaste. The market is 
sensitive to advertising, and manufacturers will go to great 
lengths to help consumers identify their product in the stores.

DRUG ST@RE NEWS 


ENTONVILLE, Ark. 
Which competitor are you most 
concerned about these days? If 
you said Wal-Mart, you're not alone. 
The $26 billion retail juggernaut out 
of America’s heartland is still sending 
tremors into dozens of new markets, 


from Texas and Florida in the south to 
Wisconsin and New York in the north, 
and coast-to-coast from Maine to Cali- 
fornia. No retailer that deals in food, 
drug or general merchandise — includ- 
ing the nation’s drug stores — is im- 
mune from the competition. 


Wal-Mart’s 1,075 pharmacies will generate more than $1 billion in prescription sales this year.

December 10, 199C 


Wal-Mart brings its strengths to bear on pharmacy 


: R greed — harmacies have already 
elt the heat. It may surprise some to 
know that Wal-Mart a ceaety pie of 
the nation’s biggest retailers of 
scription drugs. Its 1,075 in-store p ob 
macies will generate well in excess of $1 
billion in  sbigsiok. de sales this year, 
business that once went to drug stores 
and other pharmacy competitors. 

Wal-Mart has scored big gains in 
prescription sales by applying the 
same winning formula to pharmacy 
that it has applied to its other business- 
es. That strategy — combining aggres- 
sive buying and dealmaking with low 
everyday prices and high levels of cus- 
tomer service and satisfaction, in 
huge, well-stocked mass merchandise 
emporiums — has made Wal-Mart the 
nation’s most respected retailer in the 
past decade. Wal-Mart will soon out- 
strip its two chief rivals, Kmart and 
Sears, as the undisputed leader in U.S. 
general merchandise retailing. 

Since Wal-Mart does nothing in a 
small way, it is safe to say it has similar 
ambitions for the pharmacy and food 
business. The chain recently bought out 
a major food wholesaler, McLane Co., 
and has already begun testing large- 
scale grocery ecuan in its huge stores. 
Its penetration of the pharmacy busi- 
ness is older and better-established. 

What’s more, Wal-Mart is pushing to 
add pharmacies to most of the rest of its 
1,470 Wal-Mart stores, and has begun 


ning them in its 135 Sam’s Wholesale 

Claes “We're adding pharmacies 
where our lease allows it,” said Clarence 
Archer, vp-pharmacy operations. 

What gives Wal-Mart such impact is 
its enormous distribution muscle, 
which allows it to purchase merchan- 
dise — including pharmaceuticals — at 
the best possible price and pass much 
of the savings on to consumers. Adding 
to the chain’s impact is its blitzkreig- 
like growth rate; it is opening large- 
scale, one-stop megastores at the clip 
of about 200 stores a year. These units 
are being added to a nationwide retail 
ey with unprecedented mar- 

et reach and the most efficient, cost- 
effective method of delivering product 
to the marketplace in the business.

ket, and you see they’re doing a lot of 
things right.” 

Wal-Mart’s pharinacy business de- 
rives its strength from the chain’s well- 
known everyday low-price policy and its 
reputation for customer service, said 
Archer. The chain’s rapid growth and 
solid reputation are also helping attract 
career-oriented pharmacists, he said.

Walgreens wins Med-Glaser assets 


Plans to run four stores; will fold scripts, inventory into existing base 


PHOENIX — Walgreen Co. was 
awarded the assets of Medicare- 
Glaser in U.S. Bankruptcy Court 
here after winning an auction bid 
that included a plan to operate only 
four stores. 

With an offer of $12.2 million, or 
110 percent of inventory value, plus 
$50,000 to clear store leases, Wal- 
greens out-muscled bidders that in- 
cluded the St. Louis-based 
Schnuck’s Supermarkets. 

Walgreens gains all the assets of 
73 stores, including prescription 
files. A Medicare-Glaser source es- 
timated the chain’s script volume at 
12,000 to 13,000 a month. NuCrown 
Optical of St. Louis bought the in- 
ventory of five optical stores. 


The buy will greatly increase Wal- 
greens’ St. Louis market share, provid- 
ing it can hold Medicare’s customer base.

Kmart inks Price Savers takeover 


TROY, Mich. — Adding to its strength in the warehouse club 
arena, K mart Corp. agreed to purchase Price Savers Whole- 
sale Inc., a 17-store chain based in Salt Lake City. Terms 
weren't disclosed. 

Price Savers is a membership-based operation that reported- 
ly will generate $850 million in revenues in its current fiscal 
year. K mart described it as a profitable retailer that would en- 
hance its strength in the warehouse club business. 

In 1989, K mart purchased Pace Membership Warehouse for 
$322 million and merged its fledgling Makro division into Pace. 
The Price Savers acquisition extends K mart’s wholesale club 
operations into new markets in the West. 

The latest takeover extends the consolidation of the member- 
ship warehouse club industry. In November, Wal-Mart Stores 
bought out Wholesale Club of Indianapolis.

Nov. BTS show previews new lines 


NEW YORK — In addition to the upcoming Back-To-School 
Show, Thalheim Expositions announced it will hold a second Back- 
To-School Show Nov. 12-14 at McCormick Place in Chicago. 

“The November show was established to accommodate those 
retailers and manufacturers who want an early preview of new 
lines,” said David Thalheim, president of Thalheim. The New 
York show will continue to be held in February. 

The new fall show in Chicago will have a similar structure to 
the New York show. Space at the November show will be allo- 
cated initially on a seniority basis to companies that exhibit in 
the New York show. Thalheim’s Henry Dicker has been named 
show manager for both exhibitions.

—-F WNACDS study says Pharm.D. 


may be tough pill to swallow 


By Harold Cohen, R.Ph. 

NEW YORK — A five-year 
bachelor of science program at 
an accredited pharmacy 
school is more than adequate 
education for a pharmacist in a 
community practice setting, 
according to a new study com- 
missioned by NACDS. 

The study, conducted by 
SRI International, also found 
that a mandatory six-year 
Pharm.D. degree for all phar- 
macy graduates would “se- 
verely exacerbate” the cur- 
rent pharmacist shortage. 

The mandatory Pharm.D. 
issue has been debated for 
years among academicians. 
Last year, it boiled over when 
the American Council on 
Pharmaceutical Education 
(ACPE) issued a “Declaration 
of Intent” suggesting future 
accreditation would be limited 


to schools offering Pharm.D 
programs only. 

“Given the [findings of the 
SRI study], NACDS agrees 
with SRI’s recommendation 
that those who are now urging 
only a six-year Pharm.D. de- 
gree for community pharma- 
cists should re-evaluate their 
position,” said Ron Ziegler, 
president of the chain drug as- 
sociation. 


Appropriate for some 


“Of course,” Ziegler said, 
“not every pharmacist will go 
into community practice. 
Some will choose an institu- 
tional setting such as a hospi- 
tal or one of any number of 
pharmacy specialty areas. For 
some of them, education be- 
yond the five-year program 
may be appropriate.” 

The study also found that a 


patient’s quality of life can be 
improved and health care costs 
lowered if pharmacists take a 
more active role in patient con- 
sultation. But because pharma- 
cists spend most of their time 
re A phiryhny We the study 
pointed out that the use of tech- 
nicians is essential if pharma- 
cists are to provide adequate 
patient consultation. 

Before any decisions can be 
made concerning a pharma- 
cist’s degree of education, the 
SRI recommended that “lead- 
ers in the pharmacy profes- 
sion must decide on a defini- 
tion of the future roles of 
community pharmacists based 
on analyses and studies of 
needs for pharmacy-related 
health care, and a realistic ap- 
praisal of potentials for per- 
formance of such services in 
the U.S. health care system.” 


McKesson opening four DCs 


SAN FRANCISCO 
McKesson Corp. said it plans 
to open four new distribution 
centers over the next two 
years—three equipped with 
state-of-the-art materials- 
handling technology—at a to- 
tal cost of $65 million. 

The new DCs, totalling 
800,000 square feet, will be lo- 
cated in Camden, N.J.; Atlan- 
ta; St. Louis and Phoenix and 
will double capacities in each 
market. All four DCs will re- 
place older facilities, which 
the company said it will sell. 

“These were older, ineffi- 
cient warehouses that needed 
to be replaced with new DCs 
more than others,” explained 
a McKesson spokesman. 

McKesson plans to install 
automated order-picking 
equipment in the new Cam- 
den, Atlanta and St. Louis 
DCs. The high-speed equip- 
ment, which represents $10 
million of the $65 million out- 
lay, is more than four times 
faster than the semi-automat- 


ed systems the company is 
currently using. Other facili- 
ties will be converted to the 
new technology down the 
road, McKesson indicated. 

Automated order fulfillment 
will significantly improve pro- 
ductivity, said Joe Polastri, 
McKesson Drug president. 
“We will be able to react more 
quickly to our pharmacy and 
hospital customers’ needs and 
with an even higher degree of 
accuracy.” 

He added, “The addition of 
these four new centers and the 
automated order-picking sys- 
tems will make it possible for 
us to keep pace with our ex- 
panding business in these 
markets.” 


Early this year 


The first center to be com- 
pleted will be the $13 million, 
234,000-square-foot DC in 
O’Fallon, Mo., near St. Louis, 
scheduled to go on line early 
this year. It replaces an 86,000- 
square-foot DC in St. Louis.

Meyer wae te said several

and $525 million, or at least 
$21 a share. The wholesaler, 
with about $2.6 billion in annu-

the industry. A combination of 
Bergen and FoxMeyer would 
bring Bergen closer to McKes- 
son Corp., the nation’s leading 
drug wholesaler.

est in the company. The first 
was in 1985, but the merger 
was called off days before com- 
pletion when National Inter- 
group decided to acquire the 
company because of the dete- 
rioration of its steel business.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 7, 1991 


Drug Stores News gets a new look 


Question: What’s different about this issue of Drug 
Store News? 
If you answered, “It’s smaller,” you win the respect 
and admiration of our editorial staff and art director. 
Both were betting that you would not notice the 
downsizing of the publication’s depth to 14 inches from 
its previous 14% inches. Studies have shown that most 
readers are seldom aware of any but the most radical 
changes in a publication’s size and design. 
Perhaps you’re wonder- 


ing: Why did we do it? Or 
maybe: Am I getting less in- 
formation for my money? 
Since Drug Store News is the 
industry’s only publication 


IN THE MARKET with a fully paid readership, 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 
both reactions. 


In answer to the first ques- 
tion: We did it because read- 
ers told us to. In our regular readership studies, one 
consistent request has been for a smaller, handier 
publication. Readers say the newspaper should be 
able to slip easily into a briefcase. Our new size will al- 
low it to do just that. 

And, no, we have not sacrificed any information in 
downsizing our format. For the most part, we’ve giv- 
en up border space rather than text space. In a future 
issue we'll introduce a new airier and easier-to-read 
typeface that will actually provide you with more 
words per page. 

There are other changes in this issue (and in the 
works) designed to make our publication tighter, bet- 


OPINION

ter organized and easier to read. Please let us know 
what you think about the-changes. If you have any 
suggestions, let us know therirtoo.

A few years ago the representatives of the generic 
drug industry were the darlings of Washington. 

Whenever they came to town Congress would roll 
out the carpet and gush about how generic drugs 
helped hold down the nation’s health costs. 

It’s a different story today. The charges of drug ap- 
proval fraud that have been leveled against some ge- 
neric drug industry officials in recent months have 
soured Washington on generics. 

If anything, the generic drug industry is even less 
popular at the Food and Drug Administration’s head- 

quarters in Rockville, Md. In- 


directly, at least, the generic 
drug scandals already toppled 
one FDA commissioner and 
triggered convictions of sev- 
eral key agency officials 
charged with accepting gratu- 
ities from manufacturers, 
perjury, and other offenses. 

Ironically, one generic 
drug house that has never 
been particularly popular at FDA is Barr Laborato- 
ries — a major industry firm that remains untainted 
by the generic scandals. 

From the viewpoint of some FDA staffers, Barr’s 
“erimes” include belligerence against the bureaucra- 
cy. In addition to bad-mouthing the agency in testimo- 
ny on Capitol Hill, the Pamona, N.Y., generic manu- 
facturer contested FDA actions in the courts. 

Sensing a need to “rehabilitate” the firm’s image at 
the FDA, Barr came up with the idea of a public rela- 
tions/marketing campaign to offset the negative publici- 
ty surrounding the industry and to distinguish Barr 
from those companies involved in unlawful conduct. 

For help they turned to John Norris — former depu- 
ty FDA commissioner-turned-public relations swami 
— who promptly informed Barr that the company’s 
image problems were indeed severe. 

Company officials said Norris told them that FDA 
staffers view Barr “as a sleazy company which at- 
tempted to pass off poor science by using lawyers to

PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


A standup generic company takes a stand 


make agency submissions.” 

Moreover, Norris said that after discussing Barr 
with “several high-ranking managers” at the agency, 
he was told that the firm is “one of the three worst 
companies” that the FDA regulates. 

Worse yet, Norris suggested that FDA regulators 
have a habit of retaliating against “bad actor” companies 
by delaying their New Drug Approval applications. 

In a memo to officials at Barr, Norris revealed that 
“key individuals at the FDA have informed me that 
Barr’s relationships with the FDA have deteriorated 
substantially over the past several months. Although 
good relations do not guarantee approvals, bad rela- 
tions do guarantee delays.” 

“Acknowledging that “the FDA can be « tough agen- 
cy to get along with,” Norris went on to state that the 
F'DA “has threatened . . . the futures of selected drug 
companies,” especially “so-called ‘bad-actor’ compa-. 


The generic drug scandals have already top- 
pled one FDA commissioner and triggered 
convictions of several key agency officials 
charged with accepting gratuities from manu- 
facturers, perjury, and other offenses. 


nies” with “prior ‘bad records’ or ‘records of belliger- 
ence’ with FDA,” he said. 

What would it take to smooth over the rough spots 
and stop FDA drug approvers from delaying action on 
Barr’s NDAs? A long-term public relations campaign 
— managed by Norris — at a cost to Barr of $100,000 
per month for three years! 

As they explained it in testimony to Congress, Nor- 
ris’ clear implication was that “the FDA would contin- 
ue its discriminatory behavior unless Barr obtained 
the services of someone with ‘old boy’ connections.” 

To their credit, officials at Barr turned down Nor- 


ris’ $3.6 million public relations scheme.

who could?

specialty stores like Block- 
buster Raiartainwent ana

training costs were high. Mov- 


ie libraries tied up too many 
inventory dollars. The depart-

enough cross- 


merchandising 
sales, and they 
ate up too much

their presence. 

A handful of 
drug chains, like 
Wellby Super 
Drug Stores,

departments.

GENERAL MERCHANDISE 


— 


batteries 


high-voltage 


competition sparks 
battery market 


e it ever so humble, 
ioe! there’s no place like the 
battery display for fast 
turns, high-voltage competi- 
tion and frenzied promotion. 
Thanks to the continuing 
boom in the market for con- 
sumer electronics, the catego- 
ry will push past $3 billion at 
retail this year. Although unit 
sales have flattened some- 
what, and are now running 
ahead about three percentage 
points a year, the continuing 
move by consumers to higher- 
priced alkaline batteries is 
still pushing dollar gains 
ahead at about twice that rate. 
That’s no small potatoes for 
a product that one industry in- 
sider, quoted in a recent issue 
of The Wall Street Journal, 
called “probably the lowest- 
interest category in the 
world.” Indeed, the catego- 
ry’s excitement is generated 
as much by clever ad cam- 
paigns—like the Energizer 
“bunny”—as much as by prod- 
uct innovation or point-of-pur- 
chase display. 


Sparking sales 


Yet innovation continues. 
In terms of longer-life product 
development, packaging, re- 
tail support and marketing, 
battery manufacturers have 
done yeoman work over the 
past several years to spark 


sales and wrest market share 
away from their competitors. 

Consider Eveready. In ad- 
dition to its attention-getting 
ads, the company is leading a 
charge for environmentally 
friendlier products with low- 
mercury batteries, and is pro- 
moting the new, less toxic bat- 
tery at the point of sale. 

Beginning last summer, the 
company also made both its 
Energizer alkaline and Ever- 
eady Super Heavy Duty 
brands available in new print- 
ed shrink-wrap packaging to 
cut down on space require- 
ments. So-called Space Packs 
contain the same number of 
batteries as Eveready’s blis- 
ter packs, but take up one- 
third the space. Larger, 
multi-pack Family Packs are 
aimed at heavy-use custom- 
ers, who account for an esti- 
mated 73 percent of category 
volume. 


Multipacks a hit 


Larger-size multipacks 
were pioneered by Rayovac, 
the number three battery 
maker. Rayovac _ has 
achieved big sales gains in 
discount stores because of its 
commitment to multipacks, 
which are merchandised 
heavily by discounters be- 
cause they have the space to 
devote to full battery presen-
