tations. Both mass merchan- 
disers and Rayovac itself are 
aiming at the heavy battery 
user, which Rayovac profiles 
as 20 percent of Americar 
households consuming 96 
batteries a year. 

Calling itself the market 
leader in mass merchandise 
outlets, Rayovac is working 
to boost its distribution into 
drug chains and supermar- 
kets, where it has long been 
outgunned by Eveready and 
Duracell. Rayovac multi- 
packs have now found their 
way into Eckerd, Peoples, 
Thrift Drug, Big B, Perry, 
K&B, F&M and LaVer- 
diere’s, said company 
spokesman John Daggett. 
More, he said, will add the 
brand as they fight to regain 
share from the discounters 
and food stores. 

For its part, Duracell is 
capitalizing on its leadership 
in the alkaline segment of the 
battery market, which now 
accounts for roughly two- 
thirds of total sales and is the 


fastest-growing major seg- 
ment. Duracell claims it has a 
44 percent share of the alka- 
line segment, compared with 
37 percent for Eveready’s 
Energizer. In recent years, 
the company has focused ef- 
forts on boosting user life for 
its alkaline batteries and em- 
phasizing product freshness 
with date stamps. It also in- 
troduced peggable multi- 
packs in the latter 1980s. 

Duracell’s most recent inno- 
vation is its Copper Top Tes- 
ter, an in-pack bathers tester 
which came “‘in direct re- 
sponse to consumers’ ques- 
tions and concerns about bat- 
tery freshness,” according to 
Duracell U.S.A. president 
Charles Perrin. 

Duracell also jumped early 
into the growing market for 
lithium batteries, which offer 
long life, high energy se ok 
light weight and versatility. 
In the photo battery market, 
lithium sales have surpassed 
$50 million, according to the 
company. 


Chains face space 
squeeze in batteries 


attery manufacturers 

and most retailers 

agree: toa point, the 
more space available for the 
category in the store, the bet- 
ter sales respond. Batteries 
lend themselves well to cross- 
merchandising, up-front im- 
pulse-oriented display, ag- 
gressive POP promotional 
efforts and multiple locations. 

Suppliers and merchants 
also agree, however, that 
finding the space to present a 
full, well-rounded battery 
presentation and trigger im- 
pulse sales with secondary 
displays isn’t easy—particu- 
lary for smaller-format drug 
stores. 

“Space management is one 
of the biggest challenges fac- 
ing retailers in the ’90s,” said 
Gary Baker, Eveready’s vp- 


trade development. “The 
number of battery-operated 
devices is estimated to reach 
1.6 billion this year. The re- 
sulting space crunch often 
causes increased out-of-stocks 
and lost profits.” 

Added Rayovac spokesman 
John Daggett, “The sale of 
multipacks and the use of mul- 
tiple locations is the driving 
force behind battery sales 
growth in the mass merchan- 
disers.” Acknowledging that 
drug stores have lost battery 
mote. ar share to their competi- 
tors over the past half-de- 
cade—from 18 percent to 15 
percent, in Rayovac’s estl- 
mate—Daggett said drug 
stores are now fighting back. 

“The numbers are going to 
turn around for drug chains,”

Consumer demand sends

for greener pastures 


onsumers want more 
earth-friendly prod-

ers are getting the word. 
Heeding the environmental 
clarion call of the late ’80s and 
’90s, battery manufacturers 
are taking aim at both the con- 
tent and packaging of their 
vroducts. Chief on the hit list is 
mercury, a particularly deadly 
element that has long been a 
key chemical component of bat- 
teries because it helps regulate 
electrochemical activity. 
Several battery makers, in- 
cluding Eveready, Rayovac 
and the smaller Power Plus of 
America, have been touting 


lower mercury levels in recent 
years. Eveready announced 
last spring that it had achieved 
a 97 percent reduction in mer- 
cury content in its alkaline 
products, resulting in a 99.975 
percent mercury-free battery. 
The announcement capped a 
10-year effort to cut mercury 
content, according to the firm. 

Eveready also rolled out 
shrink-wrap packaging last 
year, reducing packaging ma- 
terial volume by 70 percent vs. 
blister packs. 

Rayovac was an early leader 
in cutting packaging content 
with its Smartpack multipacks.

LBO may leave Revco 
insolvent, says examiner 


NEW YORK — Reveo’s 1986 leveraged buyout probably left 
the company without enough capital to conduct its business and 
meet its obligations, and may have left it insolvent, according to 
a court-appointed examiner’s final report. 

Released Jan. 2, the 300-page report confirms preliminary 
findings made last summer. It paints a scathing portrait of an ill- 
conceived, highly leveraged buyout made at the height of the 
go-go years of the ’80s, when dealmaking and junk bond financ- 
ing were at fever pitch and caution was perhaps at its lowest 

oint. 
: In Reveo’s ease, the $1.4 billion paid to take the company pri- 
vate was largely a debt-financed deal that enriched stockhold- 
ers, former top managers, investment bankers and dealmakers, 
See Revco page 21

Over 400 to attend NACDS show 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — More than 400 chain and supplier ex- 
ecutives and 60 exhibitors will attend the National Association 
of Chain Drug Stores’ second annual conference on distribution/ 
logistics. It will be held in Grenelefe, Fla. Feb. 24 to 26. __ 

e business program is headed by Jack Futterman, chair- 
man, president and ceo, Supermarkets General. Vern Brunner, 
executive vp, Walgreens, and Mal Jozeff, Group vp, Procter & 
Gamble, will speak on retailer/supplier alliances. 

Logistics experts attending include Jim Morehouse, A.T. 
Kearney and Dr. Doug Lambert of the University of Florida. 

Subjects focused on will include Electronic Data Interchange, 
Quick Response, and the use oi telecommunications. =

Drug Emporium 3rd-qtr. net sales up 


COLUMBUS, Ohio — Drug Emporium reported that third 
quarter net sales were up 27 percent to $153.3 million, with 
nine-month sales up 25 percent to $442 million. The third quar- 
ter sales growth includes $6 million sales from three franchises 
Drug Emporium purchased in the quarter ending Nov. 30. 

Net earnings were $1.399 million compared with $1.4 million 
in last year’s third quarter, with earnings per share of 11 cents 
in both quarters. This quarter’s earnings absorbed a $700,000 
LIFO charge. 

Nine-month net income was $5.4 million, or 41 cents per 
share, versus $5.5 million, or 42 cents a share, last year. 

“Given the tough retailing environment and a full year of dou- 
ble-digit growth in same-store sales, there is no question that 
our more aggressive pricing strategy continues to achieve our 
objectives,” said Gary Wilber, ceo. 


Walgreens names dc managers 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Walgreens has named Donald Boyajian 
as manager of its newest distribution center opening this June in 
the Lehigh Valley, near Allentown, Pa. It will serve about 100 
drug stores in New ais New York, and four New England 
states. —% Sem joined Walgreens in 1979 as an assistant store 
manager. He was promoted to his most recent position, Orlando 
distribution center manager, in 1989. 

Also, Gary Ellingson was promoted as de manager at Orlan- 
do. He will be responsible in that post for merchandise shipped 
to Florida and Puerto Rico. 

Ellingson, who joined Walgreens in 1982, was most recently 
manager of operations at the Orlando facility. 


McKesson designing Wellness Centers 


SAN FRANCISCO — McKesson Drug Co. is designing Well- 
ness Centers for its customers who want to dispense informa- 
tion and health care products to their customers. Products and 
services may include blood pressure testing, cholesterol screen- 
ing, health care video rental and sales, home diagnostics, and a 
selection of health care brochures. 

The center can also include a Pharmacy Information Center, a 
touch screen kiosk that gives information on over 5,000 drugs 
and on diseases and other health topics. 

Said Fred Toney, McKesson’s senior vp, sales and merchan- 
dising: “Wellness is a key concept for the ’90s and beyond. Hav- 
ing Wellness Centers in pharmacies will help establish the phar- 
macist—already considered the most trusted professional 
according to a recent Gallup poll—as the local wellness re- 
source,” Toney said.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 21, 1991 


Collectively the Drug Store News editorial staff 
could celebrate a golden anniversary this year. Our 11 
staff editors have accumulated 50 years of experience 
writing about the industry. 

The turn of the year is the time to ponder stats like 
that. Here are a few more: Seven of our 11 staff editors 
have been with Drug Store News for at least five 
years. The longest: 10 years; the least: two days (our 

new desk editor, Carol Kear- 


ney, joined us Jan. 7.) Mean 

length service is five years, 

average just under that. 
These figures do not even 


IN THE MARKET) iclude Ken Rankin, who has 
been covering the Washing- 
BRUCE BUCKLEY ton scene for Drug Store 


- News and its predecessor, 


: Chain Store Age Drug Edi- 
tion, for 18 years. 

We’ve got two other news bureaus, one in Cleve- 
land and the other in Dallas. That’s in line with our pol- 
icy of putting our editors close to where the retail ac- 
tion is. 

From Cleveland our veteran senior editor Jim 
Frederick roams widely throughout the Midwest and 
into the Pacific Northwest. Jim probably amassed 
more frequent flyer points than any other member of 
the staff this year 

In Dallas we have Elizabeth Richardson. A native 
Texan, Elizabeth joined the staff just under two years 
ago as assistant pharmacy editor after a stint with the 
Texas Pharmaceutical Association. When a spot 
opened up in our Dallas office, Elizabeth jumped at the 
chance to return to the land of Longhorns and Aggies. 

Our editorial staff divides its efforts between Drug 
Store News and our new pharmacy magazine, Drug 
Store News for the Pharmacist, an offshoot of the tab- 
loid-sized Drug Store News/Inside Pharmacy. 
Around here the new magazine is referred to as FTP 


Veteran staff is close to the action 


OPINION 


(For the Pharmacist). It’s edited by Harold Cohen, 
who spent 15 years as a retail pharmacist before join- 
ing us seven years ago. Harold’s punchy, personal col- 
umn, Cohen’s Capsules, is probably the most avidly 
read piece of writing in Drug Store News. 

The Drug Store News group is involved in other en- 
terprises as well. Publishing for the first time this 
month is Supermarket HQ Quarterly. It’s aimed at 
non-foods executives in food chains and is edited by Al 
Heller, our executive editor. As exec editor, Al has 
been doing the daily assignments and primary editing 
for Drug Store News for almost five years: a difficult 
and important job. 

Another publication produced by our group (and 
shared with our sister publication Discount Store 
News) is FM (Food Merchandising for Non-Foods 
Retailers). It’s aimed at drug and discount store food 
merchants and is edited by Liz Parks, who has been 
with Drug Store News for almost eight years. Liz, of 
course, is the prolific editor/writer who covers the 
beauty scene in these pages. 

We’ve got two other talented senior editors in the 
New York office, both with five years experience cov- 
ering the industry. Dave Vaczek handles the technol- 
ogy beat and is one of our most tireless reporters. Last 
year he won Lebhar-Friedman’s top writing award, 
the Godfrey Lebhar plate. Susan Ball covers advertis- 
ing and promotions and has done some first-rate re- 
porting for both Drug Store News and Drug Store 
News for the Pharmacist (read her article on pharma- 
cists counseling to the elderly in the current issue). 

This column wouldn’t be complete without mention- 
ing our copy desk editors, who work long, stressful 
hours catching our dumb errors and making the publica- 
tions look good. A special thanks to Bernadette Casey, 
our senior desk editor whose laughter neutralizes our 
agita; Fred (“Freditor”) Rueckher, our newly-promoted 
assistant desk editor; and the above-mentioned Carol 
Kearney, who is still new enough to love all of this. 


Sometimes there’s no place but home 


Eighteen years after college, where I took my last 
official Communication Arts class, I have taken a re- 
fresher course. In real life. 

I didn’t exactiy choose to. 


After a car hit me and broke 
my leg last month, my usual 
100-minute commute became 
impossible. In order to keep 
working, I’ve grown keenly 
attached to on-line computers 
and modems, FAX machines 
and the call-waiting feature 
on my home telephone. 

Communication Arts holds 
new meaning for me. What I took for granted in the of- 
fice has become my work lifeline for the time being — 
not too unlike retailers, at headquarters and stores, who 
rely increasingly on new forms of communication in 
their day-to-day operations. 

EDI; daily polling of stores and warehouses by 
headquarters meinframes; third-party claims pro- 
cessing; electromc planogramming; voice mail; credit 
card authorizations; even long-distance talks with 
suppliers, managers and staffs — all are crucial links 
to effective retail management. 

Some readers don’t have to think back too far to 
know how poor communications disrupts business. On 
the day I wrote this column, Jan. 4, AT&T construc- 
tion workers accidentally severed a fiber optic cable in 
Newark, N.J. Sixty percent of long-distance phone 
and computer calls in and out of New York City that 
day didn’t work. 

Operations at airports, commodities exchanges, 
banks — and retailers — suffered. 

The snafu couldn’t affect face-to-face communication, 
however — that special art of making people feel impor- 


THE HUMAN 
SIDE 
AL HELLER 


tant, truly understanding what they want and meeting 
their needs. I know a few people whom readers might 
recognize who deserve mention for their personal skills: 
® George Jeffers, former Skaggs president who owns 
Price Less deep discounters in Sacramento. He 
cruises store aisles with an uncanny sense of when to 
approach customers. When he told an elderly shopper 
he would special-order a denture adhesive for her, the 
look of appreciation she gave him said it all. 

@ Sam Walton, Wal-Mart chairman, who exhorts his 
retail hourlies to “meet people half-way and treat 
them the way they want to be treated themselves.” 
Grand openings and annual meetings often have the 
unrestrained tenor of revival meetings, with Walton 
whoopin’ it up and building staff pride along the way 
through personal attention. 

@ Fred Canning, Walgreen board member and former 
president, who after meeting me for a moment on a 
Deerfield headquarters staircase, called me by name 
in a meeting the next day. Three months later, at 
NACDS Annual, we chatted warmly for a half-hour 
about this newspaper and his chain. 

e Chris Visocan, a former clerk at Revco in Solon, 
Ohio, who deftly handled front-end transactions on 
her new scanner while she urged a motorcyclist-cus- 
tomer to be careful, charmed merchandise from a 
four-year-old who wouldn’t listen to her mom, and dis- 
cussed cactus with a woman buying potting soil. 

Communications, high-tech or up-front and person- 
al, is an art. Take this picture, for instance. 

Some people like me better with my broken leg be- 
cause I’m easier to reach: I’m a stationary target and I 
answer my own phone. I say to them and their like- 
minded colleagues that I’ll have the last laugh. By the 
time you read this, I expect to be back at my usual fre- 
netic pace. You missed your chance.

Strong R & D efforts focal point of the ’90s 


By Harold Cohen R.Ph. 
EW YORK — Despite 
an FDA scandal that 
sent shock waves 

throughout the pharmacetu- 
cial manufacturing communi- 
ty and slowed drug approvals 
to acrawl, branded and gener- 
ic pharmaceutical manufac- 
turers continue to pump large 
sums of money into research 
and development. 

While federal officials weed 
out the last of the corrupt par- 
ticipants in the industry-wide 
drug approval scandal, the 
FDA has reorganized, naming 
Dr. David Kessler as commis- 
sioner. Hopefully, the neces- 
sary process of moving the hun- 
dreds of new and abbreviated 
new drug approvals through a 
very clogged pipeline will begin 
to pick up steam. 


Good news 


That would be good news 
for the scores of generievand 
branded pharmaceutical 
companies that have invest- 
ed millions into developing 
and bringing new drugs to 
market. According the Paar- 
maceutical Manufacturers 
Association (PMA), branded 
pharmaceutical manufactur- 
ers (also referred as PMA 
companies), spent some $8.2 
billion in 1990 for worldwide 
research and development of 
human and veterinary drugs. 

New product introductions 
from this sector of the indus- 
try is edvoioon'y vital be- 
cause of expected losses from 
drugs going off patent over 
the next five years. 

According to David Saks, 
an analyst with Wedbush 
Morgan Securities, the mar- 
ket for “brand name generics 
and peep mie source prod- 
ucts could double to $16 billion 
in sales.” Saks credits much of 
that gain to “$10.7 billion 
worth of brand name prescrip- 
tion drugs losing patent pro- 
tection between 1990 and 
1995.” (See chart) 

The best selling drugs fall 
into three therapeutic catego- 
ries; cardiovascular, central

Cardiovascular research 


According to a 1989 PMA

Alzheimer’s disease 


Drugs in development for 
Alzheimer’s disease are not 
expected to cure this deterio- 
rating condition, but ease its 
symptoms. Approximately 
four million Americans suffer

Diabetes

AIDS

account for up to 90 percent

_ According to PMA, 15 med- 
icines under investigation to 
treat AIDS fall into the cate- 
ory of biotechnology drugs. 
his category is comprised of 
several drug subcategories. 


Generics 


Generic drug approvals, 
which have virtually come to a 
standstill because of the re- 
cent FDA probe, will pick up 
and continue to grow steadily 
as patent protection on the top 
100 drugs expire over the next 
decade.

Morgan Securities analyst Da- 
vid Saks, in 1990 alone, gener-

mately 20 percent of the $40 
billion in prescription drug 
sales. His forcast is for the ge- 
neric market to double as a 
“colossal a, of generic 


ANDAs” finally get ap- 
proved.

Every phar- 
macist, at one 
| ee. time or another, 

is faced with a 

customer who 
has become addicted to medica- 
tion. This case helps to answer 
whether or not the pharmacist/ 
pharmacy andlor the drug’s 
manufacturer can be held lia- 
ble for one’s addiction. 


New York — This case 
concerns a customer addicted 
to Talwin, which she had been 
taking since 1968 for migraine 
headaches. In 1973, the patient 
told the doctor she was taking a 
trip and he prescribed Talwin 
injectable, syringes and Dram- 


— 


amine. The drug and syringes 
were purchased from a drug 
store over several years, de- 
spite their alleged nonrefillable 
status (according to testimony, 
the physician stopped treating 
the patient in 1975). By 1980, 
she was injecting Talwin every 
hour. Eventually she admitted 
to a hospital. Even as an outpa- 
tient during this period, she 
was able to refill Talwin at her 
drug store without authoriza- 
tion from the doctor. As a result 
of repeated injections, she suf- 
fered permanent damage to her 
leg and thigh. She sued. 

The jury awarded the plain- 
tiff $650,000. Liabilities were 
apportioned as follows: 65 per- 


You be the judge 


cent to the pharmacy, 18 per- 
cent to the plaintiff and 17 per- 
cent to the manufacturer. The 
manufacturer argued that, 
based on evidence of wrongdo- 
ing by the pharmacy and plain- 
tiff herself, it should not be held 
responsible. Were the liabil- 
ities apportioned fairly? 


RESULTS — During ap- 
peal, the court said it was obvi- 
ous that the pharmacy illegall 
and improperly refilled the Tal. 
win and syringe prescriptions 
as well as maintaining improp- 
er records. The court ruled 
there was enough evidence pre- 
sented that the plaintiff’s ac- 
tions also contributed negli- 


gence (for example, she 
admitted that she simulta- 
neously refilled two separate 
prescriptions for Talwin at two 
different pharmacies without 
telling either of the pharma- 
cists). Based on all the evidence 
presented to the lower court, 
the appellate court ruled that 
the trial court erred in its judg- 
ment. The matter was remand- 
ed for a new trial.

Duane Reade eyes record expansion 


Duane Reade, the New York City dis- 
count drug store chain with the highest 
sales per square foot in the industry, is 
Shins for its strongest expansion year 
ever. 

A source says the 33-unit chain hopes to 
open at least 10 stores this year and has 
four more set to open this spring. 

One store will be in Newark, N.J. and it 
will be the first Duane Reade to open out- 
side of New York. Another will be a sec- 
ond Bronx store on Fordham Rd. while 
the remaining new openings will be in 
metro-New York, Duane Reade’s core 
market. One of these stores will be down- 
town in the Wall Street area and the other 
rn be in mid-town at 57th St. and 5th 

ve.

Giant Food borrowed a page from the deep discounters last year by 
de-emphasizing its powerful cosmetics department and installing 
this Super Deals aisle in its place. A smart decision: In this 65,000- 
square-foot store in Bailey’s Crossroads, Va., weekly sales for the 
aisle soared from $7,000 to $18,000. The chain reportedly plans to 
add another Super Deals aisle featuring frozen food specials. Giant 
began the exper‘ment in this prime, center-store location with hot 
HBA items, then added food across the aisle. Tables in between fea- 
ture a mix of sizziers with the emphasis on paper and detergents. 


Snyder’s new service center 


_ Says loud ‘yes’ to shoppers 


By Susan Ball 

MINNEAPOLIS — Sny- 
der Drug’s new prototype 
store, which opened Jan. 13 in 
suburban Eden Prairie, says 
“yes” to service loud and clear 
through a variety of new fea- 
tures. 

Here are some highlights: 
e@ “Yes Express” — Snyder’s 
new service and merchandise 
center up front offers custom- 
ers: abe: vi and shipping; 
faxing; customized printing of 
wedding and other social invi- 
tations, business stationery 
and the like; photocopying; no- 
tary public; Western Talon 
money transfers; money or- 
ders; photofinishing; key mak- 
ing; postage s s; discount 
movie tickets; and gift wrap- 
ping. 

Separate staff 


Really a store within a 
store, Yes Express has a sepa- 
rate staff and a wide selection 
of distinctively Minnesota gift 
ideas — like wild rice, maple 
syrup, artwork by local artists 
and gift baskets for businesses 
and individuals. It is posi- 
tioned next to the manager’s 
office for easier control and ac- 
cess and occupies 700 of the 
store’s 8,000 square feet. 

“Our goal is to answer cus- 
tomers’ requests with a ‘yes’ 
every time,” said vp of retail 
operations Mike Pan. Ifa local 
business owner, for example, 
wants to send a gift to a client 
in California, Snyder not only 
can say “Yes, we have some 
really distinctive gifts you can 
purchase,” but can also gift- 
wrap, package for mailing, in- 
sure and ship the gift directly 
from the store. 

The centers, which will be 
rolled to more stores, will help 
Snyder set itself apart from its 
non-locally run competitors as 
a Minnesota company and a 
source of Minnesota merchan- 
dise, said Don Beeler, Sny- 
der’s chairman, president and 
ceo. He also foresees using in- 
formation gathered through 
the stores’ new POS and phar- 
macy computer systems for 
direct-marketing of Minneso- 
ta-themed gift packages and 
other merchandise.

GENERAL MERCHANDISE 


Drug store, combo and dis- 
count merchandisers are bull- 
ish about their stationery/ 
school/home office depart- 
ments. 

In a Drug Store News sur- 
vey, more than 90 percent of 
stationery category respon- 
dents said they expect cate- 
gory sales to increase be- 
tween 5 percent and 10 
percent over the comin 
year, and about one-thir 
said they plan to increase 
space for stationery/school/ 
home office products from 5 
percent to 20 percent within 
the next 12 months. No one 
said they expect category 
sales to be flat or to decrease. 


Leading chains responded 
The survey represents re- 


sponses from leading chains 
with approximately 4,000- 
5,000 stores across the coun- 
try. 

It may come as no surprise 
that more than half of the re- 
spondents see home office 
supplies as the fastest-grow- 
ing segment in the category, 
but the segment that got the 
next-highest vote—recycled/ 
reduced package products— 
may cause some buyers to sit 
up and take notice. Children’s 
art/activities was the third 
most cited segment for fast 
growth, tied with year-round 
stationery. 


Leading trends

asked to rank the strongest 
trends in the category, color

got the most first-place votes, 
with “willingness to trade up” 
second, multi-packs/buik 
packages third and price con 
sciousness fourth. Licensing, 
“sreen” products and organi- 
zational aids were generally 
ranked lower.

peak periods.

and Father’s Day and Christ-

opportunities by some.

SMG sweetens its offer 
in stock, bond buyback 


WOODBRIDGE, N.J. — 
rmarkets General’s new 
holding co increased the 
price it is offering for bonds and 
referred stock in a tender of- 
er whose deadline has been ex- 
tended for the fifth time. 
SMG-II, the holding compa- 
ny, increased the cash offer for 
13 1/8 subordinated deben- 
tures from 27 percent of their 
principal amount to 33 per- 
cent. The company also upped 
the offer for preferred shares 
to $7 per share from $5 per 
share, as it extended the dead- 
line for a response to Feb. 4. 


Part of restructure 


The offer is part of a fiscal 
restructure aimed at reducing 
interest and dividend costs 
and yeti, SMG-IT’s bal- 
ance sheet. The operator of 
Pathmark Drug stores was 
forced into a $1.8 billion LBO 
three years ago. 

The deal will “almost elimi- 
nate” a deficit in equity in rela- 
tion to long term debt. As of 
Nov. 3, that debt was $1.67 bil- 
lion, with - at minus $170 
million, sai ey Gutman, 
vp of retail development. 

In raising the price, SMG-IT 
also amended the amount of 
bonds and shares it is seeking 
to buy. It is now tendering for 
$110 million in bonds, down 
from the initial $155.5 million, 
and for 3.4 million preferred 
shares, up from 1.7 million. 

The million price of the 
restructured offer will stay 
the same, said Gutman. That’s 
the amount a group of inves- 
tors has proposed to infuse 
into the holding company in 
return for new (nondividend- 
payl i) preferred stock. 

efore the amended offer, 
the company was short of re- 
ceiving the minimuin tender 
response required by the po- 
tential investors, who include 
affiliates of Merrill Lynch & 
Co. and the Equitable Life As- 
surance Society. 

As of Jan. 16, $28.6 million in 
bonds and 696,600 of the shares 
had been tendered. With the 
new offer the minimum is re- 
duced. Now at least $70 million 
in bonds and at least 1.65 mil- 
lion shares of preferred stock 
must be tendered. 

SMG-II has also negotiated 
new covenants with its banks 
after it had said it would fail to 
meet minimum performance 


requirements. Levels on oper- 
ating profit, net worth and in- 
terest coverage have been ad- 
justed “to levels conforming to 
management’s current or- 
mance projection for (1990 to 
1994),” it said in its third quar- 
ter report to the Securities 
and Exchange Commission. 


Improved earnings 


SMG-II showed improved 
operating earnings despite a 
weak economy. 

Sales for its supermarkets 
and drug stores (and exclud- 
ing its Rickel home centers) 
were $4.59 million for the nine 
months ended Nov. 3. That 
compares with $4.61 million 
for the nine months of 1989. 

Operating earnings for nine 
months for the entire company 
were $122.5 million compared 
with $81.6 million in the period 
last year, as the gross profit 
grew to 25.1 percent, co 
with last year’s 24.3 percent. 

er gee product mix and 
retail pricing, opportunistic 
buying, and reduced inven- 
tory chvinica ge in the super- 
markets and drug stores 
fueled the profit growth. 


Thrifty reports 


lower earnings 


LOS ANGELES — Lower 
gross margins pulled third- 
quarter operating income down 
to $5 million at Thrifty Co 
for the period ended Sept. 30, 
compared with after-tax oper- 
ating earnings of $11 million the 
previous year. Sales for the 
chain’s 1,079 drug and sporting 
goods stores were basically flat 
at $768 million. 

Thrifty is showing the ef- 
fects of tough competitive and 
economic conditions in the 
West. Same-stores sales rose 
a meager 1.3 percent in the 
third quarter, compared with 
a 3.8 percent rise a year ago. 

“The decline in earnings was 
due to margins that have fallen 
below their traditional levels at 
both drug and sporting goods 
stores,” said James Ukropina, 
chairman of Pacific Enter- 
prises, Thrifty’s parent compa- 
ny. “Thrifty is improving its 0 
erations and aggressively 


acdressing inte problems 
that have contributed to lower 
margins.”

Fay’s to buy 48 Caris 


By David Vaczek 

LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — Fay’s, Inc. in a major purchase, said 
it has entered a tentative agreement to buy the Rome, N.Y.- 
based Carls Drug. Carls, operating 48 drug stores, and its em- 
ployees will be “totally absorbed” by Fay’s, with the drug stores 
converted to Fay’s stores, Henry Panasci, Jr., Fay’s chairman 
and ceo, told Drug Store News. 

“It’s our plan to assimilate the organization and the people 
into Fay’s,” said Panasci. 

The purchase significantly advances age eng to hit the $1 
billion sales mark, by adding Carls’$100 million annual drug 
store volume. Fay’s posted $526.6 million sales in 1989, and is on 
the way to being around $700 million this fiscal year, based on 
reported third quarter results.

NACDS Small Chain Conference 
is a springboard into the 1990s 


By James Frederick 

CORONADO, Calif. — 
Small-chain executives came 
here with two main goals: to 
— better relationships 
with vendors and acquire tools 
to help them survive and pros- 
per in ’90s-era retailing. 

For most drug chains, that 
means upgrading automation 
and information-gathering ca- 
pabilities without spending 
themselves into a hole. For 
the nearly 50 drug chains rep- 
resented at La Meridien Hotel 
here, these goals went hand- 
in-hand with the need to cut 
operating costs and improve 
efficiencies. 

( 1 conference photos, page 
30. 

The occasion was the annual 
NACDS Small Chain Confer- 
ence, which this year drew 
more than 70 retail executives 


representing four- to 50-store 


chains, 25 supplier companies 
and three major wholesalers. 

Since most chains here were 
small enough not to compete 
with one another, ideas and in- 
formation flowed freely. In 
panel discussions, group think 
tanks and informal get-to- 
gethers, small-chain execu- 
tives spoke eyes 

“It’s been a highly success- 


ful show, because there’s been 
a significant amount of inter- 
action among the small-chain 
operators and the manufac- 
turers,” said NACDS presi- 
dent Ron Ziegler on the last 
day of the event. 

‘This has been excellent for 
the sharing of ideas,” added 
Bill Matteucci, president of 
Drug Fair Northwest. 


Partnerships needed 


Attendees voiced the need 
for better dialogue and rela- 
tionships between retailers 
and — As Medic Dis- 
count Drug president Nat 
Lipsye put it: ‘““We have 
worked at that with every one 
of our ~~ suppliers for 
years, and I haven’t sensed a 
readiness with many of them 
to change the old ways of do- 
ing business.” 

n many cases, say both re- 
tailers and suppliers, those 
“old ways” have been more ad- 
versarial than mutually agree- 
able. In a talk entitled “The 
New Marketing Partnership,” 
retired Procter & Gamble v 
sales Lou Pritchett said, 
“These historical, adversarial, 
win-lose relationships must 
end, and we must all focus on 
the consumer in the new mar- 


a4 


keting environment.” 

“You may think these kinds 
of partnerships can only exist 
between the major suppliers 
and the biggest chains, and 
that would a reasonable 
conclusion,” Pritchett admit- 
ted. “In the old days, suppliers 
looked at retail as a necessary 
evil, a link in the distribution 
chain to the end user. . . Those 
sag Pt ending.” 

itchett gave several rea- 
sons for the change. Among 
them: the explosion of new 
product movement informa- 
tion available to retailers, 
which ers them on a more 
even playing field and helps 
both retailers and suppliers 
target individual markets and 
customers effectively; grow- 
ing consolidation among re- 

ers, which changes the ra- 
tio of suppliers to retailers; 
and new efforts by suppliers to 
shift their focus beyond just 
selling, into service and value- 
added support. At the bottom 
of it all, he said, is the growing 
realization among suppliers 
that a “win-win” partner- 
ship—in which suppliers focus 
on the needs of retail buyers in 
planning and promoting prod- 
ew both sides to build 
sales.

Panel on 1990s retailing concluded Small Chain Conference. From left: Sheldon (Bud) Fantle, presi- 
dent, Fantle’s Enterprises; Derek Hall, McKesson Drug vp-sales; Jerry Heller, president and ceo, 
May’s Drug Stores; Bob Mathews, Synercom senior vp-develepment; Derry Myers, vp-sales, Jack’s Ser- 
vice Co.; and Larry Tilton, president, Lederle Consumer Health Products. 


Panel looks at small chain concerns 


“I have tasted both the bitter 
and the sweet in this indus- 
try... you learn a lot more 
from defeat than from your 
successes.” 

—Sheldon “Bud” Fantle, 
former chairman, 
NACDS, Peoples, Fantle’s 


CORONADO, Calif. — He 
uttered that truism as he mo- 
derated a panel on 1990s re- 
tailing at the conference. 

EDI, front-end scanning, 
and other technologies were 
central issues. Fantle urged 
small-chain retailers to adopt 
scanning “as soon as you can 
use POS in any way.” 

“It’s not enough just to have 
captured the data (at the point 
of sale),” said panelist Bob 
Mathews, senior vp-systems 
at Synercom. “You've got to 
learn how to use it (because) a 
POS system will give you 
mountains of data.” 

Jerry Heller, May’s presi- 
dent, added his chain is “work- 
ing directly with IBM to de- 
velop a POS system.” 

eanwhile, Heller added, 


drug chains should stay fo- 
cused on their mission in the 
90s: “We decided a long time 
ago not to get sidetracked” by 
video rentals, optical centers, 
auto supplies and other busi- 
nesses. “It’s much easier to 
handle your financing and dis- 
tribution and build relation- 
ships with vendors if you’re fo- 
cused on one business.” 

“My personal philosophy is

at was before all of the pies got divvied 
up. Now we just try to survive like every- 
one else.”

Does your profile fit? 


We’re looking for a pharmacist who cares a lot about retail pharmacy issues — a person who 
can write about those issues clearly and strongly. 


We need a pharmacist who is at ease interacting with pharmacy professionals at all levels— 
from professional directors at the largest corporations to community pharmacists practic- 
ing at chain and independent drug stores. 


We want a pharmacist who gets excited about traveling across the country to interview 
his/her professional peers and attending national pharmacy meetings. 


We’re searching for a pharmacist who'd give anything to play a major role in shaping an ex- 
citing new pharmacy publication. 


If your profile fits our needs, give me a call at (212) 371-9400, ext. 267, or send your resume 
plus a letter to me at Drug Store News, 425 Park Avenue, New York, NY 10022. 


Bruce Buckley 
Chief Editor

Safeway net escalates 
as sales reach $14.9B 


OAKLAND, Calif. — 
Safeway reported net income 
for 1990 of $87.1 million, or 91 
cents per share, compared 
with $2.5 million, or 3 cents 
per share, in 1989. 

Sales rose 3.8 percent, to 
$14.9 billion for the year ended 
Dec. 29. Same-store sales in- 
creased 2.9 percent for the 
year and 1.7 percent for the 
fourth quarter over those pe- 
riods in 1989. 

In 1990, gross profit was 
26.7 percent of sales, versus 
25.8 percent in 1989. The com- 
pany cited significant invest- 
ment in new information sys- 
tems, which led to better 
buying practices, more effec- 
tive merchandising and 
tighter inventory control, as 
largely responsible for the im- 


provement. Another contrib- 
utor to improved gross profit 
was increased sales in higher- 
margin specialty depart- 
ments, the company said. 

Operating profit rose 15.8 
percent, to .8 million for 
the year. Operating profit was 
3.6 percent of sales in 1990, 
versus 3.2 percent in 1989. 

Capital expenditures, in- 
cluding operating lease “er 4 
tions, were $490 million in 1990, 
the first year of ima ps five- 
year, $3.2 billion capital expen- 
diture program. 

“The 30 new stores and 90 
remodels completed in 1990 
will help maintain our strong 


operating performance while | | 


enhancing long-term sales 
rowth,” said Peter A. 
agowan, chairman.

Harco doubles DC size 


NORTHPORT, Ala. — Harco recently broke ground on a 
100,000-square-foot addition to its 135,000-square-foot distribu- 
tion center here and expects it to be up and running by early 1992. 

The added space will “give us room to grow,” said Frank Ga- 
ble, director of sales at the 161-store chain, which opens 6-8 
stores a year. 

Harco plans to upgrade sortation by converting to scanning, 
which will improve accuracy and productivity, and expand the 
conveyor system, Gable added.

DRUG STORE NEWS, March 18, 1991 


fame ana 


Mal Jozoff of Procter & Gamble told a story to illus- 
trate how times have changed at the giant consumer 
products company. 

Picture this, Jozoff said: Two signal lights at sea 
flashing frantically at one another trying to avoid a col- 
lision. One signals: Change your course 10 degrees 
south. The other replies: Change your course 10 de- 
grees north. 

From the first: I’m a 


captain. Change your 
course! The reply: ’'m a 
seaman first class. You 
change your course! 
Outraged, the captain 
IN THE MARKET) _sihas his signalman flash: 
I’M ON A BATTLE- 
eeeenail SHIP! CHANGE YOUR 
COURSE! 


Comes the reply: YOU 
CHANGE YOUR 
COURSE, I’M IN A LIGHTHOUSE! 

Not so long ago, said Jozoff, P&G’s group vp, “we’d 
plow right over that lighthouse. Today the lighthouse 
is helping us to find direction.” 

The lighthouse, of course, represents Procter & 
Gamble’s retail customers, who, increasingly, are con- 
sidered partners rather than second-class colonials in 
the effort to market P&G products. 

P&G is not the only company that’s come to realize 
that the once lopsided relationship between major 
manufacturers and chains was overdue for a change. 
Part of the reason, of course, is that scanning technol- 
ogy has begun to shift the information balance. Big re- 
tailers no longer have to rely wholly on manufacturers 
to tell them what’s happening. The righting of the bal- 
ance has been mostly healthy. And in fect has been 
seen as such by more companies like P&G who are us- 
ing alliances with retailers to build sales and profits 
throughout the distribution chain. 

Jozoff, a keynote speaker at NACDS’ distribution- 


OPINION _ 


ship to shore, P&G changes ways of yore 


/logistics conference last month at the Grenelefe Re- 
sort in Grenelefe, Fla., had other comments for at- 
tendees. Much of it was targeted at an audience made 
up largely of distribution/logistics executives. Jozoff 
was quick to point out that the distribution/logistics 
function is key to P&G, accounting for some $2 bil- 
lion—second in cost only to materials purchasing on 
P&G’s ledger sheet. 

Among the areas of potential cooperation: Expand- 
ing electronic data interchange in order to eliminate 
paperwork, assure continuous replenishment, in- 
crease turns and maintain almost 100 percent service 
levels. Jozoff noted that POS data is driving this ex- 
pansion of EDI technology. “It’s not for everyone,” he 
said. “But we’re committed to working” with retailers 
at whatever level. 

Other areas of potential cooperation, he added, in- 
clude expansion of backhauling and preappointment 
delivery scheduling; internal product handling proce- 
dures to avoid damaged goods and yield “enormous 
savings to all of us”; and “helping us to improve order- 
ing, shipping and billing accuracy.” 

Most important of all, Jozoff said, was “open, honest 
communication. . .the glue to all of this.” 

“Please encourage your organization to communi- 
cate openly and freely with us,” he told the audience. 

Will it happen overnight? Hardly. A day earlier, 
Walgreens’ executive vp of marketing, Vern Brun- 
ner, pointed out how long it takes to develop a rela- 
tionship based on trust (See story, page 2). 

“We see a lot on the news today about ‘the alliance’ 
and what is working and what is not,” he said. “Let’s 
talk about alliances, about partners and partnership- 
. . -because there is a big difference between asking 
for a slot on the dance card and getting married.” 

Brunner went on: “One of the key elements for en- 
during relationships is trust. Trust—slow to develop 
and easy to break.” 

Or using Jozoff’s earlier image: easy to founder on 
the rocks at sea. 


Scene one: Jane visits her drug store to get a pre- 
scription filled. She doesn’t see the pharmacist, except 


from a distance. The pharmacist is so busy he can 


hardly look up. Jane, who is being served by a clerk, is 
anxious because she has a question about how to take 
her medicine. 

She doesn’t ask for advice because the line is backing 
up behind her and the pharmacy lacks an area for pri- 
vate consultation. 

Scene two: Cindy 1s one 


of two harried pharma- 
cists in a chain store. 
Three phone lines are 
THE HUMAN ringing and waiting cus- 
SIDE ype sareimpatient. — 

shopper, unappreciative 
— of the wait, yells: “What 
takes you so long. All you 
do is pour pills from one 
bottle to another.” 

Cindy ites her lip, and recognizes the patient as one 
who calls on the phone for advice. 

It’s a jungle out there—for pharmacists, techni- 
cians and patients. 

To minimize errors in medicine dispensing and us- 
age, 13 states have so far legislated mandatory con- 
sulting. And California came close this year. 

What do the ranks think of it? Well, one pharmacist 
in a Walgreens store that fills 400 scripts a day, said: 
“What a load. I guess the laws are well intentioned, 
but they’re not realistic.” 

Others would argue they are—in part for exactly 
that reason of time pressure. As reported in this is- 


Mandatory consultation is double-edged 


sue’s second lead story on mandatory counseling (See 
Drug Store News For The Pharmacist, page 1), Dan 
Boesen, executive director of the Arizona Pharmacy 
Association, said that “some of the greatest support 
(for that state’s recently enacted law). . .came from 
the individual pharmacists employed at the chains.” 

Consultation sets patients straight on what they are 
using, how to take it, precautions, interactions and 
special storage needs. It also forces a pharmacist or in- 
tern to spend extra time—even if it’s a minute—re- 
viewing the prescription with patients, and assuring it 
is filled properly. 

In settings that allow the time, pharmacists largely 
prefer to spend time counseling. They don’t like to 
think of themselves as highly paid pill-filler-clerks. 

But the drug chains that fill the bulk of the nation’s 
prescriptions raise crucial economic concerns: filling 
scripts will become costlier, separate consultation ar- 
eas would need to be built and broadened technician 
duties could lead to more errors in high-volume phar- 
macies. Mix in the pharmacist shortage too. 

Indeed, many chains have given consultation more 
than lip service—without legislative prompting. Revco 
launched a pilot consultation program this winter. 
Longs tested the impact of OTC counseling by fourth- 
year pharmacy students in the aisles. Many chains have 

i pharmacy counters to encourage quiet dis- 
cussions between patients and professionals. Eckerd, 
Wal-Mart and May’s are using information kiosks to ser- 
vice customers without burdening pharmacists. 

Chains have clearly made decisive moves in this di- 
rection, and that is why mandatory consulting laws 
are such a tough pill for many to swallow.

Impact of taxes 


The main effect of ongoing 
new cigarette taxes is to 
raise the price to the consum- 
er; most drug chains have 
passed taxes through to the 
retail price. That’s not true in 
all instances, with the federal 
excise tax that went into ef- 
fect Jan. 1 raising the per 
pack tax bite by a nickel to 20 
cents. 

In Tennessee, “retailers are 
reluctant to pass the full tax 
burden onto customers,” says 
Jim Hobbs, senior merchan- 
dise manager at Begley/ 
Health Mart Drugs of Knox- 
ville. Begley takes a 10 per- 
cent gross on cartons, and 20 
percent to 30 percent on 
packs. 

“It’s a low gross; plus, 
there’s a short-term float,” 
with the retailer required to

sales, while playing down the 
category through p pnint 
merchandising and little, if 
any, advertising. 

artell Drug in the state of

rettes. And that philosophy 
will prevail even if a current 
move to eliminate a gross mar- 
gin floor is successful, says Val 
torrs, Bartell’s senior vp of 
operations. 

“We have never advertised 
cigarettes and we don’t plan 
to. We don’t want to be in the 
position of encouraging peo- 
ple to buy cigarettes,” he 
said.

DRUG STORE NEWS, March 18, 1991 


(June 1990 - December 1990) 


May’s Drug has rolled out a 
new vitamin section chain- 
wide this winter, and presi- 
dent Gerald Heller is pumped 
up by its early performance. 

“We didn’t anticipate such 
increased movement, and we 
actually ran out of stock on 
some items. I’m upset that I 
underplanned it,” he said. 

The transition began a year 
ago, when May’s began to 
scrutinize vitamins. “We had a 
very, very broad line,” said 
Heller, describing how the 


Demographics 
put vitamins at 
the top at SDM 


Demographic targeting is 
the key to vitamin nek at 
Shoppers Drug Mart. The 
chain recently restaged its 
multi-vitamin line, which, ac- 
cording to Roman Niemy, 
president-corporate brands, 
‘took us over the top into a 
positive picture with vita- 
mins.” 

With the category flat, 
Shoppers sought to create ex- 
citement for its “Life” brand. 
“We wanted to get a fresh ap- 

roach to the business,”’ 

iemy said. “So, we decided 
to segment the market very 
ee 

The chain restaged the line 
along demographic lines, mar- 
keting toward teens, adults, 
50-plus, and children—a cate- 

ory Niemy says “has always 
ena big seller for us.” 

Repackaging clearly de- 
fines the new segmentation, 
and “the line should take off in 
the stores,” he added. “Our 
previous program was stag- 
nant. We hadn't had any ni 
sions for a long time.” 

A restage of single entity vi- 
tamins, he said, will be the 
chain’s next direction. 


chain kept adding SKUs with- 
out culling over more than a 
decade. 

At first, he personally 
trimmed the assortment to 
parallel today’s vitamin in- 
dustry profile. He began to 
emphasize, for example, 
higher dose units such as zinc 
d0s and vitamin C 500s, and 
added vitamin C with rose- 
rg which has become popu- 
ar. 

These additions and dele- 
tions of smaller count SKUs 
brought a new Pecans to 
the category. Vitamins still 
get 30-72 linear feet, depend- 
Jag on the store (higher in- 
come neighborhood stores 
tend to sell more vitamins) 
but repackaging and added 
color on labels modernize the 
section’s appearance. In all 
stores, vitamin displays re- 
main next to the pharmacy 
service counter. 


Heller finds the category a 
challenge—one reason why he 
tends to it himself. “Vitamins 
are my pet area. As a pharma- 
cist, 1 think I have a good feel 
for the market.” 

He characterized the ven- 
dor situation as in flux, with 
buyouts of three different 
vendors over the past few 
years, leaving Heller reluc- 
tant to turn the category over 
to someone else. “It requires a 
lot of time and energy, be- 
cause there’s such a big mix of 
product. As soon as I get it 
completely redone like I want, 
I might consider it.” 

Heller doesn’t let himself off 
the hook, just because he’s 
president of the company. 
‘Being president hasn’t real y 
given me an advantage wit 
the vendors,” he laughed. “In 
fact, all it’s done is put more 
pressure on me in my own 
company!”

Fay’s reports record 
fourth gtr. and 12 mos. 


LIVERPOOL, NY. — 
Fay’s, Inc. posted record 
fourth quarter and 12-month 
earnings for the year ended 
Jan. 25, as same-store sales 
for the year increased 8.9 per- 
cent. The results don’t include 
the 48-store Carls Drug chain 
which Fay’s has agreed in 
principle to buy. 

Annual earnings before ex- 
traordinary charges were 
$12.3 million, or cents a 
share, compared with $10.4 
million, or 68 cents a share last 
year. After charges of $1.24 
million, earnings are $11.1 
million, or 72 cents a share. 

The charges stemmed from 
the 1991 purchase of $27 mil- 
lion face value 13 34 percent 
subordinated debentures. 
Year-to-year comparison was 
also affected by an unusually 


low tax rate in 1990 due to the 
use of capital loss carry for- 
wards, Fay’s reported. 

Revenues for the year in- 
creased 17.2 percent to $672.6 
million. 

Fourth quarter net earn- 
ings were $5 million, or 43.6 
percent better than last year’s 
comparable quarter. Sales 
were $190.7 million, up 17.9 
percent. 

Expressing pleasure with 
the results, chairman Henry 
Panasci, Jr. pointed to im- 
provements in gross margin 
and operating expense ratios. 
“The current economic situa- 
tion has not dampened our ex- 
pectations. We feel confident 
that our momentum in sales 
will continue and further im- 
provement in expense ratios is 
possible,” Panasci said.

cents a share compared with 
last year’s $656,000 (ten cents 
a share).

creased 2.4 percent to a record 
$113.1 million, helping to 


drive record sales for the full 
year. Twelve month sales 
were $432 million, or 6.6 per- 
cent better than last year. Net 
earnings for the 12 months 
were $5.5 million or 82 cents a 
share, which was one cent a 
share off the record earnings 
reached in the 1989 fiscal year. 

This year’s earnings are 99 
percent better than last 
year’s.

Chains face ecological challenge 


Since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution, peo- 
ple have tended to treat the earth, airand water as either 
a vast garbage dump or an infinite source of raw materi- 
als. The results of two centuries of environmental abuse 


are now all around us. 


clear they play a big role. 


paper. 


A growing coalition of industry, government and pri- 
vate citizens has begun the massive task of reordering 
our perilous and destructive relationship with the envi- 
ronment. Consumers are clamoring for products that 
are less damaging to the ecosystem, and manufacturers 
are scrambling to come up with solutions. The so-called 
green revolution is still gathering steam. 


This revolution has major implications for retailers. 
Many have met the challenge aggressively, while oth- 
ers wait until standards are more clearly defined. Itis 


The special report beginning on page 11 of this issue 
examines the environmental crisis, its implications for 
retailers, and some possible solutions. It looks at what’s 
brewing on the legislative side, as well as what some re- 
tailers and manufacturers are currently doing to ad- 
dress the environmental concerns of consumers. 


In future issues, Drug Store News 
will continue its coverage with 
monthly articles as the “Decade of 
the Environment” unfolds.

Western DC set for Phar-Mor 


_ AURORA, Colo. — Taking the next logical step as it expands 
in new western markets, Phar-Mor is planning to open a region- 
al distribution center here to serve 11 western states. The new 
center will occupy two leased buildings totaling 189,000 square 
feet in the Upland Industrial Park near Denver. 

The off-price chain operates eight units in the state, and last 
bie opened its first stores in Arizona, New Mexico, Oklahoma, 

ebraska and Nevada. This year, Phar-Mor plans to add stores 
in markets like Phoenix, Albuquerque, San Antonio, Las Vegas 
and Oklahoma City, while opening its first units in California. 

Nationwide, the chain now operates 245 stores in 27 states, 
serviced by distribution centers in Youngstown and in Orlando, 
Fla. Plans call for a total of 65 new stores this year.

_— 


Politicians (and battlefield commanders) know that 
you can’t get too far in front of your constituents 
(troops) or you'll risk losing your office (head). 

It’s the same with retailers and customers. Retail 
leadership is important because being first can mean 
winning customers and market share, but beware of 
charging ahead too far. Your customers may not un- 
derstand. And customer confusion can be a retailer’s 
worst nightmare. 

Caution seems to be the 


approach that many lead- 
ing drug chains are taking 
on the environmental is- 
sue, as the articles in our 
special environmental sec- 
tion indicate. The chains’ 
sensitive antennas hear 
the growing public clamor 


IN THE MARKET 
BRUCE BUCKLEY 


for “earth-friendly” prod- 
ucts and actions, but they 
are nevertheless moving with care. Their customers 
may want environmental reform, but are not entirely 
certain about what’s needed. They may talk about recy- 
clable products, but not want to pay the increased cost. 
So, despite the obvious importance of supporting 
the “green” issue, cultivating a caucious and responsi- 
ble approach is sensible. As Gloria Lepik, Eckerd 
Drug’s manager of marketing research, put it: “We 
want to find a good comfortable balance between be- 
ing a zealot and being totally irresponsible.” 


OPINION 


Environmental leadership has its risks 


Consumer education is the best way of clearing 
away confusion and staying just ahead of the charging 
crowd. Supermarket companies have taken the lead in 
education (page 16), but drug chains are catching up. 
Pay Less, for example, introduced a cartoon character 
called Forest Earthwell to help educate its customers 
about environmental issues without seeming to 
preach to them. 

Pay Less is also letting its stores take the lead in lo- 
calized education actions and encouraging the ex- 
change of ideas. Sharing ideas is important. Competi- 
tion seems out of place with an issue as important as 
the environment. 

Ultimately, if the green issue is going to take hold, it 
has to make economic sense. So it’s encouraging to see 
home lighting manufacturers introducing products 
that help the environment and also save consumers’ 
dollars. Concentrated household cleaning products in 
smaller containers and tighter packaging are similarly 
producing less waste and using up less retail shelf 
space — another environmental/economic plus. 

Drug Store News decided to print this issue on recy- 
cled paper, more as a test than a self-promoting stunt. 
We found the supply of recycled, coated-stock paper 
limited and available only in a heavier and more ex- 
pensive weight. Our hope is that with increased de- 
mand more mills will begin turning out recycled paper 
and the cost will drop. 

For us, like you, idealism has to be tempered by the 
bottom line. 


It’s taken awhile, but forces of the environmental 
lobby and the free enterprise system are finally mov- 
ing on the same track. Well, at least they’re moving in 
the same direction. 

For years, most businesses either ignored environ- 

mentalism, or resisted it. 


Recently, however, 
somebody discovered gold 
under the green. Manufac- 
turers are relabeling, if 
not reformulating their 
goods to appeal to the 
public’s growing appetite 
for environmentally 
sound products. Drug 
chains are repackaging 
their private label lines in recyclable containers. And 
self-appointed “certification” organizations are offering 
environmental product endorsements——for a price. 

This is all fine. But there are some problems with 
the current commercialization of environmentalism. 
@ Some companies have gone overboard with broad 


WASHINGTON 
PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


‘There’s gold in them green hills’ 


and unsubstantiated claims about “environmentally 
pure” products or “totally recyclable” packaging. 

® No telling what standards future regulators will set 
for environmental advertising, their boardroom law- 
yers warn. Adding to these concerns: the very real 
prospect of a proliferation of rules, regulations and 
guidelines by states, cities and hamlets nationwide. 

Clearly, the boys in Washington need to set national 
standards governing environmental] product claims! 

Indeed, the Federal Trade Comniission is consider- 
ing a petition from a number of major food manufac- 
turers who want the agency to come up with nation- 
wide rules to clarify the situation for everyone. 

Under the National Food Processors Association 
plan, FTC would develop federal standards govern- 
ing five types of environmental claims: recyclability, 
recycled content, source reduction, refillable/reusa- 
ble containers, and compostability. 

There’s more than a little irony in this proposal. Af- 
ter decades of ridicule as a meddlesome “National 
Nanny,” the FTC is suddenly being viewed by indus- 
try as an environmental King Solomon. 


Letter to the editor 


Dear Editor: 

I was most interested in your “In the Market” opin- 
ion in the March 4 Drug Store News regarding Mr. 
Alan Levin’s site selection criteria. You state that 
when he is offered a potential site Mr. Levin doesn’t 
need any “heavy-duty demographic studies” to make 
up his mind. 

I am intrigued by Mr. Levin’s abilities, both in 
terms of innate ability selecting sites and decisiveness 
on making up his mind. In my 41 years performing 
“heavy-duty demographic studies” to forecast sales 
for new stores, I’ve actually met only one CEO with 
the brilliance of intuitively knowing the worth of a site 
(the late Sidney Rabb at the Stop & Shop Companies). 
If Mr. Levin is such a person, more power to him! 

In my experience with the prescription business, 
however, I’ve learned that at least one variable super- 
sedes all others in determining drug store potential; 
that is, persons over 65 years old spend in the magni- 


tude of four times that of a person aged 20. How much 
of that potential would go to Mr. Levin’s store de- 
pends, among other things, on the nature of his loca- 
tion and the nature of the competition. Perhaps he can 
handle these factors qualitatively. 

My inference is that Mr. Levin has an intuitive 
sense for demographics and knows his markets well. 
As long as the population densities close in to his 
stores are high and he is dealing with known competi- 
tors, his personal “analog system” of forecasting that 
he carries around in his head will work for him. In new 
markets, thinly populated markets or in situations 
with a different set of competitors, his intuition, I sus- 
pect, could lead him astray. Given the cost of a location 
mistake “heavy-duty demographics” are not an ex- 
pensive insurance policy. 


Howard L. Green 
president, Howard L. Green & Associates

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 1, 1991 


One of the big- 
gest by-products 
of the environ- 
mental movement 
in retailing and 
manufacturing has 
been confusion. 
Conflicting claims 
by some manufac- 
turers, and misunderstandings by 
both consumers and retailers, have 
made green marketing a tough path to 
follow. 

For one thing, there are few easy 
choices. Take the paper vs. plastic bag 
controversy: many consumers have ex- 
presage the desire for paper vs. plastic 

ags, but paper is far bulkier than plas- 
tic, takes up seven times as much landfill 
space, and eats up trees—about one 20- 


ea tree for every 700 bags, in fact. 
aper also biodegrades too slowly in 
landfills to extend their useful life, and 
its manufacture consumes more energy 
than that of plastic ~~ 
Plastic, of course, has problems of 
its own. It doesn’t break down in the 
round. It releases toxins when 
urned. It clogs waterways and chokes 
marine life when eaten or inhaled. 


Unsubstantiated product claims 


Meanwhile, claims by some manu- 
facturers that their plastic garbage 
bags and diaper linings were “degrad- 
able” backfired when it was discovered 
that the cornstarch added to the plastic 
only caused the bags to decompose into 
smaller pieces in landfills. Enraged, 
seven environmental groups called in 


Some facts about solid waste: 
problem grows, space is limited 


MANAGING THE ENVIRONMENTAL CHALLENGE 
BB cverview | 


Environmental choices aren't easy for retailers 


1989 for a consumer boycott of “biode- 
gradable” plastic bags, calling it an 
“environmental hoax.” 

“Unfortunately, a growing number of 
companies are going wild in this new 
green market,” said Jeanne Wirka, a 
policy analyst for the Environmental 
Action Foundation. “These companies 
are trying to cash in on consumers’ gen- 
uine concern for the environment b 
making misleading, unsubstantiated, 
and sometimes just plain false claims 
about the purported benefits of their 
products.” 

The confusion extends to recycling, 
as well. Manufacturers of plastic mm 
aging have attempted to clear up the 
confusion and boost recycling by cod- 
ing their products by the types of poly- 
mers used in their manufacture. 


Amid a growing clamor for standards 
to clear up the confusion, several ratings 
systems have emerged to evaluate envi- 


ronmental claims made by manufactur- 
ers. Among them are two rival certify- 
ing agencies, Green Cross and Green 
Seal, as well as in-house testing pro- 
by major retailers like » Boa 
al-Mart and major food chains. 

Many of those chains have also print- 
ed customer brochures (on recycled 
paper, of course) explaining the pros 
and cons of plastic vs. paper, the bene- 
fits of source reduction and recycling, 
and the choices all consumers must 
face. This kind of above-board, honest 
— to the problems of waste and 
pollution has cut through some of the 
confusion and won praise from envi- 
ronmentalists. 


What’s In Our Garbage Lancdfilis? 


Giass 7.1% 


Metals 8.4% 


Food Wastes 8.5% 


e@ U.S. homes, businesses and public agen- 
cies generated enough trash every year— 
more than 160 million tons, according to the 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency—to 
fill a line of 10-ton garbage trucks long enough 
to circle the earth five times. That’s roughly a 
ton of waste per person every year. 

@ Landfills for we ied cities like New York, 
Chicago and Philadelphia are expected to be 
filled to capacity within a few years. New 
York and Los Angeles each have only one re- 
maining landfill open; some experts think one- 
fourth of American cities will run out of land- 
fill space by the mid-1990s. 

@ At present, fully 80 percent of our solid 
waste is deposited in landfills, according to 
the EPA. Another nine percent is incinerat- 
ed; only 11 percent is currently recycled. 


@ Waste materials biodegrade far too slowly in 
landfills to extend their useful life. For in- 
stance, 30-year-old newspapers have been dug 
from landfills and still perfectly readable. 

@ Americans rate the environmental crisis as 
one of the nation’s four most pressing prob- 
lems, behind crime and drugs, AIDS and ris- 
ing health care costs. Nearly eight in 10 say 
they would pay more for a product packaged 
in hiedesvadabie or rec sade containers.

States have green bills pending 


By Gwen Driscoll 

Lawmakers across the 
country are prescribing 
strong medicine for the envi- 
ronment this year in the form 
of dozens of new green bills 
which could impact the na- 
tion’s drug stores. 

Bottle deposit laws may 
hike the price of beverages, 
hazardous wastes disposal 
plans may require extra ex- 
pense and labor, and recycling 
requirements could create un- 
expected shifts in consumer 
buying habits. 

me green groups hope 
the environmental movement 
will pick up enough steam this 
year to resuscitate legislation 
rejected by lawmakers in ear- 
lier sessions. In both Califor- 
nia and New York, lobbyists 
are pushing waste reduction 
plans modeled on a controver- 
sial bill that was rejected by 
voters in Oregon last year. 

Proposals to encourage or 
require recycling of various 
products are surfacing in a 
number of state legislatures 
this year. New Jersey’s Gov- 


12 


ernor Jim Florio, for example, 
recently lent support for one 
of the most ambitious state re- 
— plans yet—a 60% recy- 
cling mandate for all of the 
state’s garbage by 1995. 

A California group, mean- 
while, is pushing a Throw- 
away Packagin age | 
Act which wail require 
containers to be recycled at a 
25 percent rate by 1995, and a 
50 percent rate by the year 
2000. Significantly, the pro- 

sal would also require all 

usinesses that sell disposable 
products and packaging to pay 
the “true net cost of recycling 
them.” 

Florida and Indiana are 
debating an increase in the 
maga | deposit refund val- 
ue to at least ten cents per 
beverage container. 

Albany lawmakers are also 
debating proposed legislation 
to remove environmentally 
hazardous products from pub- 
lic reach in general. One of 
New York’s two pending bev- 
erage container bills, for ex- 
ample, would ban the sale of 


beverages connected by plas- 
tic holding devices, as well as 
single serving juice boxes. 
Another New York bill would 
prohibit the sale of items at re- 
tail which are not packaged in 
biodegradable containers, as 
well as a separate measure to 
ban the sale of non-biodegrad- 
able disposable diapers. 

Vermont introduced legis- 
lation that would ban the retail 
sale of empty polystyrene con- 
tainers while South Carolina 
introduced a measure to pro- 
hibit the sale of cleaning 
agents containing phosphates. 
In Maine, new legislation 
would eliminate all products 
containing chlorofluorocar- 
bons after January 1992. 

Colorado lawmakers intro- 
duced a bill that would require 
—os diaper packages to 
be labeled with a warning no- 
tice to consumers concernin 
the disposal impact of suc 
products. 

A proposal before the Indi- 
ana legislature would discour- 
“ deceptive environmental 

vertising claims.

MANAGING THE ENVIRONMENTAL CHALLENGE 


Light bulb man- 
ufacturers are 
betting that low- 
wattage bulbs in- 
troduced this year 
will turn on con- 
sumers—despite 
the relatively high 
ticket for fluores- 
cents and halogen bulbs. 

The environmental benefits are just 
one of the selling points for bulb lines 
launched this year by General Electric 
and GTE-Sylvania. Philips Lighting is 
leaning on halogen and fluorescent 
bulbs it launched last year. 

By their more efficient use of elec- 
tricity, bulbs save on usage costs while 
peg a about the same amount of 
ight. Suppliers are also aggressively 
educating consumers on how new lamp 
technology can bring more creative 


ducating 


shoppers about low- 
wattage bulbs is vital. 


lighting @ batteries 


lighting into their homes. 

The price question is considerable— 
with fluorescents and halogens often 
topping $20, compared with a buck or 
two per incandescent bulb. Heavy bulb 
users can easily justify the investments. 


Pay more for green products 


Ina recent poll conducted for GE, 82 
percent of consumers said they “were 
more likely to buy—and pay a little 
more for—products that positively im- 
pact the environment.” 

GE’s answer: the Energy Choice line 
of five fluorescents and four incandes- 
cents, packaged in green-colored recy- 
cled material. The 90-watt Energy 
Choice incandescent can provide energy 
costs over a 100-watt soft white. The 
more dramatic savings are in the fluo- 
rescent screw-ins. For example, the 27- 
watt Circlite fluorescent, a circled tube, 
lasts ten times longer than the 75- watt 
soft white it replaces, saving $38 in ener- 
gy costs over its life. 

GTE-Sylvania unveiled its Energy 
Saver line, also with green packaging, 
which includes lower ‘wattage incan- 
descent bulbs, replacing bulbs of high- 
er wattage, and a soft white compact 
fluorescent for home use. Aimed at up- 
scale customers, its 18 watts produce 
light comparable to a 75 watt lamp, and 
it lasts 10,000 hours compared to an in- 
candescent’s 750 hours. 

Moreover, the Energy Saver incan- 
descents are slightly smaller than the A- 
19 standard-size, using fewer raw mate- 


Vendors move to rid 


There isn’t yet 
an economical 
wa technology for re- 

m covering metals 
from ine and 
zinc-carbon batter- 
les. : 

Manufacturers 
contend that bat- 
teries account for a small percent of 
landfill space, and that their impact in 
the waste stream is benign. Eveready, 
Duracell, Rayovac and Panasonic have, 
nevertheless, moved toward lowering 
the mercury content in batteries, since 
mercury is a toxic hazardous waste. 

In addition, safe zinc-air technology, 
which replaces mercuric oxide-based 
systems in =< aids, is being used 
more and more. And suppliers have, 
for the most part, made their packag- 
ing less wasteful and more space-effi- 
cient. Eveready, for instance, went to 
shrink wrap and reduced packaging 
materials by 70 percent. 


endor initia- 


tives include less mer-

Since 1984, the industry has lowered

—— a Rayovac spokesman. 

veready, Duracell, Rayovac and

batteries’ mercury content to .025 per- 
cent, from about one percent. They’ve 
ne Mig proprietary methods to re- 
Seep the mercury, which acts as a sta- 
ilizer between the batteries’ two safe 
metals, zinc and manganese. 


Batteries still targets 


Yet, batteries remain a frequent fo- 
cus of pro-environment consumers. Bills 
are pending in many states to mandate 
mercury reduction. The vendors today 
meet the strictest levels required, but 
New Jersey and Minnesota are now pro- 
posing laws to require a mer level of 
zero. Some states and localities have 
also made proposals for collecting used 
batteries, says Charles Monahan, plan- 
“_ manager of Panasonic. 

me feel that the potential of rechar- 
eables as an environmental alternative 
as been exaggerated. “People are run- 
ning around and saying rechargables 
are the solution. They’re not,” says Pan- 
asonic’s spokesman Halaburda. 

When used properly, they can allow 
sizable savings. A single rechargeable 
can replace 100 alkalines, but don’t fill all 
battery needs. And most contain cadmi- 
um, a metal at least as toxic as mercury. 
On the plus side, rechargeables can be 

cled to some extent, and the nickel 
and cadmium metals recovered.

In Randolph, Vermont last month, 
residents capped a drive in which they 
collected aan sorted used batteries, and 
sent the cells back to the vendors. The 
ceo’s office at Eveready received one of 
the token shipments of used batteries, 
which the residents charged were haz- 
ardous waste. The box was disposed of 
in a St. Louis landfill, said Terry Telz- 
row, Eveready’s manager of standards 
and product safety. 


batteries of mercury 


Telzrow said that three major stud- 
ies in the U.S., Europe and Japan have 
found no evidence of environmental 
hazard from batteries disposed along 
with household waste. In tests, no 
metals leached from battery-contain- 
ing landfills into the ground. 

“There is no environmental problem 
with batteries. There has never been an 
incident, anywhere on the planet, where 
household batteries have caused a 
health or environment problem,” said 
Jim Donahue, Duracell’s spokesman. 


Five hundred retailers, including 
most drug stores, in Minnesota’s 
Hennepin County, which encom- 
— Minneapolis and some subur- 

an and rural areas, have been col- 
lecting “button” batteries for about 
a year. The batteries contain 
enough silver and mercury to war- 
rant sending them to a metals re- 
covery facility. 

Encouraged by the program’s 
success, the county launched a pi- 
lot program in November, in coop- 
eration with Snyder Drug and local 
library branches, to collect all bat- 
teries found in household use, in- 
cluding alkaline, zine carbon, nick- 
el cadmium and some lithium. 

The county provided 32-gallon 
Rubbermaid plastic bins wrapped in 


Retailers recover batteries 


lastic “skirts” to resemble big, 
reestanding batteries. The con- 
tainers, which have wheels for easy 
carting, are usually located up 
front, often near battery displays, 
in Snyder stores. 

“The goal is to divert the heavy 
metal in these batteries from the 
waste stream,” said Mark Oyaas, 
the county official in charge of the 
project. 

e dead batteries are collected 
by a nonprofit organization for 
hard-to-employ adults and taken to 
a special hazardous waste landfill. 
Oyaas, who said Snyder had ap- 
proached the county to help, hopes 
to expand the battery collection 
program to other retail outlets by 
summer.

COLUMBUS, Ohio — Drug Emporium said it has signed a 


letter of intent to buy the remaining 45 percent of its nine-store 
Cincinnati-Dayton teanchiat. Current store management will 


continue to direct operations, said Gary Wilber, ceo. 

Drug Emporium will issue about 1,100,000 shares of common 
stock to buy the business. The deal is subject to approval of the 
shareholders of Cincinnati Drug Distributors, Inc., the franchi- 


see. 

_ Also, Drug Emporium said it opened five new stores in March 
in the Washington, D.C.- Baltimore market, making 17. Wilber 
said plans are for ten more in the region by year’s end. 


Super Valu earmarks $121M for Cubs 


MINNEAPOLIS — Super Valu Stores has earmarked $121.2 
million, or 28 percent of its $434 million capital budget for 1991, 
for construction of two corporate Cub Foods stores, in St. Jo- 
seph, Mo., and Apple Valley, Minn. Four franchise Cubs are 
also scheduled to open this year. Funds are also budgeted for 10 

jor remodels of cororate Cub units. 

Shopko, Super Valu’s 104-store discount mass merchandiser, 
will be allocated $136 million, or 31 percent of the capital budget, 
for openings of five new stores and relocations of two units, plus 
land acquisition.
