DRUG STORE NEWS, April 22, 1991 


OPINION 


The chain drug report card is in for 1990: Not an “A” 
year, by any means, but certainly a strong B. 

Considering the economic climate, chain drug stores 
fared well. Sales rose 9 percent to $44.3 billion, and 
chains increased their share of overall drug store sales to 
62 percent. The results showed once again that provid- 
ing basic consumer needs, especially in health care, con- 
fers stability even in recessionary times. 

Not surprisingly the 
strongest gains were 


achieved in the core drug 
store categories, where 
chains have put the heavi- 
est emphasis. Leading the 


IN THE MARKET)! charge, of course, was 
BRUCE BUCKLEY pharmacy. Chain prescrip- 
tion departments racked 
up a 14.4 percent increase, 
and the price of the aver- 
age script rose more than 

$2 to $17.61. 


Most of pharmacy’s sales gain resulted from the in- 
crease in pharmaceutical prices. But there were some 
unit increases as well, as chains led with a strategy 
built around heavy health care promotion. Under 
pressure from supermarket and mass market retail- 
ers, the chains took a page from the independents and 
promoted themselves as neighborhood pharmacies 
and their pharmacists as trusted community re- 
sources. Meanwhile they used increasingly sophisti- 
cated computer technology to improve patient service 
and information and bolster their success in the ever- 
growing third-party arena. 

While pharmacy was the class over-achiever, other 


Providing basic needs equals stability 


pivotal departments were no slouches either. Strong 
to medium advances were registered in OTC drugs, 
toiletries, cosmetics, photo and stationery. Less pro- 
ductive were the general merchandise categories. 
Significantly, consumable categories—particularly 
candy and high-demand grocery products—had a 
good year. Chains used their convenient locations to 
siphon off dollars from food stores. Turnabout is fair 
play, the chains seemed to say. 

In 1991 the economic signals remain mixed, but drug 
stores for the most part continue to stand up well. 


* * * 


Often we’re asked how we compile our annual indus- 
try reports, particularly how we come by all of those 
numbers that we publish each year. The quick answer 
is that there is no single information mother-lode. The 
data is collected over several months from various 
sources, including surveys that we mail and fax to 
chains; interviews that we conduct with chain buyers 
and manufacturers; articles that we’ve run in the past 
year; the database maintained by Lebhar-Friedman’s 
Chain Store Guides; and, not least, marketing re- 
search companies like Nielsen and Towne-Oller. 

The information is gathered and analyzed and a rea- 
sonable consensus is reached for each of the dozens of 
individual product subcategories that make up our 20- 
year-old category database. The increases (or de- 
creases) have to fit like puzzle pieces within a known 
picture; that picture being the actual overall gain in 
chain drug sales as provided to us by A.C. Nielsen. 

The result is the annual report that you’re holding in 
your hands right now. Next issue we’ll report on the 
individual performances of companies in the industry. 


Drug stores’ affordable 


The nation’s middle class, buffeted by economic | 


winds of hot air, wants to descend from the blistering 
mast and enjoy life’s ride. Put in real terms, people 
who are used to working 60 hours a week or more to 
make ends meet look around and see friends who've 
done the same fall victim to cutbacks. 

The ’80s were a breathtaking era of consumption. 
The ’90s will be a time when people make more basic 
choices instead: fresh air, 
family, less glitz, more 


spirit. 
One can tick off the rea- 
sons for this mammoth 


THE HUMAN shift of consumer atti- 
SIDE tudes: higher unemploy- 
AL HELLER ment, the fall in housing 


prices, mountainous debt, 
the unmasking of Donald 
Trump and Michael Mil- 
ken and the values they 
represented, and even Operation Desert Storm bring- 
ing Americans together toward a higher purpose. 

How hard will people run to stay in the same place? I 
think they’ll make different choices—and retailers 
will have to live with them. 

Indeed, luxury car dealers and department store 
operators have wailed a lot the past year—but all that 
will help them is changing the way they conduct busi- 
ness if they want to be around when we roll into the 
next decade. 

Drug chains, for their part, should benefit by this 
back-to-basics move. If people give up their Rolexes, 
they may buy Timexes. If people spend more time to- 
gether as families, that bodes well for photofinishing 
volume. If people decide that Cuisinarts and Krups 
are too costly, they’ll opt for Oskar. 

And so on, in virtually every category sold by drug 
chains, which rarely dared to venture beyond middle- 
— price points for féar they’d lose their customer 

ase. 


format fits the ‘90s 


It was nearly a decade ago when drug chains, look- 
ing to broaden their appeal, began experimenting 
with far-afield formats and product mixes. In search 
of customers, some operators lost sense of their pri- 
mary reason for being—and suffered economically for 
that miscalculation. Most of those tests were short- 
lived, and by the late ’80s the refocus on core health 
and beauty care categories was well under way. 

Today, as drug chains are where they should be— 
intent on building core business—consumers may be 
looking to them as one more expression of rediscov- 
ered old-fashioned values. 

Few frills, no pretense, proven brands at affordable 
prices. And consultation at the pharmacy—the real 
backbone of drug stores’ image. After all, people will 
value themselves more and pay greater attention to 
their personal health care needs during the we decade 
of the ’90s. 

Drug stores, led by the pharmacies, are formats for 
the masses, and suddenly that’s become fashionable 


Letters to the editor 


Dear Editor: 

Much has been written and said about the pharma- 
cist’s role in counseling patients about their prescrip- 
tions, drug profiles, contraindications, and other as- 
pects of therapy. 

On the front page of the March 18, 1991 issue of 
Drug Store News is a photograph and article describ- 
ing the marvels of Walgreen’s new drive-up pharmacy 
window. 

My question is simply, how does a pharmacist effec- 
tively counsel a patient who is sitting outside in their 
automobile? Are we now being reduced to dispensing 
“McPrescriptions”? 


Thomas J. Nicholson, R.Ph.

Dearth of new blockbuster 


By Alan Miller 

_The 57 health and beauty 
aids categories tracked by Ar- 
bitron/SAMI generated just 
over $8.6 billion at drug stores 
during the 52 weeks ending 
December 28, 1990. This was a 
two-percent rise for the year; 
insufficient to compensate for 
inflation or product mix up- 
grading in a number of catego- 
ries. 

On a unit basis, a three per- 
cent annual decline occurred. 
And during 1990’s final 12 
weeks, units fell 4.4 percent 
and the dollar gain was only 
one percent. 

A major reason for the mod- 
est dollar growth: the absence 
of high volume, innovative 
new products in 1990. Only 20 
new brands with the power to 
produce annual drug store 
sales of $1 million-plus 
launched during the year. 
These brands are identified in 
the accompanying table, 
ranked according to their vol- 
ume during the final 12 weeks 
of the year (in order to erase 
the volume level bias for 
brands introduced early in the 
ined in comparison with those 


aunched in the waning weeks 
of 1990). 


Sales over $2 million 


Only three new brands 
showed 12-week drug store 
sales above $2 million: Vidal 
Sassoon Ultra Care shampoo, 
Dimetapp cough remedy, and 
Lotrimin Athlete’s Foot rem- 
edy. Two more new brands en- 
joyed 12-week sales of more 
than $1 million: Medi-F lu cold 
remedy, and Degree stick 
antiperspirant. Oil of Olay 
face lotion logged in at 
$952,000 during the year-end 
span. Nine of the new brands 
had 12-week dollar shares be- 
low 1 percent. 

It should be pointed out that 
the tabulations presented do 
not include line extensions, 
such as Excedrin Aspirin Prep 
or Arm & Hammer Dental 
Care gel, which may be re- 
garded by some marketers as 
new products. Also, the list of 
the most important new 
brands doesn’t include candi- 
dates in such high volume 
product categories as tooth- 
paste and powder, internal an- 
algesics, or hand and body 
creams and lotions, which are 
generally rich in new prod- 
ucts. 


Lack of innovation 


Another reason for HBA’s 
limited growth: the lack of in- 
novation in packaging, ingre- 
dients, formulation or cre- 
ative direction, which often 
spawn competitive imitations 
or “me-too” activity which can 
be counted on to expand cate- 


gory sizes. :

brands which appeared in 
1990, there were aiso a num-

| Convenience, community challenge retailers in the 90s 


i Mod cs 


ast year, American 
Stores president and 
chief operating officer 
Alan Stewart asked his divi- 
sion heads to think about 
what retailine would be like 
in the 1990s. He got anearful.

Stewart said, came up witha 
list of six major themes that 
were likely to dominate re-

Indeed, every one of the mar-

ready having a profound ef- 
fect on the way drug, 
supermarket and general 
merchandise retailers do 
business. 

Most chain drug retailers 
can guess what they came up 
with, and could probably add 
one or two more themes of 
their own. Stewart came up 
with these: 

@ The impact of the envi- 
ronmental movement on man-

Plenty of choices 


One thing is clear: in the 
1990s, consumers will have 
plenty of choices about where 
to buy prescription drugs, 
HBA, greeting cards, statio- 
nery and aslew of other prod- 
ucts that define the core of 
drug store retailing. 


Meanwhile, today’s con- 
sumer is “a mags of contradic- 
tions” in the words of one re- 
tail analyst, and 
“sentimental, romantic, and 
anxious to make his life a lit- 
tle more comfortable,” in the 
words of another, Walter F. 
Loeb of Loeb Associates. 

To compete, drug chains 
will need an array of 
strengths: better purchasing 


and distribution systems; a 
motivated workforce; a re- 
sponsive buying department 
and merchandise mix; a solid 
capital base; and a strong 
health- and beauty-care im- 
age. What’s more, they’ll 
have to practically enshrine 
the concept of convenience in 
the 1990s. 


Convenient and dependable 


“We believe the retailer 
that wastes consumers’ time 
in the 90s is committing com- 
petitive suicide,” noted Wal- 
green president Dan Jorndt 
recently. “We should simply 
be there—in convenient, 
neighborhood locations, tak- 
ing care of purchases easily 
and dependably.” 

Adds his boss, chairman 
Charles R. Walgreen III, 
“Retailing is going to change 
a lot by the year 2000. The 
days when retail giants like 
Sears, Kmart or J.C. Pen- 
ney—or Walgreens—could 
open a store, stock the 
Shelves, offer decent prices 
and wait for the customers to 
roll in are gone forever. In 
their place, we have the com- 
plexity, sophistication and 
competition that character- 
ize modern retailing.” 

So begins Drug Store 
News’ annual coverage of the 
$67.8 billion drug store in- 
dustry. In Part I, we look at 
the merchandise mix that 
“brought us to the party” and 
how it performed in 1990, as 
well as some of the marketing 
and display programs em- 
ployed by drug, combo and 
off-price chains to move that 
mix. In Part II we look at the 
chain drug players them- 
selves, from national giants 
like Walgreens to tough re- 
oem competitors like Arbor 

rugs and Big B. 

Here’s to a successful year.

rug store chains are in 
a unique position to 
shape the future of 
pharmacy service in America.

puterization, enabling us to 
serve our stores, employees 
and customers better and 
faster than before. Comput-

systems have shortened the 
distance between stores and 
headquarters, making it easi-

trends in the often diverse 
markets in which we operate. 
Perhaps more important is 
the effect the technological 
revolution in drug stores has 
had on customer service at 
the locai level.

her third party claim, pro- 
vide a synopsis of her pa- 
tient’s file or call her doctor 
to approve a generic equiva- 
lent when the computer indi- 
cates a brand name is not cov- 
ered under the patient’s plan. 
All of this can be accom- 
plished within seconds 
through a few quick taps on 
the keyboard.

graying of America and the 

om in third party coverage

in our success.

ager and the pharmacist who 
ean greet their customers by 
name, are in excellent position 
to put new corporate strate- 
gies into place and mold the 
reputation of chain stores as 
responsive members in the 
community.

New players in 
ethnic cosmetics 


Ethnic cosmetics has been 
having a strong year, and the 
future is looking even brighter 
as more major players move 
into this category. 

Posner, for instance, con- 
tinues to sell well in African- 
American neighborhood 
stores. No one questions its 
osition as the strongest 
Service cosmetics bullpen in Snyder Drug’s prototype, Eden Prai- Vons Pavilion, El Monte, Calif., develops displays with video and rand in the category—driven 
rie, Minn., maintains files on shoppers. overhead graphics that signal fashions and emphasize brands. by its advertising, fashion- 

and price-value-promotions. 

a cama ee en Now, however, Maybelline 
and Almay are launching eth- 
nic lines, and two major bud- 
get manufacturers, Artmatic 
and Pavion’s Wet ’N Wild, are 
also backing lines targeted 
specifically to women of color. 

At press time, most buyers 
had ly seen the Maybel- 
line line and their initial reac- 
tions were very positive. 
Stephanie Hayter of Genovese 
and Susan Lund of Snyder both 
welcomed a major company’s 

resence in the category. They 
th felt the Maybelline line, 
Shades of You, will start well, 
especially if promised advertis- 
ing materializes. 

“We're glad to see more man- 
ufacturers get in,” said Donna 
McManus, cosmetic buyer for 
K & B in Louisiana. K & B, like 
many chains, plans to expand 
its ethnic cosmetics planogram 
and is reviewing several other 
lines that might make good ad- 
ditions to their set. 

Among them: Shades of 
You, Simply Satin, Almay, 
Tropez from Artmatic and the 
new Wet ’N Wild ethnic line: 
Black Radiance. 


Style drives hair 
accessory sales 


Increased emphasis on 
grooming and health are pro- 
pelling sales of hair accesso- 
ries including implements 
(combs and brushes), and hair 
and head ornaments. 

While impulse sales are im- 
portant on items under $2, to- 
day’s customer also seeks out 

ue in items such as barrettes 
and—strong performers in 
1990—head bands and hair 
wraps. Head bands are a peren- 
ially strong performer. Hair 

should stay strong into 
1992, industry sources feel. 

“It’s become a basic part of 
dressing for most women to- 
day,” one source observed of 
head bands and hair wraps. 

Also strong in 1990 was the 
“ponytail” category. 

The fashion element of 
course is key in the high-mar- 
gin segment. For 1991, Goody 
is betting on its Sport line of 
hair accessories with a sport- 
ing feel to them in bright col- 
ors and in black. 

New vendors have entered 
in both the mass merchant and 
department store ends of the 
business, challenging in drug 
stores such heavyweights as 
Goody, Sekine, Conair and 
Wilhold.

Minilabs help spur sales at chain drug photo counters 


here was the action 
in photofinishing in 
1990? In more and 


more drug stores, combo 
stores, superstores and dis- 
count houses, it was at the 
one-hour photofinishing 
counter. 

The growth of on-site mini- 
labs was much of the reason 
for the steady rise in market 
share which drug stores and 
supermarkets have been carv- 
ing out of the photofinishing 
business. In 1989, the last 
year for which figures are 
available, drug stores pro- 
cessed 23.3 percent of the 750 
million rolls of film turned in 
by the nation’s shutterbugs, 
according to the Photo Mar- 
keting Association. That com- 
pares with 22.6 percent the 
previous year. 

In so doing, the drug store 
channel racked up 22 percent 
of the $5.34 billion spent on 
film developing, compared 
with 21.5 percent the year 
before. 

The percentage of that busi- 
ness which goes through in- 
store minilabs in drug outlets 
is still small, but it’s growing 
rapidly. In 1988, the in-store 
labs accounted for 1.2 percent 
of the nation’s processin 
business in rolls develope 
and 1.3 percent in dollars; by 
the next year, the numbers 
had shot up to 2.3 percent in 
units and 2.9 percent in dol- 
lars. Meanwhile, according to 
the PMA, the amount of pro- 
cessing business done by 
wholesaie labs for drug chains 
continues to decline. 

Clearly, the on-site proces- 


sors can spark business. Rev- 
enues for photofinishing 
were up another 8 percent 
last year for all drug chains 
combined, to well over $700 
million. 

What’s more, those figures 
are just beginning to reflect 
the recent installations of the 
latest generation of compact, 
easy-to-operate minilabs 
that many drug and food 
chains began installing in test 
stores over the past year and 
a half. Both Reveo D.S. and 
Perry Drug Stores, for in- 
stance, have put the PhotoGo 
ultra-compact minilab sys- 
tem in some stores in recent 
months. 

One store manager told 
Drug Store News the system 
drew a steady and growing 
business. 

Advances in mini-lab tech- 
nology have been dramatic in 
recent years. Whereas older 
systems required plumbing 
hookups, considerable floor 
space and a relatively well- 
trained crew to work them, 
newer minilabs available to 
drug stores and other non- 
photo retailers are self-con- 
tained, easy-to-operate and 
small enough to park almost 
anywhere in the store. Some 
are small enough to set on a 
countertop at the photo ser- 
vice area. 

These breakthroughs in 
minilab technology have 
been enough to lure a number 
of major drug and combo 
chains back into the one-hour 
business. Although Eckerd 
Drug in the U.S. and London 
Drugs in Canada remain the

algreens, meanwhile, has 
begun a long-overdue over- 
haul of the way it handles its 
photofinishing business at the

computerized scanning sys- 
tem at its photo counters to 
speed - rop-offs and re- 
turns. The system, built into 
the POS registers in the de- 
partment, scans photo orders 
and prints labels and receipts 
automatically. 

“It’s to the photo clerk what 
Intercom is to the pharma- 
cist,” said Walgreen president

over and over again.”

Cigarette sales grow in an increasingly complex market 


etail sales of cigarettes 
grew five percent over 
the past year despite 
the continued two percent 
downturn in unit consump- 
tion. Drug chain performance 
paralleled this trend, industry 
sources told Drug S tore News. 

Careful attention to assort- 
ments and convenient dis- 
plays lifted cigarette sales, as 
did pass-alongs of manufac- 
turer price increases and tax- 
es. Vendor price hikes on full- 
priced brands totaled $5 per 
1,000 cigarettes in 1990, and 
varied within the price-value 
segment, said John Maxwell, 
analyst at Wheat First Securi- 
ties. 

In 1991’s first quarter, a 
hike of five cents on the feder- 
al excise tax kicked in, and a 
new hike on price-value 
smokes was seen. Two more 
price increases will come in 
1991 as the vendors continue 
to cover their costs of busi- 
ness, said Maxwell. 

The average national price 
for a pack of cigarettes by 
year-end 1990 was $1.60, in- 
cluding 71 cents of taxes. 

Retailers had to pass the 
taxes and price hikes through 
to maintain decent margins, 


and in many cases conform to 
state minimum gross margin 
laws.

percent, single packs’ 20 per-

the all-time high in 1989 of $1.7 
billion, to $1.665 billon, re- 
ported the Sunglass Associa- 
tion of America. Pairs sold in 
drug stores dropped from 18 
million to 17 million.

Safeway stock sale will 
fund capital expenditures 


OAKLAND, Calif. — 
Safeway has filed with the Se- 
curities and Exchange Com- 
mission a proposed public of- 
fering of 10 million common 
shares. Proceeds will help 
fund a five-year capital budget 
that doubles spending of the 
previous five years. 

Safeway did not say how 
much it hoped to raise, but 
the stock was trading at $17 
per share at the time of the 
announcement in mid-March, 
and it closed at $21.50 on 
April 12. 

The shares would repre- 
sent about 8 percent of out- 
standing shares on a fully di- 
luted basis. Shares will be 
newly issued, and existing 
stockholders—including con- 
trolling owner Kohl erg, 
Kravis Roberts & Co.—will 
not be selling any of their 
shares, Safeway said in its 


> registration statement. 


wo of the eight million 
shares are being sold abroad, 


» with the sale making 89.3 mil- 
» lion shares outstanding. 


KKR, which purchased the 
ee. iant and took it 

» private in a LBO in 1986, will 

' own about 73 percent of out- 
standing common stock 
through two partnerships af- 
ter the offering. Before the 


sale, it owned 82 percent of 
shares. Other investors, 
mostly management, own 2.7 
million shares and options to 
purchase 6.8 million. 

Safeway is funding a $3.2 
billion five-year capital spend- 
ing budget. About half the 
amount will be for new and re- 

lacement stores, 25 percent 
or remodeling and mainte- 
nance, and the rest for support 
operations such as distribu- 
tion. The efforts will be in ex- 
isting markets, which include 
Western and Northwestern 
states and markets in western 
Canadian provinces. 

Having restructured exten- 
Sively since 1986—mostl 
through the sales of $2.4 bil. 
lion worth of assets and facili- 
ties—Safeway raised $120 
million in April, 1990 with the 
sale of 11.5 million common 
shares. 

Total debt has dropped 
from $5.8 billion at the time of 
the LBO to $3.1 billion in 1990. 
In the prospectus, Safeway 
said that sales have grown 
from $13.6 billion in 1988 to 
$14.9 billion in 1990. Operat- 
ing profits went from $398.9 
million in 1988 to $535.3 mil- 
lion in 1990, and from 2.9 per- 
cent of sales to 3.6 percent of 
sales in those years.

average of 13 percent a year.

of $83.5 million. It reduced debt 
by $100 million, preferred stock 
by $52 million, and interest and 
dividend expenses were 
slashed by $14 million total.

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, April 22, 1991 


NIFEDIPINE CAPSULES, USP 


Brief Summary 


INDICATIONS AND USAGE: 
|. Vasospastic Angina: Nifedipine is indicated for the management of va- 
sospastic angina confirmed by any of the following criteria: 1) classical pat- 
tern of angina at rest accompanied by ST segment elevation, 2) angina or 
coronary artery spasm provoked by ergonovine, or 3) angiographically demon- 
strated coronary artery spasm. In those patients who have had angiography, 
the presence of significant fixed obstructive disease is not incompatible with 
the diagnosis of vasospastic angina, provided that the above criteria are sat- 
isfied. Nifedipine may also be used where the clinical presentation suggests a 
possible vasospastic component but where vasospasm has not been con- 
firmed, e.g., where pain has a variable threshold on exertion or in unstable angina 
where electrocardiographic findings ave compatible with intermittent vasospasm, 
or when angina is refractory to nitrates and/or adequate doses of beta block- 
ers. 
ll. Chronic Stable Angina (Classical Effort-Associated Angina): 
Nifedipine is indicated for the management of chronic stable e7gina (effort-as- 
sociated 2ngina) without evidence of vasospasm in patients who remain symp- 
tomatic despite adequate doses of beta blockers and/or organic nitrates or who 
cannot tolerate those agents. 

in chronic stable angina (effort-associated angina) nifedipine has been 
effective in controlled trials of up to eight weeks duration in reducing angina 
frequency and increasing exercise tolerance, but confirmation of sustained ef- 
fectiveness and evaluation of long term safety in these patients are incomplete. 

Controlled studies in small numbers of patients suggest concomitant use of 
nifedipine and beta blocking agents may be beneficial in patients with chronic 
stable angina, but available information is not sufficient to predict with confi- 
dence the effects of concurrent treatment, especially in patients with compro- 
mised left ventricular function or cardiac conduction abnormalities. When 
introducing such concomitant therapy, care must be taken to mofiitor blood pres- 
sure closely since severe hypotension can occur fr«-n the combined effects of 
the drugs. (See WARNINGS. ) 


CONTRAINDICATIONS: 
Known hypersensitivity reaction to nifedipine 


WARNINGS: 
Excessive Hypotension: Although in most patients, the hypotensive ef- 
fect of nifedipine is modest and well tolerated, occasional patients have had 
excessive and poorly tolerated hypotension. These responses have usually oc- 
curred during initial titration or at the time of subsequent upward dosage ad- 
justment, and may be more likely in patients on concomitant beta blockers. 
Severe hypotension and/or increased fluid volume requirements have been re- 
ported in patients receiving nifedipine together with a beta blocking agent who 
underwent coronary artery bypass surgery using high dose fentany! anesthesia. 
The interaction with high dose fentanyl appears to be due to the combination of 
nifedipine and a beta blocker, but the possibility that it may occur with nifedip- 
ine alone, with low doses of fentanyl, in other surgical procedures, or with other 
narcotic analgesics cannot be ruled out. in nifedipine treated patients where 
surgery using high dose-fentany! anesthesia is contemplated, the physician 
should be aware of these potential problems and, if the patient's condition per- 
mits, sufficient time (at least 36 hours) should be allowed for nifedipine to be 
washed out of the body prior to surgery. 
Increased Angina and/or Myocardial Infarction: Rarely, patients, par- 
ticularly those who have severe obstructive coronary artery disease, have de- 
veloped well documented increased frequency, duration and/or severity of 
angina or acute myocardial infarction on starting nifedipine or at the time of 
dosage increase. The mechanism of this effect is not established. 
Beta Blocker Withdrawal: Patients recently witfidrawn from beta blockers 
may develop a withdrawal syndrome with increased angina, probably related to 
increased sensitivity to catecholamines. Initiation of nifedipine treatment will not 
prevent this occurrence and might be expected to exacerbate it by provoking re- 
flex catecholamine release. There have been occasional reports of increased 
angina in a setting of beta blocker withdrawal and nifedipine initiation. It is im- 
portant to taper beta blockers if possible, rather than stopping them abruptly be- 
fore beginning nifedipine. 
Congestive Heart Failure: Rarely, patients, usually receiving a beta 
blocker, have developed heart failure after beginning nifedipine. Patients with 
tight aortic stenosis may be at greater risk for such an event, as the unloading 
effect of nifedipine would be expected to be of less benefit to these patients, 
owing to their fixed impedance to flow across the aortic valve. 


PRECAUTIONS: 
General: Hypotension: Because nifedipine decreases periphera} vascu- 
lar resistance, careful monitoring of blood pressure during the initial adminis- 
tration and titration of nifedipine is suggested. Close observation is especially 
recommended for patients already taking medications that are known to lower 
blood pressure. (See WARNINGS.) 
Peripheral Edema: Mild to moderate peripheral edema, typically associ- 
ated with arterial vasodilation and not due to left ventricular dysfunction, oc- 
curs in about one in ten patients treated with nifedipine. This edema occurs 
primarily in the lower extremities and usually responds to diuretic therapy. 
With patients whose angina is complicated by congestive heart failure, care 
should be taken to differentiate this peripheral edema from the effects of in- 
creasing left ventricular dysfunction. 
Laboratory Tests: Rare, usually transient, but occasionally significant el- 
evations of enzymes such as alkaline phosphatase, CPK, LDH, SGOT and SGPT 
have been noted. The relationship to nifedipine therapy is uncertain in most 
cases, but probable in some. These laboratory abnormalities have rarely been 
associated with clinical symptoms, however, cholestasis with or without jaun- 
dice has been reported. Rare instances of allergic hepatitis have been reported. 

Nifedipine, like other calcium channel blockers, decreases platelet aggrega- 
tion in vitro. Limited clinical studies have demonstrated a moderate but statis- 
tically significant decrease in platelet aggregation and increase in bleeding 
time in some nifedipine patients. This is thought to be a function of inhibition 
of calcium transport across the platelet membrane. No Clinical significance for 
these findings has been demonstrated. 

Positive direct Coombs test with/without hemolytic anemia has been reported. 

Although nifedipine has been used safely in patients with renal dysfunction 
and has been reported to exert a beneficial effect in certain cases, rare, reversible 
elevations in BUN and serum creatinine have been reported in patients with pre- 
existing chronic renal insufficiency. The relationship to nifedipine therapy is un- 
certain in most cases but probable in some. 
Drug Interactions: Beta-adrenergic blocking agents: {See INDICATIONS 
and WARNINGS.) Experience in over 1400 patients in a non-comparative clin- 
ical trial has shown that concomitant administration of nifedipine and beta-block- 
ing agents is usually well tolerated, but there have been occasional literature 
reports suggesting that the combination may increase the likelinood of con- 
gestive heart failure, severe hypotension or exacerbation of angina. 
Long acting nitrates: Nifedipine may be safely co-administered with nitrates, 
but there have been no controlled studies to evaluate the antianginal effective- 


gestive heart failure during which digoxin blood levels were not measured, dig- 
italis toxicity was not observed. Since there have been isolated reports of pa- 
tients with elevated digoxin levels, it is recommended that digoxin levels De 
monitored when initiating, adjusting, and discontinuing nifedipine to avoid pos - 
sible over- or under-digitalization. 

Coumarin anticoagulants: There have been rare reports of increased pro- 
thrombin time in patients taking coumarin anticoagulants to whom nifedipine 
was administered. However, the relationship to nifedipine therapy is uncertain. 
Cimetidine: A study in six healthy volunteers has shown a significant increase 
in peak nifedipine plasma levels (80%) and area-under-the-curve (74%) after 
a one week course of cimetidine at 1000 mg per day and nifedipine at 40 mg 
per day. Ranitidine produced smaller, non-significant increases. The effect may 
be mediated by the known inhibition of cimetidine on hepatic cytochrome P- 
450, the enzyme system probably responsible for the first-pass metabolism of 
nifedipine. If nifedipine therapy is initiated in a patient currently receiving cime- 
tidine, cautious titration is advised. 

Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility: Nifedipine 
was administered orally to rats for two years and was not shown to be car- 
cinogenic. When given to rats prior to mating, nifedipine caused reduced fer- 
tility at a dose approximately 30 times the maximum recommended human dose. 
In vivo mutagenicity studies were negative. : 
Pregnancy: Pregnaricy Category C. Nifedipine has been shown to be terato- 
genic in rats when given in doses 30 times the maximum recommended hurnan 
dose. Nifedipine was embryotoxic (increased fetal resorptions, decreased fetal 
weight, increased stunted forms, increased fetal deaths, decreased neonatal 
survival) in rats, mice and rabbits at doses of from 3 to 10 times the maximum 
recommended human dose. In pregnant monkeys, doses 2/3 and twice the max- 
imum recommended human dose resulted in small placentas and underdevel- 
oped chorionic villi. In rats doses three times maximum human dose and higher 
caused prolongation of pregnancy. There are no adequate and well controlled 
studies in pregnant women. Nifedipine should be used during pregnancy only 
if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 


ADVERSE REACTIONS: 

In multiple-dose U.S. and foreign controlled studies in which adverse reactions 
were reported spontaneously, adverse effects were frequent but generally not 
serious and rarely required discontinuation of therapy or dosage adjustment. 
Most were expected consequences of the vasodilator effects of nifedipine.

Several of these side effects appear to be dose related. Peripheral edema oc- 
curred in about one in 25 patients at doses less than 60 mg per day and in 
about one patient in eight at 120 mg per day or more. Transient hypotension, 
generally of mild to moderate severity and seldom requiring discontinuation of 
therapy, occurred in one of 50 patients at less than 60 mg per day and in one 
of 20 patients at 120 mg per day or more. Very rarely, introduction of nifedip- 
ine therapy was associated with an increase in anginal pain, possibly due to 
associated hypotension.

tients. “We have a list of people with dia- 
betes by zip code and we mail promotional 
material to them,” said the buyer. “We 
also send a letter to physicians explaining 
that this is a product we have been target- 
ing to their patients.” 

ost retailers are carrying an average 
of three meters and are concentrating on 
offering the ones with the lowest price 
tags. Said Perry’s Chochol: “We’ve dis- 
continued the higher priced meters. Man- 
ufacturers are restructuring the high end 
units so that they are beginning to sell in 
the $90 range rather than at $120.” LJ 


Faster pregnancy testing kits outsell the rest 


Pregnancy testing kits are being driv- 
en by products which have become easier 
to use. Kits which show results in three to 
five minutes are outselling kits with a 
longer wait time. In fact, Warner Lam- 
bert has discontinued its EPT test with a 
30-minute waiting time in order to con- 
centrate on its four-minute product. 

Stephen Bishop, buyer at Bill’s, esti- 
mates that sales of pregnancy test kits 
have doubled there over the past year. 
“Products that are easier to use plus ag- 
- eee promotion by manufacturers 1s 

riving the category for us,” he said. The 
problem for retailers is that with so many 
products on the market, how can the 
stores stock them all? 

“No item has more than one ace said 
Bishop, “but we stock at different degrees 
of depth. Our typical store carries five or 
six different brands. That’s about double 
what we carried two years ago.” 


Broad assortment 


Page Ilderton, buyer at Kerr Drug, is 
currently carrying 10 different brands in 
the family planning section. “We carry 
practically everything on the market,” 
said Betty eg buyer at Dis- 
count Drug Mart. itehall’s Clearblue 


40 


Easy and Carter Wallace’s First Re- 
sponse products were cited by many re- 
tailers as good performers. Both have a 
wait-time under four minutes. 

Thayer’s Davis said her chain sells 100 
units of First Response a month. Clear- 
blue Easy’s single and double both have 
sales of 56 units a month at the chain. By 
comparison, Davis said that even those 
tests which take 30 minutes to get a result 
are selling at 35 units a month. Those 
sales mag be contingent on price since the 
shorter time kits can cost twice as much. 
“Sales of the 30-minute products have 
really lessened,” said Kerr’s Ilderton. 

Retailers say that it’s not just the ease 
of use that’s driving the category; promo- 
tion by the manufacturer also et a 
large part in sales. Said Terry Lehman of 
Peoples: “This category is supported by 
the vendors that support their products 
the most.” 

Those companies which are putting 
their money into keeping their prices low 
but allowing retailers to make margins 
are selling well.” Advertising makes a big 
impact, said Lehman. Manufacturers 
agree. “EPT may be a market leader be- 
cause of advertising,” said Tom McMil- 
lian, product manager for the Warner 


Lambert product. “These kits are not an 
impulse item.” 


Ovulation kits flat 


Nor are ovulation testing kits, which 
seem to be faring the least well in this cate- 
gory. Buyers cite the expense and the time 
involved in using the product as two possi- 
ves reasons. Still, they are carrying the 

its. 

“Ovulation kits are still moving slow- 
ly,” said Lehman. “There’s a lack of ad- 
vertising in this category and they are ex- 
tremely expensive, generally in the $24 to 
$34 range.” Ilderson said Kerr carries 
three brands of ovulation kits, although 
sales are slow. Thayer’s Jodi Davis is 
moving 30 First Response ovulation kits a 
month despite their $25 price tag. 

Bishop said Becton-Dickinson’s Q Test 
is the fastest seller at Bill’s. “The product 
is easy to use, although it’s certainly not 
the least expensive,” he said. 

Retailers are placing both pregnancy 
and ovulation test kits out where custom- 
ers have easy access to the products de- 
spite the risk of theft. “If they can reach 
it, they can steal it,” said Bishop. “But if 
we put the kits in the pharmacy, we 
would definitely lose sales.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 6, 1991 i 


In 1987, when Ron Ziegler was taking over the reins 
at NACDS, the association was strong and highly re- 
garded. Viewed from the pressbox, NACDS’ steady 
game seemed suited to the tasks at hand. Why tinker 
too much, we thought, with a winning organization. 
Of course, as we now know, change was not only nec- 
essary but inevitable. And in fact in the past three 
years the changes have crackled like fireworks on 
North Lee Street close to 
the banks of the Potomac. 


Under Ziegler, 
NACDS is now at a peak 
in influence and as a result 
is serving its members 
better than ever. 

Today, as the associa- 
tion’s annual meeting gets 


IN THE MARKET 
BRUCE BUCKLEY 


under way, membership, 
income and member ser- 
vices are at record levels, 
and the association’s voice in government and phar- 
macy affairs has gained in depth and resonance. Here 
are a few particulars: 

© Membership: Reflecting consolidation in the in- 
dustry it represents, NACDS’ chain drug member- 
ship has actually fallen since 1987. Today it stands at 
155 chains, whereas three years before it was 170. 
However, those 155 chains represent 24,000 stores, 
compared to 20,000 in 1987. Offsetting the decline in 
chain membership has been a 50% increase in asso- 
ciate members, to 900 from 600. Membership has also 
expanded among mass merchandisers and supermar- 


OPINION 


NACDS has made great strides in 3 years 


kets, which share a common interest in pharmacy. In 
targeting new growth, NACDS has even moved into 
the international arena. © Budget: From 1987 to 1990 
total income almost doubled, to $11.4 million from $6.3 
million, while expenditures increased to $10.6 million 
from $6.0 million three years earlier. Income after ex- 
penditures also soared — to $814,391 from $351,988. 

© Staff: In three years, the staff grew to 43 from 28. 
More important than the numbers are the areas in 
which activity has accelerated. In government affairs, 
for example, there has been expansion at both federal 
and state levels. State government affairs eis 
are now assigned to every region of the country. In the 
pharmacy and health affairs area staff membership is 
up, with more registered pharmacists handling key 
pharmacy practice and education issues. 

@ Services: A library has been added where mem- 
bers, as well as others interested in the chain drug in- 
dustry and its issues,can track down information. An 
electronic bulletin board offers news and research. 
New publications have been added, including The 
PIPEline, the Source Book and — soon to make its ap- 
pearance — Chain Drug Store Pharmacist. 

© Meetings: In addition to the strong growth of the 
traditional triad — the Annual, Marketplace and 
Pharmaceutical — NACDS has added conferences on 
Distribution/Logistics; Human Resources/Loss Pre- 
vention; and Public Conference. 

If three years has brought such great strides, one 
can only speculate about the remainder of this decade. 
The changes are sure to be as cracklingly dramatic as 
those of the first three years. 


Chain and independent drug store operators strug- 
gling to survive the economic downturn may soon find 
their job even tougher as a result of developments 
here in Washington. 

Organized labor leaders are politicking hard on 
Capitol Hill these days, and that could spell trouble for 
many companies—union and non-union alike. Indeed, 
if some members of Congress have their way, payroll 
costs in drug retailing and 
other labor intensive in- 


dustries may soon begin 
spiraling upward. 

Union lobbyists are al- 
ready pressing for a fresh 
hike in the national mini- 
mum wage, which was 
just raised to $4.25 earlier 
this spring. One scheme 
under discussion would 
boost the pay floor 35 per- 
cent to $5.75 and wipe out the current subminimum 
“training wage” in the process. 

Worse yet, some Congressional supporters of such 
legislation are also pressuring for a minumum wage 
“indexing” requirement that would mandate automat- 
ic annual increases in the hourly rate in step with 
changes in the cost of living. 

Many of these same lawmakers are also spearhead- 
ing a drive for an even more controversial “striker 
bill” designed to give organized labor activists the up- 
per hand in wage negotiations with industry. This pro- 
posal would eliminate the right of businesses to hire 
permanent replacements for striking workers. 

Although the advocates of these measures maintain 
that they are necessary to improve the economic sta- 
tus of the nation’s workforce, there’s a good deal of 
doubt about that. 

The consensus among economic researchers is that 
increases in the minimum rate eliminate em- 
ployment opportunities and do more harm than good 
for low-income workers. An indexing provision would 
aggravate those problems and create a new engine of 


» WASHINGTON 
\ PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


Wage proposal could be to labor’s advantage 


inflation, to boot. 

As for the striker bill, the last thing our fragile econ- 
omy needs is a shift in the labor law ground rules that 
would encourage crippling work stoppages. 

If these questionable proposals are implemen- 
ted, the impact would hit home at the very time that 
drug stores and other employers are beginning the 
slow climb back from the recession. 

Legislation that stalls the recovery and cripples in- 
dustry’s ability to create jobs won’t help drug stores or 
their employees. 


Letters to the editor 


Dear Editor: 

In the Dec. 10 issue of Drug Store News, results 
from the Leo J. Shapiro study were published, stating 
that in a user survey, Edge ranked 4th in brand pref- 
erence for shave cremes behind Colgate, Gillette and 
Barbasol. These findings are absolutely incorrect and 
misleading according to all other consumer and inde- 
pendent sales tracking data purchased by SC Johnson 
Wax from leading research suppliers. Consistently, 
Edge Shave Gel is positioned as the No. 1 brand in the 
shave prep category. 

In fact, according to the leading sales tracking com- 
pany, Edge Shave Gel brand is No. 1 in both dollar and 
unit sales in all classes of trade, including drug. Edge 
leads the next brand by over 20 share points in dollar 
sales. Additionally, consumer data shows Edge is rat- 
ed No. 1 by its respective users on key shave perfor- 
mance measures, like getting a close shave without ir- 
ritation. 

The above claims are substantiated by a variety of 
syndicated data. This data gives us backing to make 
and defend our No. | position claims to the trade and 
to our consumers. 


Barbara H. Jorgensen 
Public Relations Manager 
U.S. Consumer Products 
S.C. Johnson & Son, inc.

to $34.1 million from $30.3 mil- 
lion. Fully diluted earnings 
per share were 94 cents for the 
six months, versus 86 cents for 
the year-earlier period. 

For the second quarter, net 
sales gained 7 percent, to 
$1.16 billion from $1.09 billion 


for the comparable quarter 
last year. Net earnings were 
$17.1 million, or 47 cents per 
share, compared with $15.4 
million, or 43 cents per share. 

“Bergen Brunswig contin- 
ued its sales growth perfor- 
mance despite less-than-antici- 
pated results in January 
attributed in part to this year’s 
less severe flu season,” com- 
mented president and ceo Rob- 
ert E. Martini. “A higher gross 
profit margin rate, effective op- 
erating expense controls and a 
program of continuing consoli- 
dation into regional distribu- 
tion centers contributed to the 
16 percent improvement in op- 
erating earnings.” 


Arbor declares 3-for-2 stock split 


TROY, Mich. — Arbor 
Ft board of directors on 
April 2 declared a 3-for-2 stock 
split, the second 3-for-2 split in 
two years. It’s stock closed on 
the NASDAQ exchange at 
264% April 17, with a price/ 
earnings ratio of 22. 

The new shares in the form 


will be distributed May 7 to 
shareholders of record as of 
April 17. 

“We are pleased to increase 
the number of shares out- 
standing and provide better li- 
ea of Arbor stock,” said 

ugene Applebaum, chair- 
man, president and chief exec- 
utive officer.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 6, 1991 


ANNUAL REPORT PART II 


Drug industry sales climb in trying times 


elcome to Part II of 
Drug Store News’ 
annual coverage of 
the $67.6 billion drug store in- 
dustry. 

In Part I, the focus was on 
the performance of the core 
categories that form the bed- 
rock on which drug stores 
have built their businesses. 

The following pages chroni- 
cle significant events and ini- 
tiatives at some of the major 
drug chains that helped them 
grow 9 percent overall during 
1990, to become a $43.2 billion 
force in the industry. 

Faced with an uncertain 
economic climate, increased 
competition from combos and 
discount department stores 
and the changing needs of an 
ever busier and more diverse 
population, the drug chains 
profiled here have pursued 
their own set of priorities to 
meet the challenge. 

The themes of convenience 
and service—the two words 
that will be most important for 
drug stores in the 1990s—run 
as a common thread through 
all the chains’ stories this 
year. A corollary to these twin 
axioms is employee motiva- 
tion and training, which more 
and more drug chain leaders 
are seeing as key to translat- 
ing the theory of service into 
practice. 

Many chains forged ahead 
with technological advances, 
perceiving the necessity for a 
sophisticated information sys- 
tem to help them respond 
quickly te problems and op- 
portunities, better anticipate 
trends and cut overhead costs. 

Others developed pro- 
grams to build up customer

niches, such as senior citizen 
days, special mailings to new 
mothers and circulars aimed 
at teenage shoppers. Several 
chains created service cen- 
ters to offer an array of extra 
services, including faxing, 
package mailing, money or- 
ders and the like in a promi- 
nent central in-store loca- 
tion. 

The trend toward longer 
store hours, and more 24-hour 
stores, continued, in response 
to the needs of an increasing 
number of families where 
more than one adult works full 
time. 

Several chains developed 
new store layouts that f - 
tured brighter lighting, wider 
aisles, clear and simple over- 
head and shelf signage, logical 
adjacencies and anchor posi- 
tions for some of their strong- 
est departments: pharmacy, 
cosmetics, photo, HBA. 

Chains lavished special at- 
tention on pharmacies—the 
heart of their business—with 
upgraded computer systems, 
distinct niches for consulta- 
tion and an increased empha- 
sis on pharmacist-patient 
communication. 

And several chains seized 
the chance to penetrate new 
markets and strengthen their 
position in existing ones 
through acquisitional ay al 
tunities that resulted from 
other chains’ troubles: Rev- 
co’s divestiture of 712 stores, 
the sale of Peoples Drug 
Stores, the Chapter 11 filings 
by Fantle’s and SupeRx and 

edicare-Glaser were some of 
the main events that changed 
the drug chain mosaic during 
the year. 


19 


ANNUAL REPORT PART II 


Chain leaders focus on goals for the ‘90s 


Charies R. 
Walgreen Iil, 
Chairman, ceo, 
Walgreen 


executive comments 


he fundamentals of our 
industry are good. We 
have a strong consumer 
franchise, as shown by the in- 
dustry’s positive year in 1990, 
and the performance of the 
chains so far this year. Chains 
now represent 35 percent of 
the drug stores in the nation 
and fill almost 40 percent of 
the prescriptions in the U.S. 
e’re going to continue to 
see strong demand for both 
prescription and over-the- 
counter drugs in the coming 
years.. That doesn’t call for 
complacency for chains, how- 
ever, especially with the 


toughening of competition and 
the pressures on margins. 
The challenge will be to 
maintain and even improve our 
health care image, upgrade our 
service levels, and at the same 
time lower our cost structure. 
To help achieve these objec- 
tives, Walgreens is investing 
nearly $130 million in retail 


technology over three years— 
roughly $80,000 per store. 

We expect to have all Wal- 
greens drug stores on scan- 


ning by the end of the year. 
We completed satellite link- 
age for virtually all stores and 
facilities in fiscal 1990, and are 


enjoying the benefits of im- 
proved response time in the 
pharmacy, as well as expand- 
ed transmission capacity. 

We’re focused on making all 
our stores more efficient and at- 
tractive for both shoppers and 
employees. New designs are 
being tested to update the im- 
age and “customer friendli- 
ness” of the entire store, includ- 
ing cosmetics, the photo 
department and, importantly, 
the pharmacy. 

Of greatest importance to 
any business, of course, is its 
people. We will continue to re- 
cruit the best we can find. 


Boake A. Sells, 
Chairman, ceo, 
Revco 


major challenge facing 

us all is the matter of 

trust. The trust of our 
customers, of those with 
whom we're allied, such as the 
medical profession, and of the 
people who work for us. 

People participate—join in 
the process—to the extent they 
trust the organization. As dru 
store operators we need to dif- 
ferentiate our stores from oth- 
er mass marketers, and to 
make the most of markets 
which are being saturated with 
competitive outlets. We ask a 
lot of people, both inside and 
outside the organization. 

Trust is an element in shop- 
ping a drug store that it is not 
for any other kind of retailer. In 
recent weeks we’ve seen a OTC 
product-tampering scare. Over 


many months we’ve had to ad- 
dress concerns about the pro- 
duction of generic drugs. Ongo- 
ing are issues such as the cross- 
overs of prescription to OTC 
drugs, environmentalism, or 
the efforts to manage care by 
third-party administrators. 

We all have the challenge of 
making the public and our own 
people see that the product we 
sell is not just medication, but 
counsel, information, and ser- 
vice as well. 

The retail pharmacy is dis- 
tinctive by the counsel its phar- 
macists provide. We also must 
communicate to the medical 
profession that the prescriber 
and the pharmacy are a team. 
The pharmacist does not re- 
place the physician. However, 
in this busy, product-filled 


world, counsel by the pharma- 
cist is part of the therapy. 

A customer wrote to us 
about a pharmacist who provid- 
ed information about a drug be- 
ing dispensed, saying “never 
before was I given or told any- 
thing” like this information. 

“Never before” was this per- 
son treated as a participant in 
her own medication therapy. 

Many of us have been busy 
implementing new manage- 
ment information systems in 
our chains, recognizing this as a 
big need in our industry. Such 
systems deliver high-quality 
information, necessary for 
planning and cost-efficiency. 

But there’s more: informa- 
tion invites participation. And 
participation helps lay the 
groundwork of trust. 


Tim McAlear, 
President, ceo, 
Pay Less 


he turbulent economic 

climate and shifting de- 

mographics, along with 
the continued financial woes, 
mergers, acquisitions and con- 
solidation of stores in our in- 
dustry make this a challenging 
decade. 

We are battling increased 
competition from supermar- 
ket combos and discount de- 
partment stores, as they ex- 
pand their markets and add 
pharmacies. In view of this, 
we are making our pharmacy 
areas and pharmacists more 
accessible to our customers. 
We also opened a mail-order 
pharmacy—Pay Less Ex- 
press—this past year in Wil- 
sonville, Oregon. 

Our expansion plans for 
1991 are aggressive; we antici- 
pate opening 38 new stores 


this year. Most of our store 
growth will be in California, in 
order to obtain a stronghold in 
this explosive market. The 
award-winning 45 degree for- 
mat is used in all new stores 
and our rate of converting ex- 
isting stores to this layout is 
moving at a rapid pace. This 
store layout allows us to high- 
light and expand the high traf- 
fic power departments, pro- 
vide critical adjacencies and 
non-traditional departments. 
As margins tighten we are 
cutting down inventory levels 
in our stores, but still main- 
taining an in-stock position. 
Through POS scanning data 
and continued pursuit of more 
advanced technology, we can 
reduce overhead costs with- 
out compromising selection. 
As a specialty retailer, we fo- 


cus on our drug store strengths 
and pass this on to the customer 
through personalized service, 
convenient locations, quality 
products, extensive assort- 
ments of key merchandise and 
fair prices. We are constantly 
upgrading our selections and 
fine-tuning the merchandise 
mix of core categories. 

Consumer preferences are 
in a constant state of flux and 
we are actively pursuing them 
with “chunk merchandising” 
a and micro-market- 
ing. Although consumers are 
spending less and are more 
cautious when making pur- 
chasing decisions, the basics 
provided by a drug chain will 
still be in demand. However, 
pricing and service will be crit- 
ical to customer retention and 
repeat business. 


Eugene 
Applebaum, 
Chairman, ceo, 
Arbor 


oday, with the expand- 
ing lexicon of buzz- 
words, “corporate cul- 
ture” describes how an 
organization manages its op- 
portunities and challenges. 
Although Arbor Drugs is 
still a relatively young compa- 
ny, our corporate culture is 
firmly established, both in 
concept and in execution. We 
are a stores-driven oneration. 
At Arbor, every area in our 
company is here to support 
our stores’ ability to leer 


the best overall experience to 
our customers. 

It is no coincidence that ev- 
ery one of our district manag- 
ers was promoted through 
the ranks. Each one of these 
role models first served as a 
store manager at Arbor. This 
career path is an important 
component of our dedication 
to superior customer service. 
To understand the pulse of 
Arbor, one needs to have 
first-hand experience as a 
member of cur store team. 


No matter how much larger 
and more successful our com- 
pany becomes, the funda- 
mental premise of Arbor 
Drugs will not change: we 
will continue to exceed the 
expectations of customers 
365 days a year. 

That’s why we remain fo- 
cused on our customer ser- 
vice. That is why implemen- 
tation, the cornerstone of our 
corporate culture, is our stra- 
tegic advantage for the 
1990s.

Revco D.S.’s plans, an- 
nounced early last year, to sell 
712 drug stores triggered seis- 
mic acquisitional activity that 
changed the drug chain land- 
scape during 1990 even more 
than the selloff of Peoples’ 
Midwestern division did the 
year before.

new chain, RDS, had emerged 
as a major player in the South- 
west, and several chains had 
strengthened their positions 
in various markets around the 
country.

Perry’s market share in De-

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 6, 1991 


ANNUAL REPORT PART II 


store formats 


_ Chain drug designers unleash 
slew of creative new formats 


Creativity is alive and well 
in the back offices and sales 
aisles of North America’s drug 
chains. From the largest to 
the smallest, drug chains con- 
tinue to tinker aggressively 
with their store designs and 
retrofit new ideas into older 
stores at a furious clip. 

They have plenty of compe- 
tition. Food/drug combo pow- 
erhouses like Kroger, Ameri- 
can Stores, Vons, Smith’s 
Food and Drug, Randall’s, 
Tom Thumb/Page and H.E.B. 
have all unveiled radically dif- 
ferent prototypes since the 
mid-to-late 1980s, luring cus- 
tomers with seductive store 
designs that offer a vast array 
of products and services. The 
food chains are using glitzy de- 
cor, roomy aisles and dramatic 
mid-floor service islands to en- 
hance their one-stop appeal. 
It’s a powerful weapon. 

Discount chains like Kmart, 
Wal-Mart and Target have 
also gone the redesign route. 
Kmart, in particular, has be- 
gun a rapid rollout of its dra- 
matically redesigned format, 
which gives pharmacy and 
HBA stronger play and visi- 
bility at the front of the stores. 
To counter those efforts and 
maintain their competitive 
edge, dozens of drug chains 
are rolling out major and mi- 
nor redesigns of their own. In 
general, the state-of-the-art 
thinking in drug store design 
includes a much sharper focus 
on the core departments: 
pharmacy, cosmetics/fra- 
grances, greeting cards, pho- 
tofinishing and toiletries. Ser- 
vice islands, bolder signing, 
alcoves and spotlighting are 
often used to highlight depart- 
ments. 

Here’s some of the past 
year’s highlights: 

@ Genovese Drug Stores 
has opened what it calls a 
“Greenhouse Store” on Long 
Island to “grow” new ideas. 
Among them: a bar-code 
price-check kiosk for custom- 
ers; a prominent one-hour 
‘her lab and service peninsu- 

; mirrored and accent light- 
ing; snappy, simple depart- 
mental signing; sleek 
permanent aisle modules for 
special displays. 

© CVS’ Peoples division has 
begun developing a new for- 
mat to incorporate CVS mer- 
chandising techniques and de- 
cor, with lower fixtures, 
carpeting, customer-accessi- 
ble pharmacies, and a some- 
what narrower merchandise 
mix. Some 100 stores will get 


the facelift this year. 

@ Bill Edwards and compa- 
ny have completely rede- 
signed A.L. Price since its ac- 
quisition last year, with a far 
more dense and much broader 
mix. 

@ Super D Drugs in Mem- 
phis unveiled a new format in 
two stores, with front-of-store 
cosmetics counters; mini-food 


departments; and fewer pro- 
motional items. 

@ Snyder Drug Stores in 
Minneapolis rolled out its new 
prototype Jan. 13. Highlights 
include “Yes Express,” a new 
service center with shipping, 
faxing, ticketing, customized 
printing and other services; 
service cosmetics island which

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 6, 1991 


ANNUAL REPORT PART II 


technology 


Computer breakthroughs helping 


chains mind their own business 


rug chains are gaining 
more control over 
their businesses, 
thanks to new technology and 
computer-based systems. 

POS, pharmacy and direct 
store delivery systems, for ex- 
ample, give chains central con- 
trol over pricing and other func- 
tions. And headquarters can 
respond fast to local variables. 

tores reference centrally- 
maintained files for current 
data, whether it be on the 
price of a bottle of shampoo, or 
on the eligibility of a patient in 
a third party prescription 
plan. Headquarters receives 
timely windows on store activ- 
ity, particularly if files are be- 
ing updated in a “real time” 
mode. 

As chains obtain clearer, 
more frequent views of what is 
happening in their stores, 
they are better positioned to 
take the right approach with 
their customers. 

Revco and Thrift were the 
major chains reaching 100 per- 
cent rollout of advanced bos 
systems with scanning. Pay 
Less has mostly completed its 
installation. Kinney, Discount 
ee Mart and Dot Drugs vir- 
tually reached 100 percent. 

On a large scale, Tiwecne 
surged forward, with its 


equipping of 51 Fao of 
V 


from zero to 15 percent. 

Yet, not all chains are com- 
mited to scanning, though 
they may be using advanced 
systems and capturing price/i- 
tem sales by manual key-in of 
a product code. Eckerd stayed 
with a small group of scanning 
stores. Rite Aid didn’t in- 
crease scanning. Longs still 
has a small group. Genovese 
and Big B didn’t strongly in- 
crease tests. 

However, Revco foresaw 
thousands of dollars in savings 
per store per year as all 1,126 
stores were installed. Tai- 
lored software features al- 
lowed automatic discount de- 
ductions for Revco programs. 
Executives anticipated im- 
proved merchandising from 
the close sales tracking and 
fast reception of results. Buy- 
ers got monthly sales reports 
compared to the quarterly re- 
ports before. 

Checkout productivity isn’t 
as high on drug chains’ want 
lists as at groceries. The ex- 


ception: deep discounters, 


which do ery-sized_ vol- 
umes. F&M Distributors cost- 
justified its NCR POS system 
on labor savings from check- 
out productivity. 
Chains must ensure the 
rices in their electronic price 
iles at checkout match those 


market setting where shelf 
audit procedures aren’t care- 
fully observed, a high percent- 
age of prices don’t match, shelf 
audit system industry sources 
maintain. Correct procedure 
can reduce errors to 2/10 of 
one percent. 

Shelf audit systems by 
Telxon and Symbol MSI de- 
buted this year. Revco, for ex- 
ample, uses Telxon’s radio fre- 
quency system. The “RF” 
system employs the same 
“spread spectrum” technology 
used in new “wireless store” 
systems in which cash ia coe 
ters and controllers are linked 
4 radio wave. By speeding 
shelf audit, RF and the porta- 
ble terminals employed with it 
free store managers further 
from adminstrative tasks and 
allow for more customer ser- 
vice. 

Control of DSD products 
was also addressed to improve 
on the traditional “blind” re- 
ceipt of products. To be sure 
products delivered at the back 
door are the correct SKUs, 
count and price, “RF” or 
“batch” technologies are now 
being used with portable ter- 
minals. 

Receiving associates could 
be on-line to a personal com- 
puter, or files with purchase 
orders could be downloaded

HICAGO — Like the 
city in which it was 
born 90 years ago, Wal- 
green Co. makes no little 
plans. The chain drug giant 
will spend another $200 mil- 
lion this year on new stores, 
renovations, retail automa- 
tion and other capital im- 
ot ieeae in a determined 

id to outrun any signs of com- 
placency. 

Walgreen’s ongoing efforts 
should be enough to keep it 
solidly at the top of the chain 
drug industry through the 
1990s, barring some major un- 
foreseen upheaval. The chain 
has spent over $1 billion since 
the mid-1980s to expand its 
store base, increase market 
share around the U.S. and 
arm itself with the technologi- 
cal expertise to carry it into 
the 21st century. It is now 
spending roughly $130 mil- 
lion—over $80,000 per store— 
on POS scanning and inven- 
tory management systems 
over a 3-year period. 

That’s one of a slew of pro- 

ms aimed at boosting pro- 
uctivity and streamlining the 
Walgreens machine, already 
one of the most efficient mon- 
i Ptegg powers in all of re- 
tailing. The reason for all this 
effort by the nation’s most 
profitable, highest-grossin 
drug chain is simple, accord- 
ing to company executives.

Streamlined Revco struggles to emerge from bankruptcy 


WINSBURG, Ohio — 

Revco in the mid-1980s 

was an oversized, ineffi- 
cient gas-guzzler of a retail 
machine, swerving out of con- 
trol, its systems breaking 
down. 

Its retail focus was hazy and 
distorted by ill-fated forays 
into schlock promotional mer- 
chandise and poorly conceived 
buying strategies. Its opera- 
tions and support teams were 
overstretched by the chain’s 
rapid expansion, vast geogra- 
phy and shifting market condi- 
tions. Its top management 
was distracted by a bruising 
proxy fight and by a slew of 
ancillary businesses brought 
on by diversification. Need- 
less to say, Revco hit a brick 
wall at high speed following its 
debt-heavy leveraged buyout 
in late 1986. 

In 1991, Revco is a different 
company. Nearly three years 
after its bankruptcy filing, 
Revco as a retail operation is 
far smaller, better-run, far 
more cost-efficient and in 
clear touch with its basic retail 
mission. Its geographic reach 
has been cut to 10 contiguous 
states. Its top managers and 
support s are among the 
best in chain drug retailing. 
The stores are clean, many are 
remodeled, and their sales are 


steadily improving. 

Putting aside lawyers’ fees, 
accounting changes, write- 
offs and other factors, the 
stores are also profitable. Al- 
though hit hard by last year’s 
economic downturn and in- 
tense competition for custom- 
ers, they are showing steady 
gains in customer traffic and 
productivity. 

Nevertheless, Revco re- 
mains locked in a costly bank- 
ruptcy, its every move subject 
to court approval. The compa- 
ny’s beleaguered board of di- 
rectors is still struggling to 
come to terms with its credi- 
tors, and is even at odds with 
itself. Until the board mem- 
bers who hold an equity stake 
in Reveo can agree on a finan- 
cial plan with the suppliers, 
bondholders and banks to 
whom the company owes $1.4 
billion, its efforts to improve 
operations will be hampered 
by financial pressures and 
bankruptcy distractions. By 
some published estimates, le- 
gal fees have already cost the 
company $50 million, and in- 
terest costs on the unpaid debt 
are piling up. 

Recently, those pressures 
increased. In early April, the 
holders of some of heute junk 
bonds threatened to seek a 
Chapter 7 liquidation of the

changing consumer preferences has taken on new importance. Then again, some

mat—making it more cus- 
tomer-friendly and graduall 
more upscale, in tune wit 
the middle- and upper-mid- 
dle-class demographics of its 
main consumer base—that 
retail mission  hasn’t 
changed. The company re- 
mains focused on a huge se- 
lection of name-brand HBA 
at deep-discount prices as its 
main drawing card. 

The strategy seems to work 
well in all of F&M’s major 
markets, including those in 
which it is still a relative new- 
comer. 

The chain has been in met- 
ro-Minneapolis, for instance, 


for little more than a year, 
but already it has seven units 
up and running there. An 
eighth is set to open this fall, 
and Newman is planning as 
many as 12 to 15 in the Twin 
Cities within the next few 
years. 


More stores bought 


F&M also continues to snap 
up sites in Washington, 
D.C./Baltimore, which it en- 
tered via an acquisition three 
years ago. Total store count in 
those two cities will jump from 
18 to 25 this year. 

Also on tap: more stores for 
Chicago, F&M’s biggest mar- 
ket with 33 units by year-end; 
and Detroit, where two units 
will boost store count to 25 this 

ear despite the fact that it is 
&M’s birthplace and oldest 
market. 

Meanwhile, F&M is gearing 
up for its entry into another 
major metropolitan area, 
Newman told Drug Store 
News earlier this year. That 
market will be disclosed soon, 
he said.

Big B’s uphill expansion efforts are beginning to pay off 


ESSEMER, Ala. — 

Big B has been swal- 

lowing hard for the 
past two-and-a-half years to 
digest its ambitious takeover 
of 85 former Reed drug stores 
in Georgia. e 

That 1989 acquisition 
thrust Big B into the unfamil- 
iar, furiously competitive At- 
lanta market, where its man- 
agers and support people had 
to learn some tough lessons 1n 
a hurry about local consumer 
demand, regional manage- 
ment and high-cost distribu- 
tion in a market where Big B 
was an unknown. 

It was a sizeable challenge, 
and it took time to bounce 
back. Higher interest pay- 
ments and big consolidation 
and conversion costs related 


to the acquisition cut net 
earnings dramatically in the 
fiscal periods following the 
purchase. 

Then, a cut in gross margins 
to respond to tough competi- 
tion dragged Big B into the 
red in the second and third 
quarters last year, resultin 
in the company’s first annua 
loss in its 23-year history in 
fiscal 1991. 

The storm clouds, howev- 
er, appear to be dispellin 
rapidly. Despite the fisca 
year loss, Big B ended the pe- 
riod with a sharp upswing In 
the fourth quarter. Thanks to 
some higher prices in the 
stores, some cost-cutting dis- 
ciplines and steadily improv- 
ing results in the former 
Reed stores, the company re- 


)WPRUG STORE NEWS, May 6, 1991 


ported record profits of $2.45 
million for the last quarter of 
the year. Coupled with a 13 
percent same-store sales 
gain, that upswing helped 
mitigate the loss in fiscal ’91 
and marked a significant 
turnaround. 

Indeed, Big B reported 
that its Atlanta stores broke 
into the black late last year, 
for the first time since the 
takeover. 

Helping hold down operat- 
ing costs 1s Big B’s newly ex- 
panded distribution center, 
which can handle up to 500 
stores, according to the firm. 
The larger, more automated 
facility eliminated the need 
for a local warehouse in At- 
lanta and enhanced inven- 
tory control, Big B states.

’ Alliance fever runs high at NACDS Annual 


On Monday on an unseasonably hot day in late April 
the twin towers of the landmark Breakers Hotel in 
Palm Beach suddenly looked strange. Atop the south 
tower where the NACDS banner has traditionally 
flown during the association’s annual meeting was a 
different pennant bearing a green and white checker- 
board pattern. What was going on? 

It turned out that Palm Beach officialdom had sud- 

denly decided to enforce a 


10-year-old law prohibit- 
ing the display of private 
pennants, such as the one 
that had flapped atop the 
Breakers during so many 
IN THE MARKET! NACDS meetings over 
BRUCE BUCKLEY the years. If any flag was 
to be flown next to Old 
Glory, it had to be Flagler 


County standard. What- 

ever his private feelings, 
Ron Ziegler asked the Breakers to comply with the 
rule. The NACDS flag was struck. 


It was a minor setback in a meeting that set new 


standards for the depth of its business presentations 
and, as our front page story notes, in the spirit of coop- 
eration among retailers and suppliers. 

The three business sessions were outstanding. 
Playing off the theme “Alliance & Progress,” the ses- 
sions moved from the international arena—with espe- 


cially perceptive commentary on the recent Gulf War 
by John Chancellor, Pierre Salinger and Ron 
Ziegler—to business issues of paramount importance 


to the retailers and manufacturers in attendance. 


These issues revolved around the shifting patterns in 
the buyer-seller relationship, the importance of alli- 
ances and the emerging threats to the heart of the 


drug store business—pharmacy. 


The alliance aspect is well covered by Jim Frederick 


in his front page stories and by executive editor Al 
Heller in his column below. 

On the pharmacy issues, there was a highly instruc- 
tive panel discussion ably led by Pharmacy Times edi- 
tor and publisher Ray Gosselin. 

Out of all the questions, the opinions, the back and 
forth interplay of ideas, a couple of words and phrases 
shouted out for me: Chaos and collision course, the 
first describing the uncertainty of today’s health care 
climate with rising consumer expectations and dwin- 
dling resources; and the second describing the rising 
tension between the need for more patient consulta- 
tion from pharmacists and the need for fair reimburse- 
ment to cover the cost of those services. Plenty of 
questions, very few answers. But the interchange was 
important. Out of the chaos, with organizations like 
NACDS leading the way, will come new ideas and 
fresh solutions. Count on it. 

* * * 

Many U.S. companies are involved globally, but can 
you think of a drug store retailer that’s moved ir+~ the 
international arena? I can’t. But now Medicine Shoppe 
is moving into an entirely new enterprise abroad 
(Page 1). 

If plans are approved by the Taiwanese govern- 
ment, Medicine Shoppe will become a consultant to a 
company called Pro Health Care of the Republic of 
China, Taiwan. MSI will train Pro Health Care in the 
intricacies of setting up and running Medicine Shoppe 
franchises. 

Taiwan’s retail climate is vibrant and fast-evolving, 
as Elizabeth Richardson’s story indicates. Thus there 
are opportunities for new ideas and new retail for- 
mats. Says MSI’s executive vp, Ron Hofmeister: “It’s 
a tremendous opportunity to take the Medicine 
Shoppe concept to the Taiwanese people, and a tre- 
mendous opportunity for them to be leaders in inde- 
pendent pharmacy.” 


Creative alliances are currency of the 90s 


Citing that famous American philosopher Yogi 
Berra, “the future just isn’t what it used to be,” Har- 
vard Business Review editor Rosabeth Moss Kanter 
told a packed NACDS Annual Meeting ballroom audi- 
ence in Palm Beach that crisp business thinking must 
be constantly updated because marketplaces are shift- 
ing rapidly. 

“New consumer loyalties, mergers and acquisi- 
tions. . .create the need 
to assume constant 


change and plan for that 
change with collabora- 
tions,” she said. 

THE HUMAN Whether those retailer- 
SIDE supplier collaborations 
AL HELLER are balanced is another 
matter. At the outset of a 


alliance building, Kanter 
told this tale: 

A pig and a chicken were discussing their ham and 
egg breakfast. ‘Why are you so concerned?’ asked the 
chicken. ‘For you it’s a contribution; for me it’s a total 
commitment,’ said the pig. 

“There are no products anymore, just services,” 
Kanter declared. When people use products and they 
work well, that’s perceived as a service. 

Yes, she said, large chains have consolidated, have 
more information and pharmacy is more sophisticat- 
ed, so they have greater leverage. “But consumers 
have the real power and more choices than ever be- 
fore,” she added. “They have a pressured and busy 
life. They want to shop for price, but also want conve- 
nience, quality and service. That’s a daunting chal- 


lenge.” 
Kanter spoke of American Airlines as a model of 


panel she moderated on . 


“creative collaborations” that have enabled the airline 
to sidestep many troubles plaguing that industry. Its 
secret: closeness to its customers, first with its 
SABRE reservations system placed with travel 
agents nationwide, and second, with consumer mar- 
keting such as the mileage award program to build loy- 
alty. 

Clearly, the drug trade is far less high-flying in this 
area, judging by the comments of some of the panel- 
ists: 

Hal Chappelear, executive vp of Upjohn: “One of 
the first questions we hear on building collabora- 
tions is: How long is this going to last? Today there is 
more of a business focus on how we make agree- 
ments.” 

John Jennings, vp-marketing, Brooks: “The qual- 
ity of sales calls affects our time to respond. . .. It 
amazes me how many account reps don’t make use of 
available information to learn a chain’s strategic di- 
rection.” 

Vern Brunner, executive vp-marketing of Wal- 
greens: “One of our biggest challenges is how suppli- 
ers interpret their data and what they’ll bring for- 
ward.” 

Bob Hannan, president of Thrift: “The old Field of 
Dreams program of building stores and customers will 
come is over. We must find niches, which vary from 
community to community . . .The customer is not the 
retailer. The customer is the consumer.” 

Retailers in other trade classes have entered high- 
level collaborations with Procter & Gamble, for in- 
stance. Among them: Wal-Mart, Smith Managemen- 
tand A&P. This concept can be expanded in the drug 
class only if upstairs execs from both sides insist on 
such relations, peel away their adversarial facades 
and work to foster trust.

New items light up market 


New products are a driving 
force in flashlight sales. 

In the last 18 to 24 months, 
40 per¢ent of volume was done 
in new items, according to one 
industry source. 

Eveready, Rayovac, Gar- 
rity and Duracell have been 
leading innovators for the 
mass merchant channel. 
Eveready restaged its light- 
ing products line this year, 
with new products and pack- 
aging. New lights include a 
tilt-base work and auto lan- 
tern, an underwater light, a 
sport light and an outdoor area 
light/flashlight that works ei- 
ther as a regular beam or as a 
table area lamp. The area 
light/flashlight’s SRP is 
$12.99. In April, Bartell Drug 
featured the light for $8.99. 

The trend in flashlights this 
year will be European stylin 
and jewel-tone colors, accord- 
ing to Kevin Garrity, Garrity 
Industries’ vp-marketing. 

Garrity is introducing the 
Hot Lite, which features a 
“swatch-type” motif, polka 
dots and jewel-tone color. The 
company is also introducing 
Power Lite multipacks from 
$4.99 to $9.99, and Life Lite, a 
model decorated with an 
American flag that Garrity 
provided to the Desert Storm 
operation. 

Low-end plastic squeeze 
lights and personal lights 


have been successfu! in drug 
stores. Squeeze lights are 
even being put in trial size 
baskets as a unique merchan- 
dising slant. 

Eveready’s best-selling 
light is its plastic Economy 
flashlight with an SRP of 
$1.72. It’s often sold at $1.19, 
$1.29; or with two on a card 
and four batteries and an 
SRP of $6.18. 

Planograms in this categor 
are are often in disarray, wit 
multiple vendors offering sim- 
ilar lights, confusing the cus- 
tomer. Assortments have to 
be carefully planned and pre- 
sented. 

“You have to be conscious 
of your planogram, with good 
ads and off-the-shelf mer- 
chandising,” says Gary Bak- 
er, director of sales, Ever- 


one.
