Videotapes regain momentum as price-cuttin 


Blank videocassette unit sales surge in 1990, 
but dollar gains remain_hard to come by 


Units* 


For years, two major 
trends have characterized the 
market for blank videocas- 
sette tape: steadily decreasin 
prices at both the supplier an 
retailer level due to furious 
competition; and flat sales 
adhe in both units and dol- 
ars as the market matures, 
demand levels off and compe- 
tition keeps prices down. 

Now, both trends appear to 
have run their course. For one 
thing, the market regained its 
growth momentum last 
year—in unit sales, if not in 
revenues—by smashing 
through earlier projections for 
a flat year with an unexpected 
18 percent jump in unit sales. 
According to the Electronic 
Industry Association’s Con- 
sumer Electronics Group, fac- 
tory shipments of blank video- 
ro hit 338 million units in 


Recession boosts sales 


Ironically, much of the un- 
expected jump in demand was 
due to the recession that 
kicked in in the second half of 
1990. “The year finished much 
stronger than anyone had an- 
ticipated,” said John Ziemba, 
national sales director for au- 
dio/video consumer products 
at BASF. “In a ee 
period, people spend muc 
more time at home. When 
times get difficult, it’s good for 
our business.” 

Ziemba also attributed the 
gains to a “spike in retail pro- 
motions” as retailers pushed 
lower-priced products like 
videotapes to pull people back 
into the stores in a cautious 
spending climate. 

Continued price-cutting by 
manufacturers kept dollar 
gains nearly flat, however. 

Nevertheless, the rampant 
price-cutting may also have fi- 
nally have run its course. “I 
hope we’re near the bottom,” 
said Mike Golacinski, vp-con- 
sumer audio/video products 
for Maxell. “It’s an extremely 
price-driven business, but the 

ast couple of price cuts have 
een much smaller in terms of 
percentages.”

advertising strategies 


Chains create programs to increase ethnic sales — 


through stronger advertising and merchandising pro- 

groms. Some chains are thinking of ethnic products as a 
category thai needs momentum for th to materialize. More 
aggressive operators are learning that community service pro- 
grams, designed to benefit the black community, are one of the best 
ways to cultivate loyalty and build momentum. 


M any drug chains are attempting to increase ethnic sales 


Perry winners do it right 


Doo-It-Up contest receive their awards. On their left is Wm. 
Juan Roberts of Doo-It-Up, on the right, Scott Gorley of Perry. 


Perry program rewards and reaches out 


hen Perry Drug 
created Doo-It-Up 
two years ago, it be- 


came the first drug chain to 
create a consistent African- 
American advertising cam- 
paign themed to community 
service. 

Perry itself sees it as a 
milestone because it marked 
the beginning of its outreach 
to the African-American 
community, said assistant 
Raa ite: Scott Gor- 
ey. 

For Doo-It-Up, Perry 
stages an annual art procure- 
ment contest among Detroit 
high school students. Twelve 
winners each get a $1,000 
prize. The contest kicks off in 
August with a back-to-school 

romotion and ends in Decem- 

r, when award presenta- 
tions are made. 

Name brand products and 
manufacturers like Revlon, 
Posner and Carson are part 
of the program, sometimes as 
co-sponsors and sometimes 


through regular co-op adver- 
tising only. Brand name 
products at special sale 
prices are featured during 
the course of the program, 
but the primary emphasis of 
Doo-It-Up is on Perry’s ef- 
forts to reward the accom- 
plishments of talented black 
students. 

Doo-It-Up also gives Perry 
continuity with the black com- 
munity because it never really 
ends. The company uses the 
drawings and biographies of 
the award-winning students 
to enliven advertising for ev- 
ery promotion over the com- 


me ye 
e community reaction to 
the program has been so posi- 
tive that the Detroit city 
council, the Michigan state 
senate and several other 
community agencies and 
leaders have developed 
awalds of their own to honor 
Perry executives, as well as 
the honored students. 
Gorley notes that for 1992, 


Perry has dozens of civic orga- 
nizations that want to get in- 
volved in Doo-It-Up and make 
it bigger. For last year’s Doo- 
It-Up, three times as many 
schools were involved as in the 
previous year. 

One source described com- 
munity service campaigns 
like Doo-It-Up as “the next 
level beyond price/value ad- 
vertising.” It includes price- 
/value, he said, because black 
customers want to see brand 
name products advertised at 
good sale prices, but it makes 
price/ value:a secondary ben- 
efit. The primary benefactor 
is the campaign sponsor, who 
earns goodwill by putting 
something back into the com- 
munity.

ETHNIC HBA 


though no single hair 
care style is sweeping 
the black community, 
relaxed hair is still very popu- 
lar. And, some knowledgeable 
sources say the wrap look, 
which starts out with relaxed 
hair, is becoming more popu- 
lar throughout the nation. 

“In hair fashion, the popular 
styles today are all based on 
what’s easy to create and 
maintain, and what’s healthy 
and good for the hair,” says 
Mikki Garth-Taylor, beauty 
and cover editor for Essence. 

Garth-Taylor says the wrap 
is becoming more popular be- 
cause it’s easy to style and it’s 
healthy for the hair. “Black 
hair is so very fragile,” she 
said. “Hair is especially vul- 
nerable when it’s over-pro- 
cessed, relaxed or colored.” 

The wrap is created by 
ib. fs the hair around the 
head, setting it with a lotion, 
tying it with a scarf and brush- 
ing it out. 

n her sojourns for Essence, 
Garth-Taylor says she is see- 
ing a wide variety of new 
styles that don’t “stretch, 
stiffen or elongate the hair be- 
yond its natural capacity.” 


Modern versions of “culturally inspired 
styles and techniques’’—corkscrews, 
twists, Senegalese twists and coils—arethe weigh it down or make it 
latest in styling trends, says Essence. 


he wrap 
is becoming 
more popular 
because it’s easy 
to style and it’s 
healthy for the 
hair. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, May 20, 1991 


g 


She adds that textured hair 
is also very popular. “Styles to- 
day are on a variety of 
textures, whether they’re put 
in or natural,” she says. “You 
see a lot of free style bobs. 


Women are wearing braids | 


that may be twisted into the 
hair and then taken out to cre- 
ate a wrinkled look. Cork- 
screws and puffy twists or dou- 
ble-strand twists are popular.” 

She said a lot of today’s styles 
are based on African heritage- 
pir ag techniques: braids, 
coifs and twists translated into 
modern shapes. 

For both men and women, 
short cuts are still in. The 
style is to keep the short cut 
“scissor-fresh,” Garth-Taylor 
says, with mandatory trips to 
the barber or salon every 
three weeks or so. 

“Women are wearing a lot of 
caught-up hair styles that can 
be shaped and pinned rather 
than just curled or blown dry. 
Many like the sculptured look 
of the French knot or twist,” 
she said. 

Women, she added, are also 
refusing to suffer to maintain 
their looks. “Women are con- 
cerned first with their hair’s 
health. Everything else falls 
under that.” 

Because black hair is fragile 
and vulnerable to dryness and 
brittleness, Garth-Taylor 
says it is essential for both 
women and men to use condi- 
tioning products that replen- 
ish the moisture in the hair. 

That same concern with 
healthy hair styles is also caus- 
ing men and women to ques- 
tion the products used on their 
children’s hair. In its August 
issue, Essence is publishing a 
feature on how to care for the 
hair of black children. 

Again, Garth-Taylor says 
the operative vig is 
“restful hair, styles and prod- 
ucts that won’t stress the hair, 


break. The right choice of hair 
accessories is important, as is 
the right choice for shampoo- 
ing and conditioning products. 
‘The market is absolutely 
there for children’s hair care 
lines,” she adds. “A lot of chil- 
dren as young as five, six and 
seven are losing their hair be- 
cause of stressful styles and 
handling. To prevent damage 
at that young an age, we have 
to inform mothers about 
what’s good for their hair.” 
As for men, many sport the 
geometric cuts, with curly 
perms still popular and a lot 
more men wearing dread- 
locks. Dreadlocks are long and 
tubular, but whether hair is 
long or short, Garth-Taylor 
says it is essential to use condi- 
tioners and moisturizers to 
keep it healthy. 
Conssananat men and 
women are buying a lot of oils, 
gels, hair sprays, and other 
maintenance products that lu- 
bricate the hair, retain mois- 
ture, add sheen, give control 
and make hair easier to style.

now being introduced b =

Satin are primarily facial and

most needed.

for women of color.” None of

market customers.

Longs makes sales top priority 


By James Frederick 

WALNUT CREEK, Calif. 
— Longs Drug Stores will con- 
tinue to fight for its market 
share by sacrificing gross 
margins and short-term prof- 
itability to sustain sales and 
customer traffic, its leaders 
told shareholders at the com- 
pid annual meeting here 

ay 21. 

“Our plan is to increase and 
maintain Longs’ market 
share... through increased 
price sensitivity and careful 
attention to promotion,” said 
chairman and ceo Bob Long. 
He described current retail 
conditions in western states as 
“much more price-competitive 


and much more demanding” 
than in years past, adding that 
the next 12 months for Longs 
will see “an aggressive ad pro- 


Nevertheless, added new 
Longs president Steve Roath, 
“promotional sales cannot be 
an end in and of themselves. 

“Some retail segments are 
more vulnerable than others, 
and we need to be selective of 
the competitors we promote 
against,” Roath told share- 
holders. “Our promotional 
strategy should support our 
core business by providing a 
value-added reason for shop- 
ping at our stores.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 10, 1991 


It was the spring of 1986. For the Jack Eckerd Cor- 
poration, an era was ending, a new one about to begin. 
I remember attending Eckerd’s last annual meeting 
as a public company in April. I recall it as a time of nos- 
talgia and hope. Long-time shareholders came to 
share remembrances with Jack Eckerd and others 
who had built the chain into one of the most dynamic in 
the nation. 

Now five years later it 
is plain that the mixture of 


hope and optimism shown 
by the new management 
team at that meeting was 
well justified. The finan- 
cial package they crafted 
so carefully has stood up 
to the rigorous tests im- 
posed by the marketplace. 


IN THE MARKET 
BRUCE BUCKLEY 


In a time when the letters 

LBO have come to be as- 
sociated with the financial excesses of the "80s, Eck- 
erd’s leveraged buyout serves as a model for what 
might have been done by others, had they not reached 
out for quick and risky solutions. 

Consider that the company and its LBO partner, 
Merrill Lynch Capital Partners, were able to take ad- 
vantage last year of Revco’s misfortunes by laying out 
$80 million for 223 of the stores put on the block by the 
Ohio-based drug chain. The deal added sales. It built 
muscle in key Sunbelt markets. And it had the mark of 
a confident and aggressive player able and willing to 
dig deep for future returns. 

Kckerd’s remodeling program carries the same 
mark of confidence. By now the story of the chain’s 
substantial and continuing investment in creating a 


REC 


Eckerd shows muscle, even in its heart 


OPINION 


“customer-friendly” atmosphere in its stores is well 
known. Since 1986 some 1,200 stores have been re- 
modeled: Uncluttered, fresh, appealing, easy to shop 
are the words that come to mind in describing the 
changes that have taken place in Eckerd’s second 
most important asset. 

The first, of course, is people. That’s where the com- 
pany has had its greatest success. It has managed to 
instill a feeling of ownership pride among its asso- 
ciates, from headquarters, to distribution centers to 
its more than 1,700 stores in 14 states. Part of the rea- 
son is financial: stock ownership plans for key employ- 
ees and profit-sharing for everyone. But financial 
packages can only go so far. The intangible benefit of 
working for a company that values enterprise, cre- 
ativity and hard work is much more important in the 
long run. And that, it seems to me, is where Eckerd 
excels. 

Not long ago Eckerd announced that it would 
make sure that the 52 National Guard members and 
Reservists called up in the Persian Gulf crisis would 
not suffer financially as a result of their sacrifice. 
The company said it would make up the difference 
between their military salaries and the amounts 
they earn as civilians. “We adopted this policy sim- 
ply because we thought it was the right thing to do,” 
Stew Turley wrote in the company’s recently issued 
annual report. 

Exactly. It was the right thing to do. It also sent out 
a message of caring to all of the thousands of Eckerd 
associates and millions of Eckerd customers from Tex- 
as to Florida to New Jersey. Talk about the intangible 
rewards of people investment! 

Is it clear that I’m a fan of this kind of enterprise? It 
would be hard not to be. 


Shoppers need comfort 


Retailers seem so preoccupied today with technol- 
ogy, inventory management and lean operations, they 
mustn’t lose sight of the backbone of their business: 
the customers. 

The need to tailor store design to lifestyle concerns 
and a grayer shopping base is crucial. With so many 
retail alternatives open to consumers, often the most 
comfortable store gets the business. 

“It’s not a matter of, 
say, Revco vs. Eckerd. It 


is everyone competing for 
discretionary dollars. No 
one is serving new mar- 
kets. We are overstored,” 
said Paco Underhill, man- 
aging director of Enviro- 
sell, a design firm with ex- 
tensive credits in the 
department store, spe- 
cialty chain, banking and 
packaged goods areas. The company makes unusual 
time-lapse film studies of shopper flow around and 
within stores. 

“Amenability and profitability are inextricably 
linked,” Underhill declared during a recent presenta- 
tion at the law offices of Gibney Anthony & Flaherty in 
New York City. “Shopping is a social process. Most 
decisions are discretionary.” 

Underhill, whose firm was involved in the recent 
development of Revco’s prototype, offered some in- 
sights on store design: 
© Account for “rear-brush factor,” people’s unwilling- 
ness to examine products on a busy or narrow aisle be- 
cause others who walk by will likely rub against them. 
Women are more sensitive to this, he says, explaining 
why the romance novei section generally has more 
room than other classifications in bookstores. 

Indeed, in one of his studies, a rack of new men’s ties 
in Bloomingdale’s rated far greater attention when 


THE HUMAN 
SIDE 
AL HELLER 


in order to spend 


moved five foot over from a main traffic aisle to a less- 
busy department aisle. 

The drug store application: display new cosmetics 
items slightly away from a main traffic spot, on a 
curved showcase perhaps, where a woman can handle 
the product comfortably. 

“So many store planners are men,” says Underhill. 
“They don’t appreciate that with a suburban audience, 
if a stroller can’t get to it, near it or by it, a significant 
part of the shopping audience will never visit that part 
of the aisle. 

“Shoppers can’t negotiate and shop at the same 
time,” he added. 

@ In drug stores, shoppers are more prone to impulse 
buys after they take care oftheir primary purchase, 
such as filling a script. Promotional ends and floor- 
stands may have more impact if set to attract traffic 
moving from the back-of-store to the front. 

® Less than five percent of drug store shoppers pick up a 
carry basket or wagon. Since there is a direct correlation 
between transaction size and carry- aids, stack these 
baskets around the store near impulse items. 

@ Drug stores need to understand the age of their 
shoppers: for seniors, comfortable seats help deter- 
mine where scripts are filled and money spent; for 
younger crowds, keep a visual axis between pharmacy 
and baby care. 

@ Given the absolute predictability of who shops when 
in a mall, shift merchandise by the entrance appropri- 
ately to draw traffic. Since 60 percent of people ap- 
proach from the right side, cant the goods for maxi- 
mum visual impact. That is, after all, the shoppers’ 
first impression of a store. 

“How stores work in Lafayette, La., and Grand 
Forks, N. Dak., are distinctly different,” said Under- 
hill. “I appreciate some cookie cutter approach, but 
chains succeed by letting local management take re- 
sponsibility for stores and accept the consequences of 
increases and decreases.”

eye cosmetics 


Lip, face and nail were all strong for last year, and eye color is coming on hot for the first half of 1991. 


A makeup sights should aim at 18-49 set 


ye ‘olor is the third most highly 
usec! color cosmetic category, ac- 
cording to Gallup. Two-thirds of 
all American women use eye color 
products. Half of all women are mas- 
cara and eye shadow users, and four 
out of 10 use liners. 

Eye color, however, is not necessar- 
ily something to advertise to attract 
mature women 50 and older. 

Gallup found that just 25 percent of 
all eye shadow users are women 50 and 
older and just 19 percent of mascara 
users are 50 and older. 

These are products to advertise in 
beauty programs aimed at attracting 
younger women. Three out of 10 mas- 
cara and eye shadow users, for exam- 
ple, are women aged 25 to 49, and two 
out of 10 are 18 to 24. 

Women aged 18 to 24 are also fre- 
quent users of eye cosmetics, with 85 
percent of all women in this age seg- 


ment reporting that they use an eye 
cosmetic at least once a day or more. 


Favorite brands 


Far and away, the American fe- 
male’s favorite eye brand is Maybel- 
line. Thirty percent of all the women in 
Gallup’s survey named Maybelline as 
their favorite eye color cosmetic. 

Maybelline’s share of votes was 
nearly three times greater than its 
closer rival, Cover Girl, cited by 11 
percent. Avon came in third with eight 
percent mentions; Mary Kay, six per- 
cent; L’Oreal, five percent, and Rev- 
lon, four percent. 

Maybelline was the strongest with 
consumers 25 to 34 (36 percent) and 18 
to 24 (32 percent). Cover Girl went 
over the biggest with girls 18 to 24 (20 
percent), and was the weakest (seven 

reent) with women 35-49. Avon had 
its greatest strength with women 35 to 


and bring it to the house. 


49. Twelve percent of women this age 
chose Avon as their favorite mascara 
brand. 

Revlon’s mascaras were weak with 
women 18 to 34, but were the favorite 
of 10 percent of women 50 and older. 

L’Oreal was also weak in popularity 
among women 18 to 24, like Revlon, 
picked by just two percent of these re- 
spondents as their favorite brand. But 
eight percent of women 25 to 34 picked 
L’Oreal as a favorite. 

Maybelline’s overwhelming popu- 
larity among all age segments, howev- 
er, suggests that if retailers want to 
use mascaras to draw traffic, they can 
probably reach the broadest number of 
consumers across all age segments by 
featuring Maybelline. 

However, if they want to add some 
special incentives to attract more wom- 
en 25 to 49, they should aiso consider 
featuring Cover Girl and L’Oreal.

in beauty sales derby 


allup reports that more than 

four out of 10 cosmetic users 

currently buy their cosmetics 
“most often” in a drug store. Making 
up this total, 19 percent frequent a con- 
ventional drug store such as Wal- 
greens or Eckerd, and 23 percent visit 
deep discounters such as Drug Empo- 
rium or F&M. 

Gallup found that the strongest com- 
petition for cosmetic sales isn’t coming 
from department stores, but from dis- 
counters such as Kmart and Wal-Mart 
(19 percent) and direct marketers Avon 
and Mary Kay (15 percent). Just 11 per- 
cent of women said they buy “most of- 
ten” in department stores. 

Indeed, Nielsen Marketing Re- 
search, which tracks the sales of cos- 
metics and beauty aids through mass 
channels, has consistently reported 
that discount chains are building a 
greater presence. Wall Street analysts 
who follow the cosmetic industry con- 
cur that department store share is de- 
clining. 

Store without walls 


Not only are discount stores as well as 
food/drug combination stores intensify- 
ing their merchandising and advertising 
programs for cosmetics, direct market- 
ers such as Avon are also aggressively 
pursuing this customer. 

Avon executives have told reporters 
that they view their company as a 
store without walls, and they have said 
they want to increase the volume of 
business they do in beauty aids. 

Other direct marketers Mary Kay 
and Amway are also introducing new 
beauty care products and lines, and ob- 


viously pitching much more whole- 
heartedly for cosmetic and beauty aid 
sales. 

Gallup’s profile of where women 
shop “most often” for beauty care 
products shows that door-to-door com- 
a like deep discount drug stores, 

ave been most successful in appealing 
to women 25 and older, and least suc- 
cessful in cultivating the 18 to 24 year 
old female shopper. 

Just 7 percent of all 18 to 24 year old 
respondents, for example, said they 
bought their cosmetics “most often” 
from a door-to-door rep, and just 11 
percent said they bought them “most 
often” in a deep discount drug store.

climbing, and nail, while strong at many 
chains, 1s slowing down in some areas.

that lip and face cosmetics continue to 
do exceptionally well this year. In 
some chains if eye cosmetics are do- 
ing well, nail sales are weaker; at oth- 
er chains, the opposite is true. In 
most chains, cosmetic organizers and 
a ei are selling exceptionally 
well.

Pierce, who supervises the cosmetics

growth categories year-to-date are 
eye and lip color, up about 10 percent,

letries, and it’s really blowing out the

“Eye Defense is phenomenal,” said

it in stock.” ; 

“When store managers start notic- 
ing an item and calling in to reorder it, 
you know it’s good,” said Genovese’s

she’s had managers call up and order

Revlon’s new packaging for its eye 
care lines has been well received by 
consumers, most chains reported. 

In Seattle, Bartell sold out within a 
few weeks of the first shipment. The 
chain is back in stock now, and Pierce 
said everything in the line is still sell- 
ing well, and the quad- and single-pan 
shadows are doing exceptionally well. 

“When they first shipped, we had 
the quads for.two days and they were

Bay area drug competition gets white-hot 


By James Frederick 
First of a two-part series 
COLMA, Calif. — eee, 

over the densely stacke 
aisles of the Drug Barn store 
in this suburb south of San 
Francisco is a fitting symbol of 
the new era in Northern Cali- 
fornia retailing. It is a huge 
overhead banner proclaimin 
everyday discounts of up to 
percent. 

Across the San Francisco 
Bay in suburban Walnut 
Creek, the Longs drug store 
closest to headquarters has 
taken a similar tack. The 


“Cadillac of drug stores” is 
now sprinkled throughout 
with shelf tags that shout low 
prices and unadvertised spe- 
cials. 

The signs that fill the mar- 
ket’s first deep-discount 
store and its best-establish 
chain drug stores used to be an 
anomaly in the once-quiet, 
well-defined wor!d of Bay 
Area drug store retailing. 
a with eng esti call to 
ower prices, they symbolize 
all that has happened in this 
massive population center, 
and all the changes that are 


still to come. 

Northern California drug 
retailing is quickly evolving 
from a state of friendly rivalr 
into a furious battle for turf. 
Traditional sivas 3 goa 
and traditionally high gross 
margins are under assault as 
never before. 

Caught in the middle, as 
usual, are the handful of inde- 
pendents that remain here, 
and any retailers still sleeping 
at the wheel. Those that can’t 
adapt quickly--with technol- 
ogy, lower operating costs, 
better dealmaking abilities, 


lower prices and real custom- 
er service--aren’t likely to 
make it through the gauntlet 
of the 1990s. 

Two major forces are 
scrambling consumer loyalties 
and retail strategies here. One 
is the rapid influx of new drug, 
combo and discount stores; 
the other is an economic slow- 
down that forced consumers 
into retrenchment and cur- 
tailed bank lending for new re- 
tail development.

30-year career that I’ve had to

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 24, 1991 


NACDS is waging a strong and laudable campaign 
to block an effort to require the six-year Pharm.D as 
the entry-level degree for pharmacy practice. The as- 
sociation has assembled some clear, and in my opinion, 
irrefutable arguments in making its case. The most 
persuasive: the severe impact that a mandatory six- 
year degree would have on the already difficult phar- 
macist shortage. 

In its latest Executive 
Newsletter, NACDS 


weighs in with another 
telling point: the effect 
that a six-year require- 
ment will have on women, 
minorities and the poor. 
Retaining the five-year 
degree, the association 
says, offers the best op- 


IN THE MARKET 
BRUCE BUCKLEY 


portunity for members of 
these groups to enter a re- 
warding profession. 

The association cites statistics showing that pharma- 
cy has become an increasingly attractive choice for 
groups that. on the whole, have long had fewer career 
options and less chance for advancement. Women, for 
example, now comprise almost 62 percent of the stu- 
dents enrolled in the nation’s pharmacy schools. Minor- 
ity group members (including African Americans, His- 
panics, Native Americans and Asian Americans) make 
up almost 20 percent of pharmacy school enrollment. 

A mandatory six-year degree, with its higher edu- 
cational costs, will put a damper on the growing enthu- 
siasm of these groups for careers in pharmacy, says 
the association. A big loser, of course, would be retail 
pharmacy, the largest employer by far of the coun- 
try’s pharmacists.

The recent brouhaha over market share figures in 


OPINION 


Another big pitfall of mandatory Pharm.D 


the Greater Detroit area points up the difficulty that 
outside research firms have in assembling an accurate 
picture of the relative standing of retail companies in 
individual markets. 

It also demonstrates how sensitive retailers are to 
reported numbers. When Metro Market Studies 
showed that Arbor Drugs had overtaken Perry in 
metro Detroit, Perry execs saw red. They quickly re- 
leased sales figures for the seven-county market 
which they said put Perry three points ahead of its 
nearest drug store competitor, which, of course, is Ar- 
bor. 

Two observations on the Detroit flap. First, Drug 
Store News has occasionally used Metro Market Stud- 
ies as a market share source for various articles be- 
cause it is the only objective outside firm we’re aware 
of that publishes these figures. We do, however, ex- 
amine the numbers closely in the light of our own 
knowledge of these markets. 

Second, the fierce rivalry for market share in De- 
troit makes better retailers of all the players there. 
The beneficiary is the consuming public.

What a conversion! I’ve become a “voice mail” fan. I 
used to hate those recorded messages when I dialed 
business offices. Couldn’t they get a real person to an- 
swer the phone? Often I just hung up. 

Now Drug Store News has a new phone system that 
includes a voice-mail feature, and I have to report: It’s 
great. No more lost messages buried under a ton of 
press releases. No more messages delivered two days 
after the call (“Sorry, I forgot.”) 

Now I’m getting my messages on time and return- 
ing calls immediately (Try me: my new direct number 
is 212-756-5227. I’d like to hear from you). 

A complete list of Drug Store News direct lines is on 
page 1. I hope the change will improve our service to 
you, our readers and customers. 


A little more than a year ago, the Food and Drug 
Administration hit rock bottom. 

Repeated funding cuts by Administration penny 
pinchers had eroded the agency’s enforcement mus- 
cle, while the deepening generic drug approval scan- 
dals sapped FDA’s will and destroyed staff morale. 

Health and Human Services Secretary Louis Sullivan 
appointed ex-FDA Commissioner Charles Edwards to 

- head a blue-ribbon adviso- 


ry panel to study the agen- 
cy’s problems and recom- 
mend solutions. 

No big deal. Here in 
Washington they form 
special advisory panels 
every ten minutes or so. 
Bureaucrats and politi- 
cians love these study 
groups because they’re a 
way to delay painful but 


m= WASHINGTON 
m® KEN RANKIN 


inevitable change. 

In the case of the Edwards Committee, however, 
the Washington bigwigs got more than they bar- 
gained for. Indeed, ears are burning all over town. 

The picture of FDA painted by the study group is of 
an agency literally stretched to the breaking point—a 
regulatory body that is “not prepared to cope” with 
the responsibilities assigned to it. 

There’s more than enough blame to spread around, 
according to the report. 

The Administration deserves much of it for loboto- 
mizing FDA’s rulemaking authority and submerging 
the agency into a bureaucratic Bermuda Triangle 
within the Public Health Service. 

Congress deserves its share, and then some, for 


Committee raises hackles with FDA picture 


heaping new responsibilities on FDA without appro- 
priating funds to properly carry out those duties. 

Militant special interest groups ranging from true- 
believers in the animal rights movement to shrill- 
voiced AIDS activists have made an almost impossible 
job even more difficult for FDA. 

State legislators from Maine to Maui have tried 
to undercut F'DA’s authority over foods and drugs by 
designing their own conflicting regulatory standards. 

Even us in the (gasp!) news media contributed to 
the agency’s internal paranoia by subjecting day-to- 
day decisions by FDA officials to intense scrutiny. 

In short, it’s a wonderful report packed with conclu- 
sions and recommendations certain to infuriate just 
about every possible side. 

The solutions recommended by the committee, 
however, may be even more controversial. 

HHS Secretary Sullivan—the guy who called for 
the study in the first place—is less than thrilled with 
the panel’s proposal to slash his Department’s author- 
ity over FDA. 

House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair- 
man John Dingell (D-MI)—the person who stirred up 
the generic drug hornets nest in the first place—is liv- 
id over criticism about Congressional micro-managing 
of the agency. 

The army of self-appointed “consumer advocates” 
and special interest radicals who roast FDA at every 
opportunity are furious that some of the heat has been 
turned in their direction. _ 

The wine and quiche crowd in Sacramento is having 
fits over suggestions that FDA should veto their plans 
to concoct their own politically correct labeling re- 
quirements for drugs and cosmetics. 

I love it!

continue at Arbor Drugs 


TROY, Mich. — Arbor 
Drugs maintained its stron 
growth momentum with a 22. 
percent jump in net income 
and a 22.2 percent sales in- 
crease for the third quarter 
ended April 30. 

_Net earnings for the period 
hit a record $2.8 million on 
sales of $101.2 million. Same- 
store sales were up a sharp 
10.5 percent. 

For the first nine months, 
net has increased 15 percent to 
$9.6 million and sales have 
climbed 19.4 percent to $301.4 
million, with same-store sales 
up 10.0 percent. 

Arbor chairman and ceo Eu- 
gene Applebaum attributed 
the sharp gains—which have 
become standard for the 112- 
store chain—to excellent sales 
growth, expense disciplines 
and continued success in new- 
store expansion. “Over the 
past 12 months, the company 


has added 20 new drug stores, 
and we are enthused by their 
performance,” he said. “The 
proceeds from [Arbor’s recent 
additional] stock offering will 
further enable the company to 
expand its existing base of 
stores.” 

Applebaum added that Ar- 
bor’s double-digit compara- 
ble-store gains “demonstrate 
the fundamental strength of 
our base business.” 

Arbor recently declared an- 
other 3-for-2 stock split, and 
sold another 1 million shares of 
common stock (1.5 million 
shares on a post-split basis) in a 
public offering to raise addi- 
tional capital. Concurrently, 
Applebaum offered 1 million 
shares of his own holdings in 
arbor to the public, reducin 
his stake in Arbor from 4.3 mil- 
lion shares or 45.1 percent own- 
ership, to 3.3 million shares, or 
31.4 percent ownership.

ued success in new store expansion.

DRSN GALLUP REPORT 


bath care 


Lotions, creams, talcs and dusting powders that women stroke on their bodies after bathing are the most popular items, usec 
by 56 percent of the women in the study. 


With proper merchandising, 
simple bathing becomes ritual 


Thanks to the growing popularity of body care specialty stores like The Body Shop and HO Plus, American women have begun to 
transform their bathing and moisturizing rituals into highly sensual experiences. 
_ Through their romantic advertising and product presentations, Body Shop stores are conditioning women to think of soaps, gels, dust- 
ing powders and moisturizers as indulgent experiences. 
Fragranced lightly with the natural oils and extracts of flowers and fresh fruits, body care products can make a woman feel pampered, 
silky, and as innocently erotic as nature itself. 


Now drug stores and other mass retailers are beginning to see that they can also merchandise the bath and skin care category as sensual 
enhancements. 


Some of the more progressive chains like Drug Emporium, Eckerd and Genovese have begun expanding their bath planograms and 
some are creating bath centers in their cosmetic skin care sets or on highly visible endcaps. 


Buyers are also reporting strong growth in bath care products, especially for premium positioned lines like Yardley, Jean Nate, L’Ef- 
fleur, Sarah Michaels and Natural Essence. 
In our exclusive Gallup Consumer Survey report, Drug Store News discovered another reason for thei success of specialty chains like 


The Body Shop and HO Plus: they’ve tapped into a large market of women who use body care products sensually, and who sincerely 
| cherish these products for their ability to provide such luxurious indulgences.

ealth, fitness and

have succeeded in

These days, women don’t 
want to wait until their skin 


No one wants to look any older than they have to, which helps ex- 
plain why 69 percent of adult women use face moisturizers. 


has been damaged before they 
start to protect it. They’ve 
been taught that the best way

As health, fitness and fash- 
ion magazines continue to 
publish articles warning 
against the damaging effects 
the environment can have on 
human skin, the incidence of 
use can be expected to grow. 

Given the usage rates they 
now command, moisturizers 
are a perfect category for 
chain drug stores to advertise. 
Women will be looking for new 
products offering the latest 
technological breakthroughs 
in innovative formulas. 

Some will respond to the 
stores that offer the lowest 
prices and broadest selec- 
tions. They’ll have questions 
about what is best for their 
skin types, and retailers with 
knowledgeable staffs will be in 
a strong competitive position. 


Replenishment rates high 


Since most women today 
tend to use moisturizers at 
least once a day, oe 
ment rates are relatively high. 

Certainly if women can be 
persuaded to buy their mois- 
turizers in one particular 
store, that store will benefit 
from frequent repeat pur- 
chases. And the more women 
a store attracts, the more like- 
ly that store is to generate oth- 
er incremental impulse pur- 
chases. 

Gallup found that women 
who wear facial moisturizers 
apply them often. 

ndeed, 84 percent of all 
women 25 to 34 apply them at 
least once a day, and 33 per- 
cent say they use them “more 
than” once a day. 

Facial moisturizers also 
have psychological benefits 
for the user. In addition to giv- 
ing users a sense of security 
based on the protection they 
provide, vig | also leave a 
woman’s skin feeling soft and 
silky to the touch. 

As the day wears on and the 
moisturizers wear off, women 
can feel their skin tightening. 
The quickest way to remedy 
the problem? Stroke on a little 
more moisturizer. 

Facial moisturizers help 
women feel good as well as 
look good, beauty experts say.

the most popular moisturizing 
brand among American wom-

@ For years now, FDA has taken a 
hard line on sunscreen products, 
maintaining that there is no extra 
benefit to those with “Sun Protec- 
tion Factors” (SPFs) above 15. 
That line appears to be softening, 
however, and officials at the agen- 
cy’s Division of OTC Drug Evalua-. 
tion are indicating that FDA now 
sees a role for sunscreens with 
SPFs as high as 30. 


@ Seems like pharmacy’s ethical 
Standards are changing faster than 
they used to. In the 100 years fol- 
lowing the adoption of APhA’s 
Code of Ethics in 1852, it was re- 
vised only once. Over the last 40 
years the APhA code has been up- 
dated four times (1952, 1968, 
1975 and 1981) and now the asso- 
ciation has decided “‘it is appropri- 
ate to review the code once again” 
in light of ‘the evolving mission of 
pharmacy and the changing health 
care environment.” Pharmacists 
are being asked to suggest possi- 
ble code changes to APhA.

By Elizabeth 
Richardson 
EEVILLE, TX. 
— Some things in 
Beeville aren’t 
buzzing as they used to. 

Independent pharma- 
cy, in this town 90 miles 
south of San Antonio, is 
close to being obsolete. 
Just six short years ago, 
six independents served 
a population of 15,000. 
Three have shut down 
since January. st two 
have survived the latest 
forces to hit the market. | 
And more trouble is on 
the way. 

Beeville has seen 
many indications of trou- 
ble over the last several 
years forshadowing the 
current state of affairs. 

Within the last 10 
years, two chains have 
emerged on the scene— 
Eckerd and H.E.Butt, 
the regional combo store 
operator. Each has of- 
fered cheaper prices 
than Beeville residents 
had previously seen. In 
addition, Kmart and 
Wal-Mart have moved 
in. The two discounters cur- 
rently don’t have pharmacies. 
Yet over 30 businesses closed 
after their arrival, including 
“mom and pop” businesses, 
and hardware, lumber, auto 
and clothing store retailers. 

Meantime, the local econo- 
my has suffered. The declin- 
ing oil economy of the mid- 
1980s, and recent crop failures 
from drought and vig | 
have battered farming an 
ranching, the region’s pre- 
dominant industries. 

The area’s naval base, 
Chase Field, is being closed. 
Chase Field has employed 
2,250 people, or 35 percent of 
the county’s jobs. 

Although the state is build- 
ing a maximum security pris- 
on in the area—slated to open 
in late 1992—not all of the Jobs 
lost from the naval base can be 
replaced. 

‘All of these factors have 
_ been very devastating to the 
@ommunity,” says Bill Mor-

pentane age” who just moved to

years of business.

third party having four per-

five percent. Reduced rates, 
slow pay, and restricted cash

NEW YORK — There are strong indications 
in the latest Generic Drug Substitution Study 
that the underlying strength of the generic 
drug industry is proving to be the catalyst for 
strong and growing retail confidence in the in- 
dustry’s products. 

The 1991 study conducted by Drug Store 
News for The Pharmacist covers mailed replies 
from pharmacy directors representing some 
3,000 pharmacies operating by drug chains, su- 
permarkets and mass merchandisers. 

The study shows that the directors are much 
more positive about the generic companies that 
came through the 1989 scandals untarnished. 
As one director put it: “We still have a high lev- 
el of confidence in the generic manufacturers 
we buy from.” 

Wrote another: “We were tentative at first. 
We’re more positive now.” 

Indeed the study shows that the large major- 
ity of the chains in the sample have increased 
their purchases of — drugs in response to 
growing demand from consumers, physicians 
and third-party payors. Asked about the trend in 
generic prescriptions, more than three-quarters 
of the respondents (78 percent) said the number 
had increased, while 22 percent said it had re- 
mained the same. No one reported a decline. 

In comparison, 17 percent of the respondents 
to last year’s survey reported a decline in ge- 
neric prescriptions. 

One reason for the growth, of course, is that 
physicians have been writing more prescrip- 
tions either generically or substitution permit- 
ted. The study showed a small increase in both 
generic and substitution-permitted prescrip- 
tions and a small decline in brand-only scripts. 

Asked tc rate the key factors in deciding to 
substitute a generic, pharmacy directors

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 15, 1997 


Like many people who live in the city, my wife and 
I didn’t pay much attention to the threat of Lyme 
Disease. Unlike country friends and family who 
make a nightly ritual of scrutinizing legs and bodies 
for swollen little ticks, we blithely ignored any pos- 
sible threat to ourselves. After all, no deer roam the 
little park a block away from where we live in 
Queens, N.Y. 

In fact, my wife would 
tell me later, when she got 


= ; BRUCE BUCKLEY 


calls from worried parents 
about the threat of Lyme 
Disease, she treated them 
casually. She’s an RN who 
works in a pediatric office 
in Manhattan, and she 
gets a lot of calls like that. 
Lyme Disease? Not to 


IN THE MARKET 


worry. That’s not to say 

she put them in the same 
class as diaper rash or the common cold. She just 
didn’t share their feeling of dread. 


Possible spider bite 


That’s all changed. One night a couple of weeks 
back, she asked me to check out a couple of bites on 
her leg. They had begun to itch during the day. She 
was afraid it was the work of a spider. Ever since her 
hand blew up after being bitten by a spider on a wil- 
derness canoe trip several years ago, she’s been ter- 
rified of spiders. I looked at the bites. They weren’t 
swollen, so they couldn’t have been caused by mos- 
quitoes, as I first suspected. They were surrounded 
' by ariny, like the moon when a storm’s coming. A 
red ring. 

Lyme shot into my mind, but I didn’t say any- 
thing. “Might be a spider,” is what I did say. The 
next day I said, “Maybe you ought to have a Lyme 
test done in the office.” She was skeptical. Where 
could she have been bitten? Perhaps on a weekend 


OPINION 


Lyme Disease hits home for two city folk 


trip to Vermont on the Memorial Day weekend, I 
suggested. 


Magic bullet 


A week later the result came back from Stony 
Brook Medical Center on Long Island. Reactive, 
meaning positive. Not even borderline. For her, ina 
way, it was a relief to know what was causing those 
achy knees and shoulder joints and periodic feelings 
of utter exhaustion. It was caused by a nasty little 
organism that can burrow deep and bring on severe 
illness if left undetected. Fortunately pharmaceuti- 
cal science has provided some swift magic bullets to 
combat the little invaders. Fortunately, too, the on- 
set was diagnosed quickly. 

For Joan the magic bullet was the systemic tetra- 
cycline named Declomycin. Taken twice a day for 
two weeks, the drug is said to be highly effective 
against the spirochete that causes Lyme. She’s in 
the middle of the two-week course of treatment, but 
no longer worried. The aching joints have — to 
subside. 

As asidelight, it wasn’t easy to get the drug. Our 
local chain pharmacy, where we do most of our drug 
store shopping, was out of stock. The pharmacist 
called around to several nearby stores in the chain, 
and they had none either. Could we wait a day for an 
order to come in? No way, my wife said. 


Warning 


The pharmacist, who knows my wife is a nurse, 
did taik about precautions. Don’t take any antacids, 
she said, and stay out of the sun, you can broil. Inter- 
estingly, the pharmacist staffing the independent 
drug store where my wife finally located a supply af- 
ter many calls offered no such warnings. 

This pharmacist silently took the $100 and handed 
her the package. So much for stereotypes about 
chain and independent pharmacists. People are just, 
well, people. 


Strange things are happening here in Washington. 
Over at the the Supreme Court, First Amendment 
advocates are arguing that nude bar room dancing is a 
Constitutionally-proteeted expression of speech. 
Meanwhile, six blocks away at the Federal Trade 
Commission, an administrative law judge effectively 
ruled that drug stores have no right, constitutional or 
otherwise, to jointly discuss the pros and cons of being 
in various third-party pre- 


scription drug programs. 

According to the FTC 
ALJ, Oakfield, N.Y.- 
based Peterson Drug ille- 
gally conspired with a 
number of other New 
York state drug chains to 
boycott a third-party pre- 
scription drug program 
during the mid-1980s. 

The judge’s decision 
caps some three years of investigations and regulatory 
proceedings surrounding an aborted attempt by admin- 
istrators of a third-party prescription plan for New 
York state employees to set unrealistically low reim- 
bursement levels to pharmacies. 

Following meetings to discuss the new reimburse- 
ment plan, many chains, as well as independent drug- 
gists, declined to take part in the program. So many re- 
jected the arrangement that the state recanted and 
developed a more acceptable reimbursement formula. 

FTC antitrusters in Washington cried foul and 
charged a number of chains and independents with 
conspiring to engage in an illegal boycott of the New 
York plan. All the defendants except Peterson settled 


WASHINGTON 
\ PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


ls discussing third-party programs a conspiracy? 


with FTC by signing consent orders agreeing to re- 
frain from third-party “boycotts.” 

Last month’s ruling against Peterson, if upheld, will 
not only bar the chain from entering into third-party 
boycott agreements in the future, but will also prohibit 
the company from informing other pharmacies whether 
it will participate in various third-party drug programs. 

There are legitimate reasons for Peterson Drug to 
discuss the advantages and drawbacks of participa- 
tion in third-party drug plans—reasons that have 
nothing to do with conspiracies to boycott programs. 

Third-party programs establish the terms for partici- 
pation by pharmacies and offer those terms on a take-it- 
or-leave-it basis. Sometimes, reimbursement levels are 
set so low that participating pharmacies may actually 
lose money by filling these prescriptions. But ifa signifi- 
cant number of drug stores in the area participate in that 
program, it may be financial suicide to turn down the 
third-party’s reimbursement ultimatum. 

However, not all third-party plans attract high lev- 
els of pharmacy participation. Drug stores can safely 
decline to participate in these programs if reimburse- 
ment terms are unreasonable. 

The point is that drug stores have a legitimate rea- 
son to determine the degree of participation in third- 
party plans by other retail pharmacies. Indeed, with- 
out this information, it may be impossible to make an 
informed decision on whether or not to participate. 

Does the sharing of this information constitute 
proof cf a conspiracy to boycott third-party plans? I 
don’t think so. 

As long as pharmacies don’t mutually agree on a 
course of action, shouldn’t they be allowed to discuss 
their options with one another?

points, eye-catching and so- 
phisticated display techniques 
and promotional activity—has 
also fueled growth. At I got it 
at Gary’s, for instance, in-line 
hosiery is positioned near the 
cosmetics section and occa- 
sionally at the checkstands to 
pull traffic and boost impulse 
sales, said Edevane. 

Also fueling dollar growth 
in the category has been grow- 
ing demand for newer, less 
traditional fashion colors like 
black, off-black and navy. 

“We see a lot of interest in 
the sheer blacks and in ivory, 
and people are starting to ask 
for navy,” said one buyer.

U.S. marketing for Canada’s 
Siebruck Hosiery, “Navy blue 
is making trenendous gains, 
and black and off-black shades 
have replaced a lot of brown 
and suntan shades in some 
markets.” 

NAHM’s Howard acknowl- 
edged that “the basic nude and 
brown pantyhose are still the 
biggest sellers,” but added that 
“colors are a growth niche. We 
now seeing pale blues, pinks 
and greens, and a lot of ecology 
colors and earth tones.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, July 15, 1991 


Revco files reorg. plan 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Ina 
series of painstaking steps 
aimed at lifting itself out of a 
three-year bankruptcy, Rev- 
co D.S. has filed both a 
—_ disclosure statement 
and a plan of financial reorga- 
nization with U.S. Bankrupt- 
ey Court in recent weeks. 
Both must pass muster with 
Revco’s battery of creditors 
and with the court before the 
1,100-store chain can begin to 
emerge from Chapter 11. 

The disclosure statement, 
filed June 27 and now under 
review by Revco’s three 
creditors’ committees, exam- 
ines in detail how each class 
of creditor will be treated un- 
der the reorganization plan 
filed by Revco’s board earlier 
in June. That plan calls for 
the chain to swap its $1.45 bil- 
lion in debt obligations for a 
combination of equity in a 
post-bankrupt Revco, cash 
and new debt payment terms 
the company can manage out 
of existing cash flow. 

If the & is approved, sup- 
liers ‘tho are owed millions 
y Revco, as well as holders of 

its several classes of junk 
bonds, would trade in their 


claims against the company 
for a big chunk of ownership in 
the reorganized firm. 

The board’s plan, which 
along with the disclosure 
statement is still under review 
by creditors, also seeks the 
dismissal of most litigation 
arising out of the company’s 
1986 leveraged buyout. How- 
ever, Revco’s plan would still 
allow for court action against 
Salomon Brothers, which act- 
ed as principal investment 
banker for the LBO, and 
against former Revco manag- 
ers Sid and Mare Dworkin and 
Bill Edwards. 

U.S. Bankruptcy Court set 
an Aug. 2, 1991 hearing date 
for approval of the disclosure 
statement. Once approved, it 
will be sent with the reorgani- 
zation plan to all creditors and 
stockholders for a vote that 
could determine the compa- 
ny’s future. 

“This is a very important 
step toward bringing Revco 
out of bankruptcy,” Revco 
chairman and ceo Boake Sells 
said of the disclosure state- 
ment. “We believe our plans 
will fairly distribute Revco’s 
value.”

®@ Responding to criticism from 
retail pharmacists, the Arthritis 
Foundation has scrapped its 
controversial mail order drug 
program. The flap erupted when 
officials at NARD made the 
“shocking discovery” that CIBA 
was distributing Coupons in 
pharmacies offering purchasers 
of its Q-Vel leg cramp remedy 
discounts on membership in the 
foundation's mail order drug pro- 
gram. The druggists squawked, 
CIBA promptly cancelled the 
promo, and the foundation fol- 
lowed suit by ditching mail pro- 
gram altogether. 


@ Look for some key changes at 
FDA to cut the backlog of generic 
drug approvals and speed the 
ANDA process. One proposal 
would concentrate approval en- 
ergies on “blockbuster” gener- 
ics—drugs likely to produce sig- 
nificant economic savings in the 
marketplace. Another FDA plan 
would “encourage” pioneer drug 
manufacturers to share produc- 
tion tips with generic competitors 
in return for a carrot: extended 
patent life for their products.

Retailers rebound 
under the ‘Big D’ 


By Elizabeth Richardson 


ALLAS — The rebound is under 
way for retailers in “Big D.” 
deeply recessed in the late 
’80s, Dallas has recently experienced 
more upbeat economic conditions, and 
that is welcome news for pharmacy oper- 
ators in this highly diversified market. 
Yet, Someries A is different in Dallas 
than in most markets. With the successful 
retailing experiments of the ’70s, “Big D” 
evolved into “Big C”—indicative of the 
combination stores that have developed 
into such retail powerhouses here. 


Combo hotbed 


Since the short-lived Skaggs-Albert- 
son’s partnership of the ’70s, Dallas has 
been a hotbed of food/drug combo experi- 
mentation. Currently, the market. hosts 
seven combo operators. Together they 
command a 42 percent share of the pharma- 
ey market, according to the most recent 
igures compiled by Metro Market Studies. 

They are nationally operating Albert- 
son’s, Kroger, Winn Dixie and American 
Stores’ Skaggs Alpha Beta; and heavy 
hitting local players Tom Thumb Page, 
Minyard Food Stores (and its Sack ’N 
Save division) and Brookshire’s. 

Since the departure of Revco, Eckerd 
Drug and Drug Emporium remain the 
only national drug chains with strength in 
the Dallas market. 

The Metroplex also houses strong local 
chains, including True Quality and Town 
and Country, as well as several hundred 
independents scattered throughout the 
area. Also roiling the market are deep

Location: key to loyalty

the market, with so many choices avail- 
able. More often than not, in a market 
where an automobile is not just a conve- 
nience but a necessity, price and service 
have less impact than where the store is 
located, how accessible the parking lot is 
and whether involvement in major traffic 
areas is necessary in reaching the loca- 
tion. 


Niche touches and musts 


While operators in the area are highly 
involved in customer service, each has 
carved out a specific niche in which to 
lure its customers. These niches don’t 
necessary involve tactics that might be 
considered selling points in other mar- 
kets, however. In the energetic Dallas 
market, prompt checkout isn’t just a 
nice touch, its a must. Twenty-four 
hour stores aren’t just an advantage 
they’re a given. 

Tom Thumb Page, which operates 37 
combos, 15 free-standing drug stores 
and two discount stores in the area, 
pulls in its customers with flexible mer- 
chandising mixes. “Your particular im- 
age to the customer is what makes you 
different,” said Lee Roy Treadway, vp, 
pharmacy operations. “Our primary fo- 
cus is high merchandise levels. We’re 
competitive in pricing, but we’re not a 
low price leader and don’t try to be.” 

Skaggs Alpha Beta, strong in this 
market since its venture with Albert- 
son’s in the ’70s, will have new chal- 
lenges to face as it becomes part of the 
Osco drug network. Since February, 
the stores have been under the umbrella 
of American Drug Stores, giving the 
Oakbrook, Ill.-based Osco operational 
and merchandising control. The move 
promises to bring the Skaggs stores into 
the forefront with improved merchan- 
dising, new formats and even a new 
name. 


New identity for Skaggs 


While the stores still flag the Skaggs 
Alpha Beta banner, David Maher, ceo 
and president of American Drug Stores, 
told Drug Store News that the stores 
will be headed under the Osco name 
eventually. 

Kroger nurtures its strength in the 
market by allowing more leverage with 
decisions at the local level. This proves 
to be a big advantage for store managers 
to grab their share of the pie in the high- 
ly competitive Dallas market. Chain- 
wide, the company is placing more em- 
phasis on the service components of 
pharmacy, such as computerized re-

tion of insurance eligibility, which helps 
Kroger stand out as a service-oriented 
company. 


A roar from afar

have to contend with a new entry in the 
market by the beginning of next year. 
Food Lion, the eastern grocery chain 
firebrand is entering the market, with 
40 stores slated for the area within a 
year. The company has already been 
promoting ads featuring slashed prices. 

Food Lion’s stores won’t house phar- 
macies, which may cause them some 
problems. “This area is used to one-stop 
shopping,” said one Tom Thumb Page 
pharmacist. “Sure, customers may shop 
there a few times to check out their 
prices, but once they need their medica- 
tions, they’ll realize it’s easier and more 
convenient to shop us, rather than hav- 
ing to make two or three additional

OPINION 


Whatta rock! 

I mean a gem, a perfectly faceted, virtually flaw- 
less, one-carat sparkler that fits the finger like a 
glove. I don’t know why, but a diamond is what came 
to mind when I thought about Carls Drug. 

There have been a bunch of acquisitions over the 
past few years in the chain drug industry, but few 
seem as perfectly matched as the recently completed 
marriage of the Syracuse-based Fay’s drug chain and 
its smaller Rome, N.Y., 
cousin, Carls. 


I use the word cousin, 
rather than neighbor, de- 
liberately because the two 
chains spring from the 
Same Panasci family 
roots. Henry Panasci once 
worked as a pharmacist 
for his uncle Carl Panasci, 


IN THE MARKET 
BRUCE BUCKLEY 


for whom Carls is named. 

But the merger is much 

more than the story of family ties renewed. It’s the 

story of growth and promise for Fay’s in a relatively 

static period for retailers in general and chain drug 

companies in particular. For the most part, real estate 

developers have been sitting on sidelines, taking a 

breather; the once overflowing stream of potential 
sites has shrunk to a trickle. 

For Fay’s—a Northeastern powerhouse before the 
acquisition, with 199 drug stores in New York and 
Pennsylvania—the 43 new Carls stores represent at 
least two years of growth at about 10 percent per year. 
But few chains are achieving 10 percent growth in the 
currently stagnant real estate climate, and many are 
not growing at all. 


A diamond is a chain’s best friend 


Thus, a 20 percent expansion spurt coming on top of 
Fay’s existing store development plans is phenome- 
nal. The Carls stores represent an even better oppor- 
tunity than most. As a group, they’re mature, contrib- 
uting $100 million in sales right out of the gate. As 
they begin to reap the benefits of Fay’s strong hand in 
operations and merchandising, their per-store sales 
average is certain to begin to approach the current 
$3.4 million generated by a mature Fay’s drug store. 

Carls stores also fill in gaps in Fay’s market strong- 
holds in upstate New York, and thus fit in quite neatly 


Real estate developers have 
been sitting on the sidelines, 
taking a breather; the once 
overflowing stream of retail 
sites has shrunk to a trickle. 


under their parent’s advertising and distribution um- 
brella. What’s more, their size is compatible with 
Fay’s merchandise mix. Finally, they come supplied 
with experienced store personnel. Who could ask for 
more? 

The acquired stores already sport the Fay’s logo 
and feature its merchandise mix, but when the re- 
make is total and when all the stores are equipped with 
Fay’s new POS scanning system, the result is going to 
be dynamic. 

Diamonds may or may not be forever, but they can 
certainly cause a lot of excitement for now. 


Rebecca C. is a frail 82-year-old pharmacy customer 
in Daviess County, Ky. She has grown hard of hearing 
in recent years—enough to warrant purchase of a $400 
hearing aid last year. But since her less-than-nimble 
fingers couldn’t deftly maneuver the battery door, 
that broke off the hinge. And since her straining eyes 
couldn’t read the engraving on the miniature battery, 
that was never replaced. 

These problems, plus a hard-to-overcome sensitiv- 

ity about being hard of 


hearing, caused her to 
cope without using the 
hearing aid until her 
daughter visited from 
New York this spring. 
The daughter, Elizabeth, 
grew hoarse repeating 
herself and shouting to be 
heard. Determined to get 
her mom communicating 
freely, Elizabeth marched 
her off to an audiologist, hearing aid in hand. | 

Dr. Etienne, the audiologist, had been promoting a 
new, more flexible hearing aid. Rebecca and Eliza- 
beth were prepared to invest in another unit, reason- 
ing that it would be worth the outlay, if mom would be 
more disposed to use it. Etienne instead repaired the 
old hearing aid and, speaking slowly and distinctly, 
gave mom tips on how to use and maintain it. Mother 
and daughter were ecstatic. 

Rebecca visited New York this summer, in part to 
see another doctor about another medical problem. 


THE HUMAN 
SIDE 
AL HELLER 


Listening to the elderly has its rewards 


The day before this appointment, the battery 
“squeaked and died,” said Elizabeth. 

Concerned that her mother wouldn’t be able to hear 
the doctor the next day, Elizabeth went to her local 
chain drug store to buy more batteries, but the phar- 
macist said the numbers on mom’s battery didn’t cor- 
respond to the batteries in stock. 

At 11 p.m., Elizabeth was on the phone with a Wal- 
greens store manager in nearby Yonkers, who said he 
carried about 15 specialty batteries and if she came to 
the store he’d help her find the correct replacement cell. 

Elizabeth’s husband persuaded her not to make a 
late-night trip, reasoning that all chains probably sold 
the same kinds of batteries. 

The next morning, Elizabeth, still worried, left the 
doctor’s waiting room, hearing aid in hand, and scur- 
ried across the street to Schoonmaker Medical Phar- 
macy, an independent in Scarsdale. 

Once again, a pharmacist took the time to examine 
his battery assortment, going so far as to open a pack- 
age he thought contained an equivalent cell. (Battery 
makers, take note.) He was right, and within minutes, 
mom’s ear was turned on. 

“It’s so easy to think that elderly people’s minds 
wander, but they can understand so much when they 
can HEAR you,” said Elizabeth, who admitted “talk- 
ing around, across and over her (mom) because she 
wasn’t participating in the conversation.” 

Elderly customers may not be the loudest or buy the 
most, but they are the demographic group of the fu- 
ture for retailers. And they can teach us all a few les- 
sons—if we will only listen.

SUMMARY: The market for 
paperback books and maga- 
zines went into a tailspin late 
last year, feeling the brunt of 
the economic downturn. 
Nevertheless, periodicals 
represent a major traffic 
draw in chain drug outlets 
and a source of almost guar- 
anteed return on investment. 
What’s more, some success- 
ful startup publications have 
created some bright spots. 


By James Frederick 

The recession hasn’t been 
kind to the book and magazine 
industries. Single-copy sales of 

eriodicals were off significant- 
y in 1990 and early 1991, and 
hundreds of publications folded 
or were merged with rivals. 

Although the $3.6 billion in 
retail sales racked up by mag- 
azines last year would have 
looked good back in the mid- 
1980s, it marked a 4.1 percent 
decline in revenues from the 
industry’s record-setting level 
of 1989. And if it hadn’t been 
for a strong first half, the 1990 
decline would have been far 
worse: second-half sales were 
off a whopping 9.3 percent in 
dollars and 9.8 percent in units 
versus the year earlier. 

For paperback books, the 
story was even worse. Paper- 
back book sales were off 10.9 

ercent in dollars last year, to 
$2.11 billion, and off a star- 
tling 17.4 percent in units, to 
440 million retail copies sold.

reading public with extra value.

the spigot on new publica-

the Magazine Publishers of 
America, 536 new magazines 
debuted in 1990. That’s 68 ti- 
tles fewer than the number in- 
troduced the previous year. 
The survival rate for those 
1989 rollouts has been 50 per- 
cent or less, the industry 
group reports. 

The slackoff in demand— 
combined with the magazine

Technicians: Boon or bane to busy pharmacists? 


By Susan Ball 


n some states, the “T” 

word—as in pharmacy 

technician—doesn’t offi- 
cially exist. 

In other states, pharmacy 
technicians, although they 
may be termed “ancillary” or 
“supportive” or “nonlicensed” 
personnel, are not only legally 
recognized, but tightly regu- 
lated as to what they can and 
cannot do. 

One state, for exampie, may 
stipulate that techs can’t take a 
drug off the pharmacy shelf, 
but can put it back, while anoth- 
er state allows techs to fill a pre- 
scription from shelf back to 
shelf, so to speak, as long as 
they’re under a pharmacist’s 
supervision. Some states speci- 
fy a 1-to-1 tech-to-pharmacist 
ratio in retail settings and a 2- 
to-1 or 3-to-1 ratio for institu- 
tions such as hospitals, while 
others don’t address ratios. 


States split on recognition 


A survey published -in 
APhA’s American Pharmacy 
in June, conducted by a group 
from the University of Tennes- 
see College of Pharmacy, found 
that 25 states recognize phar- 
macy technicians by statute or 
regulation and 25 do not. 

hether techs are licensed, 
certified or registered also 
varies by state. 

In summary, “It’s a patch- 
work quilt of different regula- 
tions from state to state,” said 
Mike Eaton, director of opera- 
tions, Association of Pharma- 
cy Technicians (APT). 

But whereas even two or 
three years ago, the main is- 


he arena is shifting, with some vehe- 


ment exceptions, toward not only tolerating 
techs behind the Ra counter, but lobbying for 
more of them, with expanded responsibilities. 


sue was whether pharmacy 
technicians should be counte- 
nanced at all, the arena is 
shifting, with some vehement 
exceptions, toward not only 
tolerating techs behind the 

harmacy counter, but lobby- 
ing for more of them, with ex- 
panded responsibilities. 

As a pharmacist who once 


DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, August 26, 1991 


worked for a large drug chain 
put it, “Yeah, we had techs— 
we had to. We constantly 
begged for more!” 

ne force thrusting techs 
into the spotlight is the spread 
of mandatory consultation. In 
California, where mandatory 
counseling goes into effect Jan. 
1, a bill to recognize pharmacy 


technicians is making its way 
through the Legislature, and 
among its proponents on record 
are Pay Less and Longs. Said 
John Young, vp-pharmacy ser- 
vices in charge of Pay Less’ 
pharmacies in California, “If 
mandatory counseling goes into 
effect without pharmacy tech- 
nicians, it would be a Catch 22 
situation—the worst possible 
scenario.” 


Pharmacist shortage factor 


Another impetus is the 
movement to make Pharm.D 
the entry level degree for 
pharmacists. “The use of 
aon technicians will 

ave to go up, in light of man- 
datory counseling and 
Pharm.D’s impact on the 
pharmacist shortage,” pre- 
dicted a senior pharmacy ex- 
ecutive at a large mass mer- 
chandise chain. 

He added, “Technicians can 
relieve pharmacists of yscogom 
and pouring and licking an 
sticking—which isn’t what they 
went to pharmacy school for— 
so pharmacists can do what 
they’re sup to do, which is 
counsel an rvise.” 

California’s current legisla- 
tive activity illustrates man 
of the crosscurrents surround- 
ing pharmacy technicians. 
The state has tried before, un- 
successfully, to legislate the 
use of pharmacy techs, but 
those HF rescten for the current 
bill are “cautiously optimistic” 
of its chances. 

The bill, AB 1244, would per- 
mit the use of pharmacy techni- 
cians, with specified restric-

cuts in pharmacists’ jobs or

that safety will be jeopar-

only), Alaska, Hawaii, Mon-

States take action on voluntary certification 


Michigan and Illinois al- 
ready have voluntary certifi- 
cation processes in place and 
are beginning to franchise 
their programs to other 
sta’ es. 

Michigan was the first state 
to establish a voluntary certifi- 
cation process, in 1981. Its pat- 
ented Pharmacy Certified 
Technician (PCT) program con- 
sists of a manual and examina- 
tion. The exam is designed to 
cover the body of knewledge 
needed by both community and 
ae pharmacy technicians, 
said Lou Sesti, ceo, Michigan 
Pharmacists Association, 
which funded the p ’ 

“Certification has helped 
people get jobs and get better 
salaries,” Sesti said. “It’s 
strictly a voluntary program 
to measure knowledge. Michi- 
gan has left it to the market- 
place to determine what train- 
——— be required.” 

ince 1981, the test has 
been taken 3,604 times (some 
take it more than once), and 
the pass rate is about 50 per- 
cent. Sesti said those seeking 
certification are about evenly 
split between community and 


hospital technicians. The day- 
long exam was initially given 
once a year, but is now offered 
on two consecutive days twice 
a year, because of demand. 


Other states interested 


Iowa is working out a licens- 
ing 5 to use Michi- 
gan’s PCT program, and Arizo- 
na has it under consideration, 
Sesti said. Michigan’s manual 
will be supplemented with 
Iowa law, and the first exam 
will be offered next spring, an 
Iowa Pharmacy Association 
spokesman said. 

“What I feel is that techni- 
cians will be getting recogni- 
tion,” said Ronda Chapman, a 
pharmacy technician in a Wal- 
greens in Des Moines, who is on 
a committee preparing a bro- 
chure to inform pharmacists 
and techs about the program. 
“Also, it will help pharmacists 
know which ie Glace, who 
take the exam and become cer- 
tified, know a little bit more 
about pharmacy.” 

Illinois’ voluntary certifica- 
tion program was funded by 
the Illinois Council of Hospital 
Pharmacists (an affiliate of the 


American Society of Hospital 
Pharmacists), which “saw a 
need to recognize the knowl- 
edge base that working tech- 
nicians already had,” and 
weed out those with insuffi- 
cient knowledge, said Jan 
Keresztes, a member of the 
council’s certification task 
force and coordinator of the 
technician training program 
at South Suburban College, 
South Holland, II. 


Advantages of certification 


Keresztes ticked off some 
advantages certification af- 
fords technicians, including 
job security, higher salaries 
and more responsibility. 

South Carolina is in the pro- 
cess of contracting for the IIli- 
nois voluntary certification 


prog 

If Michigan and Illinois con- 
tinue to franchise their volun- 
tary certification programs to 
other states, either program 
might become the embryo of a 
model voluntary certification 
program to roll out nation- 
wide. Thus, the goal the 
ASHP set in June could be on 
its way to attainment.

By Elizabeth Parks 

NEW ORLEANS — The 
second annual Exclusively 
HBA show, which ran here 
earlier this month, had some 
weak spots, but as a whole at- 
tendees rated it fairly high and 
many small to mid-size vendor 
companies said they had a 

t show. 

Many of the retailers who 
attended also gave the show 
good marks, with plenty to see 
and lots of leads to follow up. 

Although the show is pri- 
marily skewed to mass mer- 
chandise accounts, wholesale 


membership clubs and whole- 
saler/distributors, there were 
a fair number of drug chains in 
attendance. 

According to Jay Spauld- 
ing, the show’s principal and 
ceo, drug chains accounted for 
10 percent of the companies in 
attendance and 13 percent of 
the buyers. 

Among the major drug com- 
panies walking the floor this 

ear were American Drug, 

ig B, Hareco, K&B, Drug 
Emporium, Revco, Sid’s Get 
it For Less and Thrifty. 

As it turned out, many drug 


and food chains did elect to 
pass on this show because, as 
several told us, it duplicates so 
much of what they’ve seen at 
trade shows sponsored by the 
National Association of Chain 
Drug Stores and the Food 
Marketing Institute. Howev- 
er, the consensus among the 
drug and food retailers who 
came was that the show was 
worth attending.

combo chain just before the start of the football season to

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 30, 1991 _ 


OPINION 


Carrots work. But sometimes sticks are better. 

Wal-Mart took the latter approach when it informed 
vendors earlier this year that it would no longer toler- 
ate a casual approach to UPC product coding. Make no 
mistake: Wai-Mart carries a big stick. 

The discount giant told its product suppliers that 
it would impose stiff fines for violating UPC stan- 
dards: 10 percent of the purchase order for a first of- 

fense and up to $100,000 


(or 10 percent—whichev- 
er is higher) for three- 
time losers. 

Privately, some of Wal- 
Mart’s approximately 


IN THE MARKET) 5,000 vendors expressed 
outrage at the penalty 


BRUCE BUCKLEY 
system. But, of course, 
* nobody rebelled. Selling 


products into Wal-Mart 


stores is a pretty strong 


incentive for compliance. 

The result of the get-tough policy? Scanning accura- 
cy has improved from the 91 or 92 percent level to 95 
percent, Curtis Arend, administrative manager of 
Wal-Mart’s UPC item file, told Drug Store News se- 
nior editor David Vaczek. For Wal-Mart, the goal of 
98 percent is going to require continuing vigilance, 
plus resolving some of its own problems with internal 
coding procedures, Arend said. 

In improving the integrity of its product file, Wal- 
~ Mart gains in its ability to buy and manage inven- 
tory. The discounter already sets the standard for 
distribution efficiency, but if it is to achieve its long- 
term growth goals, it cannot afford to rest on its 


Wal-Mart carries a big stick and will use it 


achievements. 

Advantages also accrue to Wal-Mart’s vendors. 
Cleaner UPC files mean more accurate and timely 
national and regional product movement informa- 
tion, better forecasting and stronger marketing all 
around. 

Accurate UPCs also benefit the drug store indus- 
try, many of whose companies are now fully scan- 
ner-equipped or rolling out systems. Wal-Mart’s 
“stick” may thus cast a longer shadow than anyone 
anticipated. 

* * * 

Retailing may be in the doldrums because of the 
sputtering economic recovery, but it would be hard to 
tell that from the robust activity of the three leading 
deep discounters profiled in this issue. Their growth 
has been nothing short of phenomenal. 

While many other chains have gently tugged on the 
expansion reins, Phar-Mor, Drug Emporium and 
F&M have taken off at a furious pace, galloping into 
new markets with a loud clatter. 

They are also relentlessly increasing their penetra- 
tion of existing markets. They may eventually bang 
into some restraining wall out there, but they have not 
seen it yet. Overstoring is a word not found in their 
dictionaries. 

In today’s economy, it’s imperative to understand 
what’s motivating customers. The Big 3—and oth- 
ers in this rapidly expanding retailing segment— 
have a firm grasp on the worrisome forces confront- 
ing consumers. 

Their price-driven approach in high-demand prod- 
uct categories is a tonic that will propel growth both 
now and well into the future. 


Kids needie Va. governor on drug abuse 


A statewide drug abuse essay contest, sponsored 
by 85 Cardinal Drug Centers in Virginia, elicited 
sharp observations, fresh wisdom—and some disturb- 
ing comments—from the 200 five-to-fourteen-year- 
olds who entered. Their job was to write a two-page 
— to Governor Wilder, telling him how to halt drug 
abuse. 

The contest was conceived by a marketing team at 
five-store-operator Rich- 
mond Apothecaries, 


owned by pharmacist Dan 
Herbert, who signed onto 
the Cardinal network 
about 13 months ago. Lau- 
ra Peery, a consultant for 
Cardinal, took the idea 
networkwide, using Car- 
dinal’s greater statewide 
presence to involve more 
people. 

Cardinal, the franchised coop program of wholesal- 
er Owens & Minor, has for the past year hosted an 
hour-long program, Kids and Drugs, every other 
Thursday on BLAB, a cable television station broad- 
cast throughout Greater Richmond. 

The anti-drug messages aired here, posters hung in 
stores, and cooperative work with the Greater Rich- 
mond Informed Parents group, got some young juices 
stirring during the summertime contest, which ended 
with winner Jason Daugherty and 12 runners-up be- 
ing feted at a Triple A Richmond Braves baseball 
game on Aug. 29. 

From Jason, age 12 of Shacklefords, Va.: “Keep 
kids busy doing activities that are fun and benefi- 
cial. . school projects, state highway cleanups. . . 
Construct a facility in schools. . .where kids can talk 
to other kids about taking drugs and what could hap- 
pen. . .train kid counselors to talk to other kids 
. . -put books, cassette tapes and videotapes in public 
and school libraries.” 


THE HUMAN 
SIDE 
AL HELLER 


From 9-yeai-old Merenda Garnett Kranz, second 
place, of Louisa, Va.: “Have one person for each school 
that has the experience of drugs. That person will tell 
what they went through. They will also tell what other 
drugs do to you. 

“The person might be from jail. People from jail who 
don’t do drugs anymore and are going to be let out of 
jail can do that for a job.” 

From 11-year-old Robert Brown, third place, of 
Richmond: “Taking drugs is like melting iron. Tak- 
ing drugs is killing all good memories. Let’s keep our 
memories alive!” He urged that drug users surren- 
der their cars, be treated longer in hospitals, hear 
loving words from their families and be educated 
better. 

Herbert, 48, who served as president of the Vir- 
ginia Pharmaceutical Association in 1987, ex- 
plained: “Parents say the problems are in school, the 
school says it’s at home. We wanted to hear from the 
kids what they think people around them should be 
doing about drugs.” He termed the contest a “quali- 
ty success,” but noted that the back-to-school pro- 
motion and contest tie-in raised BTS sales in his 
stores just 15 percent (“the recession,” he says), 
compared with gains in prior years of 20 percent to 
25 percent. : 

Next year, Cardinal will extend the program into 
September and possibly January for greater school in- 
volvement, said Peery. Herbert said he’d like to see 
1,000 entries in 1992. 

The need for balance in anti-drug messages was 
brought home vividly by five-year-old Maria Black- 
well of Richmond, who wrote: “No drug stores. Only 
groceries with medicine. Throw them in jail.” 

Said Herbert: “Young kids don’t distinguish be- 
tween legal and illegal drugs. We have a generation of 
kids growing up associating drug stores as bad places. 
We need long-term education about the positive role 
of pharmaceuticals in life, and teach that drug stores 
are not the source of drug abuse.”

conditioners and bergamots.

care product
