Hair styles, fashion trends 


Comb kits and cur! kits, 
however, are down, reflecting 
the changes in hair styling 
away from the curl. 

From the fashion perspec- 
tive, there is only one new hot 
hair style shaking up the mar- 
ket, and that’s the wrap, which 
everyone says is getting more 
and more popular each day. 

“The wrap has become very 
popular and it’s getting 
stronger and stronger,” says 
Pearlman. Because of the 
wrap, a new product segment 
has emerged: wrap lotions.” 

“The wrap continues to be 
hot all across the country,” 
says Jones, “and that’s been 
great for the sales of styling lo- 
tions that women need to keep 
the style in place.” 

Jones also notes that black 
men are still wearing their hair 
short. The high top look is still 
popular with the sides tapered 
and the hair on top cut high and 
flat. “Texturizers are selling 
well to men,” Jones says. “They 
help make hair more manage- 
able, and you see guys still us- 
ing lots of gels and lotions to 
keep their hair set in place.” 

J.M. Products has an Iso- 
plus Wrap Lotion that is doing 
very well at retail. Other 
brands also singled out are 
Revion’s Wrap & Tap, doing 
well in the salon market place 
as well as at retail when it’s 
available, and Pro Line’s 
Wrap Lotion, one of the first 
wrap products to go retail. 

Pearlman says another new 
look is starting to develop at the 
salon level: the Waffle Wave. 
He says it’s too soon to tell how 
big it may get or how long it will 
last, but he describes it as a 
“nice look” which requires the 
use of curling rods and setting 
lotions to maintain. 

“The waffle wave is not a 
curl,” says Jones, “it’s reall 
waves, but they’re all throu 
the hair, not just at the ends. 
It’s quite attractive, and it 
also requires the use of styling 
aids to lock in the hair.” 

_ Jones also sees another styl- 
ing trend emerging. “What’s 
old is new again,” she says.

| Buying better raises 
Genovese’s net income 


| |. MELVILLF, N.Y. — Genovese Drug Stores raised its net 

income 54.5 pent for the second quarter and 44.7 percent for 
the first half ened Aug. 16. Jerome Stengel, vp and treasurer, 
said the dramatic increases were largely attributable to control- 
ling expenses and “buying better.” 

Net income for the quarter was $1.2 million, on sales of $100.5 
million, compared with net income of $795,000 for the year-ago 
period, on sales of $96.9 million. 

For the half, net income was $2.7 million, on sales of $233.5 
million, versus net income of $1.9 million, on sales of $225.4 mil- 
lion, in the previous first half.

The bout continues over mail order pharmacy 


By Dianne Tharp, R.Ph. 

What are your feelings about 
mail order haveaie? 

Those three little words evoke 
strong emotions, con and pro, 
from people in pharmacy—with 
no middle ground apparent. 

The most visible battle today 
pits NARD against the Ameri- 
can Managed Care Pharmacy 
Association (AMCPA). NARD, 
the national association repre- 
senting independent pharma- 
cists, has ~~ as its priority a 
campaign to discredit and he 
mantle organized mail service 
pharmacy. In its monthly jour- 
nal, it devotes a page to © Mail 
Order Alert’—a series of items 
detailing victories, alleging 
bi ge ae pricing and tax 

reaks, documenting misfills 
by mail, and offering strategies 


to compete. 
Old adversaries 


But this is not a new war. In 
1983, NARD established a mail 
order problems clearinghouse 
with the Michigan Pharmacists 
Association to — ammuni- 
tion for its escalating battle. In 
NARD literature, mail order 
pharmacy and pharmacists are 
often ni Bao to as “second- 
rate, unregulated, . . .danger- 
ous’ and a “public health 
threat.” 

The battle spills over to the 
legal front, too. The Insurance 
Competitive Pricing Act 


nsurance Competitive Pricing Act: 


hopes to repeal insurance companies’ 


exemption from antitrust prosecution. 


[H.R.9/S.430] is the latest legal 
attempt to loosen the foothold 
home-delivered prescription 
services have gained in society. 
H.R.9 hopes to repeal insur- 
ance companies exemption 
from antitrust prosecution— 
which is how health insurance

forces patients to use mail or- 
der, according to NARD. And 
NARD’s latest complaint is 
with HCFAs draft regulations 
for OBRA ‘90, moons Orn or- 
der firms from the verbal coun- 
seling requirement. 

All this seems to have pushed 


oe mail order organization too 
ar. 

In an August 16 letter to the 
Federal Trade Commission, 
AMCPA executive vp Delbert 
Konnor urged the FTC to de- 
clare NARD’s campaign unlaw- 
ful, and to take action to “pre- 
vent consumers from bein 
misled by NARD’s unfair an 
unsubstantiated claims.” 

NARD responded by firing 
off its own letter to the FTC ask- 
ing for an investigation into 
AMCPA pricing procedures. 
Stay ‘enn for the next volley. 

The AMCPA is a trade associa- 
tion comprising 11 mail order 
firms, with 11 pharmaceutical 
manufacturers (brand and gener- 
ic) as associate members. as- 
sociation was organized to de- 
fend and promote the efforts of 
mail service pharmacy. Estab- 
lished in 1975 as the National 
Mail Service Pharmacy Associa- 
tion, the organization changed 
its name four years later. 

While ‘some people suggest 
that the name change was an at- 
tempt to disguise its mission, 
AMCPA insists that the new 
name symbolizes a change in fo- 
cus from the seviinn ate prod- 
uct to the provision of a service, 
which includes information 
management, prescription 
monitoring and other value- 
added services on the clients re- 
quest. But all this service has a

price to Del Konnor, “Only if 
the program beneficiaries are 
willing to pay for service will

Konnor describes mail ser- 
vice as highly structured, cen- 
tralized dispensing with cost 
containment and cost efficiency 
achieved through low over- 
head, generic dispensing, vol- 
ume-buying power, the effi-

dispensing process. 


Cost benefit? 


But does mail order really 
save money, and for whom? 
While third parties like Virginia 
Blue Cross and New York Med- 
icaid are adding a new mail or- 
der benefit in the belief that it 
does, and Medco Containment 
Services now fills 450,000 pre- 
scriptions per week, some who 
have experience with mail or- 
der are dropping this provision 
in their health 3 ag According 
to Marion's Managed Care Di- 
gest study of 1990, 16 percent of 
HMO ’s had mail order in 1988; 


only 8 percent had it in 1989. 

Other benefits managers see 
no a with mail order phar- 
macy plans. Henry Blissen- 
bach, vp of pharmacy programs 
for UHC’s Diversified Pharma- 
ceutical Services “has not found 
one [mail order company] in- 
cluding the largest, that would 
save us any money. In Third 
Party Rx newsletter, Richard 
Eckstrom, president of Cost 
Containment Corp., was 

uoted as saying that most of 
the savings in mail order benefit 
he has studied go to the em- 

loyee. He said he stresses to 
bis clients that mail order is less 
likely to be a cost saver for the 
employer. 

Asked if mail order saves mon- 
ey for the benefits provider, 
Mitch Wasserman, vp of corpo- 
rate development at Insurex, 
Inc., replied: “It depends on the 
plan design and the mail order 
vendor. Interestingly, Wasser- 
man noted that employees tend 
to view mail order pharmacy ser- 
vice as an enhancement to their 
benefits which could enable em- 


ployers to cut other benefits, 
whether or not mail order actual- 


ly saves money. 

Dr. Ken Kirk, Texas College 
of Pharmacy at Austin, ana- 
lyzed his own university s pro- 
posed mail order plan and dis- 
covered that, in his opinion, 
“adequate data was not pre- 
sented to show that Medco 
would save money over retail 
[pharmacies].” 

And Beach Hall, recently re- 
tired director of health care op- 
erations for General Motors, 
told execs attending the 
NACDS Pharmaceutical Con- 
ference, that GM's seven-year- 
old mail order benefit is, “at 
best, a break-even operation. 
He added that the auto giant's 
mail order scripts are stable at 7 
percent, and not a threat to 
well-run retail pharmacies ac- 
tive in patient interaction. 
Asked if he would use the mail 
order benefit himself, Hall re- 
oan that he will continue to 

ave his prescriptions filled at 
his community (independent) 
pharmacy. 

What about all the studies of 
mail order that are touted by 
proponents and opponents with 
such fervor ae certitude? 


Kirking and Ascione in “An 
Analysis of Research on Mail 
Order Pharmacy Services cri- 
tiqued 10 adios comparing 
mail order with community 
pharmacy services. They ex- 
plain the conflicting results of 
various studies is partly the re- 
sult of variations in types of 
plans and populations studied. 
The bottom line of their analy- 
sis: “A definitive assessment of 
the economic issues related to 
mail order pharmacy services, 
along with patient satisfaction 
and other measures of quality, 
cannot be made based on exist- 
ing research.” 

They conclude that objective, 
readily available, quality re- 
search comparing mail order to 
community pharmacy services, 
including quality of care issues, 
identifying drugs better suited 
for longer term dispensing and 
optimum days a apr medica- 


tions, has yet to be done. 

This need for more informa- 
tion is supported by Wasserman. 
He said that until recently, most 
studies were comparing mail or- 
der services to card programs.

Insurex also collects data on in- 
demnity programs, and, since 
75 percent of employers pro- 
vide prescription drug benefits 
through major medical pro-

In spite of the apparent defi- 
ciencies in existing studies, or- 
ganizations such as the AMA 
and the ASHP use them to sup- 
port their positions. AMA says 
that mail order pharmacy is ap- 
propriate for patients with long- 
term chronic illnesses who have 
been adequately informed 
about their medicines. And 
ASHP says mail service phar- 
macies are “viable alternatives’ 
for maintenance meds. One 
pharmacy benefits manage- 
ment company run by pharma- 
cists, which asked not to be 
identified, offers mail order as 
an alternative, but focuses on 
walk-in pharmacies as the back- 
bone of its business based on ex- 
isting studies. 


A new pilot program 


Hopefully, a better basis for 
deciding about mail order will 
come from studies like the 
Tufts/PCS maintenance drug 
program. 

Robert C. Johnson of PCS, 
co-sponsor of the study, cites 
the price emphasis of the past, 
and today’s shift to cost-effec- 


tive health care as the reason 


for the Tufts study, which be- 
gins this month. The Massa- 
chusetts HMO will use PCS’ 
RECAP to dispense mainte- 
nance medicines to the chroni- 


cally ill as an alternative to 
mail order. The major differ- 
ence between this program 
and mail order are the initial 
dispensing of a trial quantity, 
with refills at maintenance 
quantities, so less waste is an- 
ticipated. 

Also unique to this study: 
pharmacists will be reimbursed 
at a 25-percent fee increase for 
each additional 30 days supply 
dispensed. In effect, the phar- 
macist will receive more money 
for playing a role in compliance 
and managing patient care. As a 
result of this study, the hope is 
that payors will better under- 
sank the important role of 
pharmacist hands-on patient 
care, says Johnson. 

Not only are traditional phar- 
maceutical suppliers paying at- 
tention to eh order, but also 
some pharmacy educators have 
expressed concerns regarding 
new educational opportunities. 
Today's students learn face-to- 
face communication, physical as- 
sessment, patient observation 
and clinical intervention. 

Does the curriculum need to 
be modified to better prepare 
the pharmacy students who 
elect to practice in the mail or- 
der environment? A recent em- 
ployment ad for National Rx 
Services touts a four- or five-day 
week, free nights and week- 
ends, and part-time hours, if 
desired. From a scheduling 
perspective alone, mail service 
pharmacy can offer students an 
advantage over most chain out- 
lets, and may be in the students 
future employment plans. 

So, given the great concern of 
all noted, controversies over 
study results and negative cam- 
paign efforts of organized phar- 
macy groups, how do we ac- 
count for the continued growth 
of mail order? It has been sug- 
gested that aggressive market- 
ing by mail nodes companies to 
corporate buyers is one of the 
reasons for the growth. If so, 
community pharmacies can 
compete if they establish the 
value of their pharmacy servic- 
es with benefits managers. As 
farfetched as it might seem, 
even greater effectiveness 
would result if chains and inde-

garg market together to 
oth benefits managers and 
customers. 

The fact that community 
pharmacies can also compete 
on price is being demonstrat- 
ed. Rx-1, for example, is a co- 
operative of 40 independents 
in 14 states that put together a 
pricing handbook to beat ev- 
ery AARP top 100 price, and 
have experienced an increase 
in business as a result. 


What’s in store? 


With all these alternatives be- 
ing offered to mail order, what is 
the future of mail order pharma- 
cy service? Del Konnor predicts 
greater than $6 billion, or 15 per- 
cent of all prescriptions filled in 
1995, will by provided by mail 
service pharmacies. John Mc- 
Hugh, president of Retired Per- 
sons Services, Inc., does not feel 
the industry has matured, but is 
more conservative in his growth 
prediction. 

Konnor sees three key 
growth areas for mail order 
pharmacy: 
® information ——— 

@ performance and account- 
ability 
® patient services 
He believes mail order will 

lay a major role in a national 
health care scheme with such 
value-added services as timely 
management data reports, pre- 
scriber and patient reports, a 
system to monitor compliance 
and drug interactions, and clin- 
ical services like patient educa- 
tion and compliance monitor- 
ing. Those who hope to 
compete should take note. 

Since the first mail order pre- 
scription was shipped by the Vet- 
erans Administration in 1946, 
some opponents are gradually 
coming to realize that there may 
be an acceptable, limited role for 
the service in contemporary 
pharmacy practice. 

Although a policy statement of 
the AMCPA equates Freedom- 
of-Choice legislation with eco- 
nomic protectionism, their vp 
has perhaps said it best: “. . .the 
consumer has been and will con- 
tinue to be the best judge of the 
acceptance of home-delivered 
pharmacy services.” =

Gerald Heller honored 


NEW YORK — Gerald Heller will be honored with the Torch 
of Learning Award at a dinner at the Grand Hyatt on Dec. 5 by 
the Pharmacy and Mass Merchandising Divison of the American 
Friends of the Hebrew University. Heller, president of Tulsa, 
Okla.-based May’s Drug Stores, is being recognized for his com- 
mitment to pharmacy research and education. 

_ Heller is a member of the Oklahoma Pharmaceutical Associa- 
tion, is chairman of the University of Oklahoma College of Phar- 
macy’s Dean’s Advisory Committee and serves on the NACDS 
board of directors and executive committee. 


Stone, cfo, named to Perry board 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores senior vp and cfo Jer- 
ry Stone has taken a seat on Perry’s board of directors, filling a 


vacancy left by the resignation of former president and chief op- 
erating officer David Schwartz. 


Stone joined Perry in April, 1989 after a stint as vp-manufac- 
turing for Talon, Inc., and 23 years at Arthur Andersen & Co. 


Arbor exec tops Michigan Rx board 


TROY, Mich. — John Enokian, vp-health services at Arbor 
Drugs, has been elected chairman of the Michigan Board of 
Pharmacy. The six-year board member will direct meetings, 
oversee pharmacy activities in tho state and serve as liaison be. 
tween the board and the National Association of Boards of Phar- 
macy (NABP). 

_At Arbor, Enokian handles third-party contract negotia- 
tions, represents the company in government affairs and han- 
dies other pharmacy-related issues. He began his pharmacy ca- 
reer at Arbor’s first store in 1965.

McKesson: progress on waste issue 


ATLANTA — McKesson Drug Co. has contracted with BFI 
Pharmaceutical Services on a new controlled substances return 
and waste disposal program, making it the first pharmaceutical 
and HBA wholesaler to establish such a system. _ 

The contract, slated to begin this month, is for a pilot program 
at the wholesaler’s distribution center in this city and is limited 
to the disposal of controlled pharmaceutical products. That con- 
tract may be ded to include returns of all classes of pre- 
scription and other products.  —__ 

BFI Pharmaceutical Services, a division of Browning-Ferris 
Industries, uses a computerized tracking and waste profiling 
system which assists manufacturers and wholesalers in credit- 


ing procedures for the processed products.

By Elizabeth Parks 

NEW ORLEANS — From 
a product perspective, there 
was a lot to see and learn at 
this_year’s second annual Ex- 
clusively HBA Show here. 

Over 340 suppliers on the 
floor showed their wares to 
the 541 retailer/wholesaler 
buyers in attendance. In com- 

arison to the NACDS Mar- 

2 Spied show, Exclusively 
HBA skews more to toiletries 
and to the smaller or second 
tier cosmetic companies. 

The biggest. cosmetic com- 
panies there were Revlon/AI- 
may, L’Oréal, and Max Fac- 
tor; except for Factor, these 
companies have strong toilet- 
ry and cosmetic divisions. 

Although many buyers at the 
show said they hoped io see 
more cosmetic companies on 
the floor next year, it still isn’t 
clear what direction this show 
will take when it convenes in 
Denver next September. 

One source for a company 
that attended said he was im- 
pressed with “the caliber” of 
the buyers who did attend. 

There were no dramatic 
launches here, but there were 
hundreds of well thought out 
promotions for the first and 
second quarter of 1992 plus 
hundreds of new niche items 
and clever marketing con- 
cepts. Given all the excite- 
ment that’s happening with 
kids’ toiletries this year, the 
new body sculptured carded 
cosmetics from Ducair Tsu- 
mura stood out. 

This newest addition to the 
Kid Care family features 
three Little Mermaid groom-

accessories, and two Turtle 
accessories—each with the 
shape of the characters sculp-

service staffers. Jonee offers 
19 treatment products ad- 
dressing specific needs like 
nail biting or fungus. 

But how can a consumer 
know which does which if 
there’s no cosmetician to help 
her? Jonee’s lets the consumer 
educate themselves by read- 
ing a little color-coded dot af- 
fixed to each treatment prod- 
uct. Each dot now specifies 
what each treatment can do.

Florida lawsuit over risqué photo has 
drug chains weighing exposure 


TAMPA — A lawsuit currently pending 
a Eckerd and some former employees— 
which alleges that a staffer duplicated a partial- 
ly nude photo of a customer without authoriza- 
tion—may prompt drug chains to reevaluate 
their photofinishing policies. _ 

The saga began when Wendy Ellington’s 
friend snapped a picture of her partially nude, 
then sent the roll of film to Eckerd to be devel- 
oped. Matthew Powell, her attorney, said EI- 


lington saw the photo, burned it and the - 


tive, and forgot all about it—at least until the 
rey ny y turned up at a party three years 
ter to haunt Ellington—and Eckerd. 


“The employee had made a duplicate of the 
photo and put it in an album with 297 other pho- 
tos he had copied,” claims Powell. That album is 
now in the hands of Vivian May, an attorney 
drafted by the court to represent others in a class 
action suit whose pictures are in the book. 

Ben Will, the attorney for Eckerd, said: “I 
can’t say the oa id make duplicates of 
photos; in fact they deny it. But if they did, it 
was against Eckerd policy which forbids dupli- 
cating photos. This was an action of the em- 
Lee es acting as individuals, not as employees 
of Eckerd.” He also said media attention has 
made too much of the nudity in the photo. 

When pictures may be pornographic, “we 
turn them over to the authorities so they can 


set standards on what’s acceptable and what’s 
not,” Gene Ormond, Eckerd’s director of public 
relations, told Drug Store News. 

“The issue is — theft,” he stressed. 
“Lets say someone took a picture of a rock star 
at a concert and brought it in to be developed. If 
an employee ee it and blew it up toposter 
size, that’s theft. Our policy clearly prohibits 
employees from copying any customer photos. 
If it had come to our attention that the employ- 
ees had been doing that (when employed by 
Eckerd three or four years ago), they would 
have been fired.” 


Other chain approaches 


Pay Less, based in Oregon, follows state 
laws when categorizing photos as nude or por- 


nographic and is looking into a new policy that 
would balanes mn 


ples’ rights with the law, said 
merchandiser Face 


ers. 
And at Snyder’s Drug Stores in Minnesota, 
employees cannot open sealed photo . 
Said Snyder’s Dave Vacaud assistant vp- 
store operations: “That’s an invasion of privacy 
and the employee would be terminated if 
caught doing so.” ’ 
But Snyder adds that no matter how strin- 
nt policies are, much of the day-to-day photo 


usiness (and drug retailing business in gener- 


al) is left to employees’ good judgment. 
DRUG STORE NEWS, October 14, 1991 


The name doesn’t soar. It doesn’t light any rockets. 
But it works: Affiliated/Associated Drug Stores, the 
organization with the glaring redundancy in its title 
and the once tenuous lease on life, has become the 
Chain Drug Marketing Association. The new name 
works because it fits. It describes exactly what the as- 
sociation is about. | 

Actually a slight alteration is likely to occur soon. 

New York State won't 


permit a “for-profit” or- 
ganization like CDMA to 
use the word association 
in its title, so the Chain 
Drug Marketing Associa- 
tion may soon become 
Chain Drug Marketing 
Associates. That may ac- 


IN THE MARKET 
BRUCE BUCKLEY 


tually be a slight im- 
provement, since it has more of a “partners” feel to 
it. On the other hand, it may sound too much like a 
consulting firm. 

Whatever. CDMA is poised to fly. The past year has 
been a watershed for the 65-year-old New York buy- 
ing organization. Many industry people were writing 
its epitaph 13 or 14 months ago, when Jim Devine was 
hired to strap himself into the freefalling association 
and pray that his experience, exuberance and drive 
would act as a kind of personal bungee cord to snap 
things back. 

Even those most committed to preserving the orga- 
nization admit to having more than a few doubts about 
the long-term prospects for survival. NACDS had put 
its Marketplace into orbit as the premier drug store 
merchandise show. And a lot of key vendors were 
grousing that there were already too many shows to 
attend. If any shows seemed expendable, industry 
people said, they were the far smaller Affiliated/Asso- 
ciated events. 

Undaunted, Jim Devine and a group of committed 
members warmed up earlier this year with the suc- 
cessful mid-April merchandise show in Dallas. This 


OPINION 


AADS has a new name, new lease on life 


past month CDMA seemed solidly back on track with 
its show in Atlanta (as our coverage in this issue de- 
tails). Vendor attendance was at an all-time high, and 
retail members came to do business. Out of the 75 
members, 61 sent representatives to work the booths 
and exchange ideas. More orders were written than 
ever before. 

The New York-based buying group has always 
prided itself on being not just the impresario of twice 
yearly shows, but a year-round marketing resource 
for its members. In recent years, however, the orga- 
nization’s energies seemed drained, its efforts a bit 
shop-worn. The challenge was to reignite the fire, es- 
pecially among those smaller regional and local chains 
for whom the efforts of a dedicated marketing staff 
could mean so much. 

Devine and some hard-working members spent 
the better part of a year digging deep into the struc- 
ture of the organization and setting a course to fulfill 
the needs of members and suppliers. In talking 
about those efforts, members like Harco’s Jim Har- 
rison III, the new chairman of the board, use words 
like “focused,” “energy” and “exciting.” And they 
credit not only Devine, but all of the members and 
associates who worked so hard to chart the new 
course. 

Devine was ebullient in the aftermath of the re- 
cent show. Characteristically he credited others. 
The support from the members, he said, was “fan- 
tastic.” 

True, it was a team effort. But it’s doubtful that it 
could have been done without Devine. His long expe- 
rience in the industry and friendships bought the asso- 
ciation the time to allow changes to take place. His en- 
thusiasm and flexibility fueled the excitement of 
members and staff. 

Devine himself admits to having a few uncertainties 
at the start of the adventure some 13 months ago. “But 
I just renewed my lease in Guttenberg, N.J.,” he told 
me with that great chortling laugh of his. “And I hada 
comfortable feeling about it.” 


rights have retailers 


Drug store employees, like any other workers in 
this country, have a right to join labor unions. Labor 
unions, in turn, have a right to organize workers and 
picket non-union establishments. 

But what about the rights of employers? Do drug 
stores and other businesses have the right to seek pro- 
tection from harassment by union activists? 

Suppose labor organizers target your store? What if 
union recruiters set up 


picket lines in your park- 
ing lot, harass employees 
on their way to work and 
urge your customers to 
shop elsewhere? Do the 
labor laws protect retail- 
ers from such tactics? 

That’s a question that 
may soon be answered 
here in Washington by the U.S. Supreme Court. 

The case at issue involves the plight of retail tenants 
at the Lechmere Shopping Plaza—a 14-store strip 
center in Newington, Conn.—who were literally over- 
run by union organizers a few years ago. 

Despite protests from the retailers, non-employee 
activists from the United Food and Commercial 
Workers picketed the plaza, distributed leaflets to 
customers in the center’s parking lot, entered stores 
and buttonholed employees as part of their recruiting 


WASHINGTON 
PERSPECTIVE 
KEN RANKIN 


When Lechmere sought a state court order to pre- 
vent this trespassing, the union responded by filing an 
unfair labor practice complaint with the National La- 


in labor disputes? 


bor Relations Board. 

Those federal charges effectively checkmated the 
Connecticut retailers who were told that once unfair 
labor practice charges are filed with NLRB in Wash- 
ington, the state courts lose jurisdiction over the mat- 


‘ter. 


A similar situation erupted in West Virginia 
where the state’s Supreme Court of Appeals also 
held that retailers may not secure protection against 
union trespassers once a federal NLRB complaint is 
filed. 

Both of those union trespass cases are now before 
the U.S. Supreme Court and retail industry lawyers 
are keeping close tabs on developments there. 

But for my money, there’s another even more dis- 
turbing union picketing case in the pipeline—one that 
has antitrust as well as economic implications for drug 
stores. 

This one involves an unusual provision in a contract 
negotiated between unionized store workers and re- 
tailers in Ohio. 

Under the new contract, the Ohio retailers may re- 
duce wages to their workers if competing merchants 
continue to pay lower wage rates. But here’s the kick- 
er: the union can avoid those wage cuts by picketing 
the lower paying, non-union retailers! 

Critics of this agreement contend that it represents 
an unholy alliance between retailers and labor 
unions—an anticompetitive conspiracy to punish com- 
peting non-union retailers. 

Again, the U.S. Supreme Court will ultimately 
have to call the shot.

Harco Drug 


At Harco in Alabama, hair 
care is flat and dull—although 
buyer Charles Monk says 
Harco has an opportunity to 
expand in professional hair 
care, and he’ll manage that 
over the next few months. 

Monk says he wants to run 
schools on professional hair 
care educate the cosmeticians. 
He is already sending more 
product information into the 
stores for them to read. 

In the sham category, 
Monk says the big trend is that 
consumers are buying more 
and more two-in-one sham- 

/conditioners, led by Pert 
lus and Vidal Sassoon. 

In — aids, the gels and 
mousses have peaked, so 
Harco is dropping slower 
movers and giving more space 
to top sellers. He singled out 
the Clairol styling aids and 
L’Oréal’s Studio Line, partic- 
ularly Pumping Curls, as 
among his best sellers. 

John Frieda’s Frizz-Ease 
has done very well in Harco 
stores, selling well even at its 
full $9.99 retail. Now Frieda is 
launching 4 aumber of line ex- 
tensions, which Monk feels 
will make the manufacturer’s 
line a top seller. 


Bill’s Drug 


At Bill’s Drug in Benicia, 
Calif., buyer Sharon Schrage 
says professional hair care 
lines, and the L’Oréal Studio 
Line, particularly the brand’s 
styling aids for curly hair, are 
setting the sales pace in the 
category. 

At press time, Bill’s was 
‘eng’ s to advertise Frizz- 

ase. Schrage said that based 
on what she’s seen in other 
chains—a good ad plus place- 


ment on a ighly visible end- 
cap—should be effective. 
Kinney 


In Gouverneur, N.Y., Kin- 
ney buyer Robert Burtis says 
styling aids are turning the 
fastest for him, but he’s wait- 
ing for the next big marketing 
trend to emerge. 

“In hair styling, we’ve gone 
from regular hold to super to 
ultra to spritz to freeze, and 
now we've got to have one step - 
beyond that. I’m waiting for 
the — Glue Special,” Bur- 
tis said. 

He knows that teenage girls 
are still driving the growth in 
hair styling. “I went to a girl’s 
soccer game recently, and 
they were out there playing 
for hours in the burning sun. 
One girl came off the field and 
her was drenched in 
sweat, but she didn’t have one 
hair out of place.”

Rite Aid reports record 
earnings for 2nd atr. 


SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — Rite Aid Corp. reported record 
earnings for the second quarter ended August 31. During the 13 
weeks, corporate revenues rose 9 percent to $900.7 million from 
$826.2 million. Quarterly earnings grew 11.5 percent to $25.1 
million from $21.5 million. 

Drug store sales were up 8.7 percent to $849.0 million in the 
quarter, com 
earlier. Net dru 
cent to $23.6 mi 
earlier period.

lion, and net income advanced 14.3 percent to $50.0 million. 
Same-store sales were up 7 percent for the quarter and 7.3 per- 
cent for the 26-week period. The retail drug division sndded the 
quarter with 2,439 drug stores. 

Sales for Rite Aid Corp.’s specialty retailing arm, American 
Discount Auto Parts, were up 15.7 
quarter to $22.5 million, compared with the year-earlier peri-

$571,000 from the year-earlier’s $464,000. ADAP opened three 
stores in the quarter to end the period with 86 retail locations.

Fay’s qtr. revenues up; 
sets sights on 2nd half 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — 
Fay’s posted net earnings for 
the second quarter of $1.25 
million, or 8 cents a share, 
compared with $3.25 million, 
or 21 cents a share in the sec- 
ond quarter last year. Reve- 
nues in the rie ended July 
27 increased 27.8 percent to a 
record $207.4 million, as com- 
parable store sales climbed 5.7 
percent. 

Chairman Henry Panasci, 
Jr. said earnings were affect- 
ed by lower than expected 
gross margins, store expan- 


sion costs and sales weak- 
ness in the Paper Cutter divi- 
sion. 

“With the costs of absorbin 
the Carls stores behind us an 
recessionary pressures eas- 
ing, we expect that second half 
results will be more in line 
with expectations,” said Pan- 
ascl. 

First half net earnings are 
at $3.1 million versus last 
year’s $4.2 million, with six 
months sales of $384.6 million 
against $315.5 million in last 
year’s comparable period. 


Albertson’s qtr. net income up 10.9% 


BOISE, Idaho — Albertson’s 
reported record sales of $2.19 bil- 
lion for the second quarter ended 
Aug. 1, a 5.7 percent increase 
over the $2.07 billion in the com- 
parable period a year ago. 

Net earnings rose 10.9 percent 
for the quarter, to $58.7 million 
from $52.9 million, and operating 
profit gained 15 percent, to $93.8 
million from $81.6 million. Same- 
store sales increased 1.4 percent. 

For the first half, sales were 
$4.35 billion, a 6.6 percent gain 
over the $4.08 billion for the peri- 
od last year. Net earnings rose 
12.7 percent, to .3 million 


from $104.1 million. Same-store 
sales increased 2.5 percent. 

Gross margin was 23.41 per- 
cent for the half, compared with 
22.95 percent last year. The com- 
pany said the increase was a re- 
sult from improved retail store 
contributions and from distribu- 
tion center efficiencies. 

Albertson’s said the second- 
quarter sales, while a record, 
were somewhat below expecta- 
tions, and that it aimed to im- 
prove same-store sales and de- 
crease operating expenses as a 
percent of sales during the second 
half.

rose 10 percent, to $162.8 mil- 
lion from $148. million in the

uarter sales rose 8 percent, to 
.40 billion from $7.78 billion.

Rich leaves Thrifty 


By David Vaczek 

LOS ANGELES — Eve Rich has resigned 
as Thrifty Drug’s president because of a con- 
flict in management styles with William Yin- 
gling, who was named ifty Corp. chairman 
and ceo in August, according to company 
sources and others. 

Yingling, hired by Pacific Enterprises, the 
parent of Thrifty, to help spearhead a turn- 
around in the oo said that Rich, 50, 
“decided to leave se of differences over 

ement matters. 

“We had hoped to work out our differences, 
but realized in the end it was a case of having 
different basic management styles,” said Yin- 
ping, the 47-year-old former president of 

ucky Stores’ Southern California division. 

In an apparent cordial parting, Rich said 
“the chain is on the right track and that its turn- 
— will succeed under Bill Yingling’s lead- 
ership.” 

Some sources expressed surprise at the de- 
parture by Rich, who was the drug chain indus- 
try’s highest-ranking woman, because PE ex- 
ecutives expressed full suppert for her agenda 
to reorient the chain. 

Yingling, a highly regarded executive, is 
seen as ag a mass merchandising dimen- 
sion to lity, which boasts new senior mer- 


chants hired by

NHMA cancels fall show 


NEW YORK — The National Housewares Manufacturers 
Association (NHMA) has cancelled its 1992 fall show, and is 
scheduling just one show for the year. 

The group’s board of directors also voted to hold only one 
show a year as long as it faces soft demand for a second yearly 
event, NHMA officials said at a press conference here. 

“The marketplace has spoken, and the board has listened,” 
said Tom Conley, NHMA executive director. 

“At the present time, it’s clear that the industry support for the 
Atlanta show [planned for September 1992] just doesn’t exist.” 

The move to one sag show was sparked by declining ven- 
dor enrollment at the fall show and dwindling retailer atten- 
dance, Conley said.

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 28, 1991 


Like the cooling breeze, the performance of two 
leading chain drug players—Walgreens and Arbor— 
provided welcome relief in a summer marked by the 
highs and lows of an uncertain economy. 

Around the country there are drug chains that are 
managing to weather the problems caused by consum- 
er anxieties. Some chains are even thriving. But none 
is doing better than Walgreens and Arbor, who re- 
ported their year-end re- 
sults this month. 


Though the two chains 
‘ are vastly different in 
scope, they share many 
retail principles and ap- 


IN THE MARKET) proaches. It is those prin- 


BRUCE BUCKLEY ciples and approaches that 
are at the heart of their 


strength, and neither 


chain makes a secret of 
them. These principles 
are simple, basic retailing combined with a healthy 
dose of modern technology. 
What is hard—and what Walgreens and Arbor do so 
well—is the execution: 
@ They stick to the product mix that customers expect 
from them and promote those expectations heavily. 
That means prescriptions and OTC drugs, cosmetics 
and toiletries, greeting cards and photo and consum- 
ables and limited general merchandise. 
@ They pay close attention to their changing customer 


OPINION 


a“ 


Two chains find what works & stick with it. 


mix so they are not left high and dry when demograph- 

ic tides shift in their various markets. 

@ ‘They use technology and improved information 

gathering to buy smart and smooth the flow of goods 

= their stores. Turnover benefits, and so does cash 
Ow. 

@ They do “alliance-building” with suppliers, but in a 

measured and hard-headed business way. 

e They invest in stores, keeping the look fresh, and 

they increase their presence in markets that make 

sense to them. 

@ They don’t try to be price leaders; instead, they 

rely on promotion, efficient service and convenience 

to draw customers. 

© Most important, they make their employees feel 

that they’re a crucial part of a winning team. 

This last point was emphasized by Michael J. O’Con- 
nor in arecent, throughtful article on “Lean Retailing: 
An Idea That Could Make a Revolutionary Change”, 
published by Arthur Anderson’s International 
Trends in Retailing last spring. 

O’Connor, a retail consultant for Anderson and for- 
mer president of the Super Market Institute (prede- 
cessor to FMI), wrote about the importance of em- 
powering employees. “People want to feel that they 
matter. People want to feel that what they do has 
some importance and that they can progress. And 
people find it hard to work for a person or company 
they do not respect.” Respect for employees and cus- 
tomers is a given at Walgreens and Arbor. 


Congress’ illegal alien legislation backfires 


Congressional “immigration reformers” are begin- 
ning to acknowledge that they made a serious mistake 
five years ago by approving legislation holding drug 
stores and other employers legally responsible for 
screening illegal aliens out of the workforce. 

But, just as Congress begins debate on a new bill 
to repeal those controversial employer sanctions, 
officials at the Immigration and Naturalization Ser- 
vice (INS) are talking up 
proposals of their own 


that would create even 
greater compliance has- 
sles for the industry. 


. WASHINGTON That law at the center 


\ PERSPECTIVE of the controversy—the 
KEN RANKIN Immigration Reform and 


Control Act (IRCA) of 
1986—shifted the burden 
of policing the nation’s 
immigration laws from 
the federal government to private employers. 

For the last five years, that law has required em- 
ployers to verify the immigration status of all new 
hires and to maintain records to document that they 
did obtain **» appropriate evidence from incoming 
employees. 

Additionally, IRCA leaves businesses vulnerable 
to stiff federal penalties for violations of these require- 
ments—including minor paperwork infractions. 

Still another provision establishes government 
sanctions for employers who implement the law in a 
way that results in job discrimination against individ- 
uals who look or sound foreign. 

Now, after five years, it’s clear to many that em- 
ployer hiring sanctions have failed to curb illegal im- 
migration and businesses have been subjected to cost- 
ly paperwork and recordkeeping burdens 
unnecessarily. 

“Tllegal aliens continue to pour into this country,” 
and “a cottage industry in counterfeit and fraudulent 
documents has flourished” because of IRCA, said Sen. 
Orrin Hatch (R-Utah), the point guard for the biparti- 
san effort to repeal the employer sanctions. 


Sen. Edward Kennedy (D-Mass.), a co-sponsor of 
Hatch’s repeal bill, openly admits that “Congress 
made the wrong move” in enacting employer sanc- 
tions. “We aimed at illegal aliens—but we hit law- 
abiding Americans, and it’s time to correct our mis- 
take.” 

Despite support for the repeal legislation from all 
points on the political spectrum, federal bureaucrats 
responsible for policing the employer sanctions aren’t 
getting the message. 

Indeed, INS is considering plans to grant immigra- 
tion agents sweeping new powers to subpoena records 
from business in order to measure employer compli- 
ance with the controversial hiring rules.

and have no therapeutic al-

or ddI) has been tested in 
more than 30,000 patients 
with advanced human immu- 
nodeficiency virus (HIV) who 
are intolerant to or not bene- 
fiting from AZT (zidovudine). 
Many treated patients have 
shown an increase in T4-help- 
er cells and lower levels of 
p24 antigen (which indicates 
the presence of HIV), without 
the significant bone marrow 
suppression seen with AZT. 
The manufacturer, Bristol- 
Myers Squibb, has priced Vi- 
dex to retail at less than 
$2,000 per year. The Videx 
Reimbursement Helpline (1- 
800-662-7999) provides a | oa

cy for probable sources of é 
funding for treatment.

Retiree script plans 
may be too costly 


Private sector and government third- 
party experts fear that soaring health care 
costs will force employers to reduce or 
eliminate prescription drug benefits for re- 
tirees. 

A study by PCS found that the average 
annual Rx cost for employed individuals is 
now between $37 and $180. The cost for 
retired Americans is three times as much: 
an average of between $240 and $535. The 
Congressional Budget Office (CBO), 
meanwhile, issued a study showing that 
six out of 10 senior citizens have no outpa- 
tient prescription drug coverage. The . 
tunate ones with Rx benefits through re- 
tiree health plans “are at risk of losing this 
beer ini because of rapidly rising 

ealth care costs, CBO warned. 


The best price scheme 
has begun to unravel 


The controversial new system of requir- 
ing pharmaceutical manufacturers to offer 
their “best prices’ on drugs to Medicaid is 
already beginning to unravel. 

Instead of sharply lowering Rx prices to 
Medicaid, pharmaceutical ae ieee 
responded to the “best price” mandate by 
eliminating “giveaway prices to the De- 
partment of Veterans Affairs. That’s poetic 
justice to retail pharmacists who have com- 
plained for years about ingrained “discrimi- 
natory pricing’ in the Racca in- 
dustry. 

But now VA officials are squawking at 
having to pay full price for drugs. VA’s price 
on some Rx products has jumped more than 
1,000 percent since the best price law took 
effect, and House Veterans Affairs Com- 
mittee chairman Sonny Montgomery (D- 
Miss.) is pushing legislation to exempt 
prices to VA and other government agen- 
cies from the calculation of the “best” Med- 
icaid price. 

Pharmaceutical manufacturers don’t 
mind that so much, but they are opposed 
to ae agicy in the bill requiring them to 
roll back VA prices to September 1990 
levels. 


Kennedy is seeking 
expanded rebates 


Meanwhil: Sen.- Edward Kennedy (D- 
Mass.) wants to expand the “best price” Rx 
rules. Pharmaceutical manufacturers 
would be required to extend Medicaid- 


10 


| drug watch 


style price rebates to federally funded pub- 
lic health clinics, under his new “Public 
Health Clinic Prudent Pharmaceutical 
Purchasing Act” (S.1729). The legislation 
would permit government-subsidized drug 
treatment facilities, abortion clinics, AIDS 
treatment centers and other health care 
outlets to purchase pharmaceuticals only 
from manufacturers who have signed re- 
bate agreements. Prices would be capped 
at levels charged by participating drug 
manufacturers on September 1, 1990. 


McKesson testing 
disposal program 


On Oct. 1, McKesson began testing a 
new controlled substance return and waste 
disposal program with BFI Pharmaceutical 
Services. BFI assists manufacturers and 
wholesalers in crediting procedures for the 
processed products with a waste tracking 
and profiling computer system. 

Douglas Thompson, senior vp of distri- 
bution services at McKesson, said that “this 
new and innovative program . . . ensure|[s] 
the proper disposition of controlled sub- 
stances in an environmentally safe manner 
in accordance with all state and federal 
laws’ and added that “the potential for ille- 
gal diversion is Palle reduced.” 

If the initial pilot is successful, use will be 
expanded beyond controlled substances to 
all classes of pharmaceuticals and drug 
store products. 


New drugs tested 
for bowel diseases 


Ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease 
sufferers have persistent diarrhea, fever 
and weight loss due to the immune system 
inappropriately attacking the bowel wall. 
Treatment to date has been with some 
combination of sulfasalazine and steroids. 
Because some patients experience intol- 
erable side effects, new therapies are 
sought. 

e University of Chicago is conducting 
trials of promising new agents, which in- 
clude: 
® Zileutin, a lipoxygenase inhibitor that 
blocks early inflammation. 
® Budesonide, a steroid that is active local- 
ly in the intestine. 

@ Methotrexate, a cancer chemotherapeu- 
tic agent. 

® Cyclosporine, an immune suppressant. 
@ Short-chain fatty acids, nutrients thought 
to be deficient in these patients. 

For more information, or to volunteer for 
Fi _— contact Pat Schultz at (312) 702- 


Unapproved medicines 
get the American OK 


The Wirthlin Group, a national public 
opinion research firm, in its September 
survey, found that 79 percent of Americans 
believe that “. . . patients with fatal and in- 
curable diseases, in consultation with their 
doctors, should have the power to decide 
whether to take an experimental drug while 
it is under FDA review.’ Unapproved ther- 
apies for serious diseases like AIDS, can- 
cer, Alzheimer’s disease, and even diabe- 
tes, heart disease and arthritis should be 
accessible on patient and doctor choice. 


Should individuals with these 
diseases be allowed to try drugs 


not yet approved by the FDA?

Wart remover patch 
especially for kids 


PediaPatch Wart Remover 
System for Children, from Tsu- 
mura Medical, is a nonprescrip- 
tion strength removal product. 

It utilizes a patented gum- 


based, transdermal-like patch 
containing a 15 percent salicylic 
acid solution that eliminates 
common warts and plantar 
warts with regular nightly ap- 
plications. The medicine con- 
tinuously and painlessly breaks 
down the wart. The patch can 
be trimmed to fit the size of the 
wart so there is less chance of 
surrounding skin irritation. The 
patch is affixed for the night 
with a colorful, protective ad- 
hesive bandage, so a high level 
of compliance is generated. 

It’s available in a6 mm. patch 

and is packaged with 20 medi- 
cated patches and 24 protective 
bandage tapes. 
Tsumura Medical, Div. of Tsu- 
mura International, Inc., 1000 
Valley Park Dr., Shakopee,

1990: A banner year 
for drug wholesalers 


By Elizabeth Parks 


their best years ever. 

Joe Polastri, chairman of the board 
for the National Wholesale Druggists As- 
sociation (NWDA) and president of 
McKesson Distribution Group, the indus- 
try s largest drug wholesaler, sums up 1990 
as a year of strong accomplishments. 

He describes the industry performance 
as a significant achievement against the 
backdrop of a softening economy.’ 

Indeed, according to the 1990 NWDA Op- 
erating Survey, sales for the industry were up 
18.1 percent to $30. 18 billion. Gross margins 
reversed their historical decline and rose to 
7.35 percent, compared to 7.30 percent on a 
composite-average basis in 1989. 

NWDA also reports that operating ex- 
penses, as a percent of sales, declined again 
in 1990, dropping 2.7 percent to 4.72 per- 
cent compared to 4.85 percent in 1989. 

But, despite the industry’s sterling per- 
formance in 1990, Polastri and other whole- 
salers warn that there are some indicators 
and trends that are not totally encouraging. 

Polastri cautions that wholesalers “may 
be approaching maximum efficiency” as the 
historical declines in operating expenses 
appears to be slowing. 

Polastri and a number of other wholesal- 
ers are also concerned that intensifying 
competition for market share, 
combined with a reduc- 
tion in manu- 


j n 1990, drug wholesalers had one of 


facturer price increases, will hurt margin 
stability in 1991, and possibly again in 1992. 

Many wholesaler executives also feel 
that mid-sized and smaller companies will 
continue to find it hard to compete in to- 
day's marketplace, and may be forced to ei- 
ther merge with a larger, more technologi- 
cally advanced company to survive. 

Many wholesalers believe the industry 
may shrink to 50 companies in the next few 
years from the present 83. 

At Bergen Brunswig, President Phil En- 
gle reports that while the 1990 calendar 
year was up for Bergen, the last half of the 
fiscal year, which ended in August, was 
more difficult. 

“I'm not predicting that profit margins 
for the industry are going to go up again in 
1991,” Engle says, “because the competi- 
tive environment in the last three and four 
months is as strong as I've ever seen it. 

The big players are all after share of mar- 
ket, and to get that youve got to take 
business from the smaller guys.’ 

“Margins are based on our ability to do 
forward buying,” says Polastri. 

“Right now, because of the pressure from 
Washington for cost containment, we re 
not seeing many price increases. 

If that continues, you will see 
wholesaler margins

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, October 28, 1991 


ERYTHROMYCIN ETHYLSUCCINATE 
AND SULFISOXAZOLE ACETYL 
FOR ORAL SUSPENSION 


INDICATION 


For treatment of ACUTE OTTITIS MEDIA in children that is caused by 
susceptible strains of Hemophilus influenzae. 


CONTRAINDICATIONS: 


Known hypersensitivity to either erythromycin or sulfonamides. Infants less 
than 2 months of age. 


Pregnancy at term and during the nursing period, because sulfonamides 
pass into the placental circulation and are excreted in human breast milk 
and may cause kernicterus in the infant. 


WARNINGS 


FATALITIES ASSOCIATED WITH THE ADMINISTRATION OF SULFONAMIDES, 
ALTHOUGH RARE, HAVE OCCURRED DUE TO SEVERE REACTIONS 
INCLUDING STEVENS-JOHNSON SYNDROME, TOXIC EPIDERMAL 
NECROLYSIS, FULMINANT HEPATIC NECROSIS, AGRANULOCYTOSIS, 
APLASTIC. ANEMIA, AND OTHER BLOOD DYSCRASIAS. 


Clinical signs such as sore throat, fever, pallor, rash, purpura, or jaundice 
may be early indications of serious reactions. 


- ERYTHROMYCIN ETHYLSUCCINATE AND SULFISOXAZOLE ACETYL FOR 


ORAL SUSPENSION SHOULD BE DISCONTINUED AT THE FIRST 
APPEARANCE OF SKIN RASH OR ANY SIGN OF ADVERSE REACT 10N. In 
some instances a skin rash may be followed by a more severe reaction, such 
as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epiderma! necrolysis, hepatic necrosis 
and serious blood disorders. 


COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT SHOULD BE DONE FREQUENTLY IN PATIENTS 
RECEIVING SULFONAMIDES. 


Usage in Pregnancy (SEE ALSO: CONTRAINDICATIONS): The safe use of 
erythromycin or sulfonamides in pregnancy has not been established. The 
teratogenic potential of most sulfonamides has not been thoroughly 
investigated in either animals or humans. However, a Significant increase 
in the ixridence of cleft palate and other body abnormalities of offspring 
has been abserved when certain sulfonamides of the short, intermediate 
and long-acting types were given to pregnant rats and mice at high oral 
doses (7 to 25 times the human therapeutic dose). 


The frequency of renal complications is considerably lower in patients 
receiving the most soluble sulfonamides such as sulfisoxazole. Urinalysis 
with careful microscopic examination should be obtained frequently in 
patients receiving suifonamides. 


PRECAUTIONS 


Erythromycin is principally excreted by the liver. Caution should be exercised 
in administering the antibiotic to patients with impaired hepatic function. 
There have been reports of hepatic dysfunction, with or without jaundice 
occurring in patients receiving oral erythromycin products. 


Recent data from studies of erythromycin reveal that its use in patients who 
are receiving high doses of theophylline may be associated with an increase 
of serum theophylline levels and potential theophylline toxicity. In case of 
theophylline toxicity and/or elevated serum theophylline levels, the dose of 
theophylline should be reduced while the patient is receiving concomitant 
erythromycin therapy. 

Surgical procedures should be performed when indicated. 


Sulfonamide therapy should be given with caution to patients with impaired 
renal or hepatic function and in those patients with a history of severe allergy 
or bronchial asthma. in the presence of a deficiency in the enzyme 
glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, hemolysis may occur. This reaction 
is frequently dose-related. Adequate fluid intake must be maintained in order 
to prevent crystalluria and renal stone formation. 


ADVERSE REACTIONS 


The most frequent side effects of oral erythromycin preparations are 
gastrointestinal, such as abdominal cramping and discomfort, and are dose- 
related. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea occur infrequently with usual oral 
doses. During prolonged or repeated therapy, there is a possibility of 
overgrowth of nonsusceptible bacteria or fungi. If such infections occur, the 
drug should be discontinued and appropriate therapy instituted. The overall 
incidence of these latter side effects reported for the combined 
administration of erythromycin and a sulfonamide is comparable to those 
observed in patients given erythromycin alone. Mild allergic reactions such 
as urticaria and other skin rashes have occurred. Serious allergic reactions, 
including anaphylaxis, have been reported with erythromycin. There have 


been isolated reports of reversible hearing loss occurring chiefly in patients - 


with renal insufficiency and in patients receiving high doses of erythromycin. 
The following untoward effects have been associated with the use of 
sulfonamides: 

Blood Dyscrasias: Agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, 
leukopenia, hemolytic anemia, purpura, hypoprothrombinemia and 
methemogiobinemia. 

Allergic Reactions: Erythema multiforme (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), 
generated skin eruptions, epidermal necrolysis, urticaria, serum sickness, 
pruritus, exfoliative dermatitis, anaphylactoid reactions, periorbital edema, 
conjunctival and scleral injection, yhotosensitization, arthralgia and allergic 
myocarditis. 

Gastrointestinal Reactions: Nausea, emesis, abdominal pains, hepatitis, 
diarrhea, anorexia, pancreatitis and stomatitis. 

CNS Reactions: Headache, peripheral neuritis, mental depression, 
convuisions, ataxia, hallucinations, tinnitus, vertigo and insomnia. 
Miscellaneous Reactions: Drug fever, chills and toxic nephrosis with oliguria 
and anuria. Periateritis nodosa and LE phenomenon have occurred. 

The sulfonamides bear certain chemical similarities to some goitrogens, 
diuretics (acetazolamide and the thiazides) and orai hypoglycemic agents. 
Goiter production, diuresis and hypoglycemia have occurred rarely in 
patients receiving sulfonamides. Cross-sensitivity may exist with these 
agents. 

Rats appear to be especially susceptible to the goitrogenic effects of 
suifonamides, and long-term administration has produced thyroid 
malignancies in the species.

distribution centers and four semi-auto- 
mated facilities equipped to become full 
automated once it achieves the needed 2 
lar volume in sales—from $250 to $300 mil- 
lion per facility. 

The wholesaler is also investing in addi-

open in mid-1992. Both will be semi-auto- 
mated, but designed so they can be upgrad-

required volume. 

In these centers, instead of the two pick-

Bindley Western 


At Bindley Western, chairman and ceo 
Bill Bindley feels the most significant ac- 
complishment in the past year has been the 
transition to “full lines and full service.” 


Bindley has 12 d.c.'s now. The average 
center generates $200 million. In 1987, the 
average d.c. was doing $100 million. 

All centers have mezzanines, which al- 
lows Bindley to use air space to maximize 
efficiency. They also have a standard lay- 
out, so the way items are picked and rotated 
in one facility is exactly the same as it would 
be in any other. 

Bindley’s new facility in San Demos, 
Calif., is doing well, the company dou- 
bled the size of its Charlotte, N.C. center. 
Bindley is also adding more space in its India- 
napolis facility. The company also has a new 
100,000-square-foot center in Orlando. . 

Bindleys newest facility, in Stanford, 
Conn., will open in 1992, and will consoli- 
date three smaller centers. 

The wholesaler will also move into a new 
facility in Atlanta within the next six 
morths, and will push deeper into the 
northeast market by opening its first Penn- 
sylvania facility in Harrisburg toward the 
end of this year. 

Bindley has used technology to improve 
its data processing systems. “We've devel- 
oped new software programs for ourselves 
and our customers. We have a variety of 
p.c.-based programs to help retailers man- 
age their businesses. We also have a new 
nursing home pharmaceutical package that 
is comparable to our retail i Nurs- 
ing homes has been another growth area for 


us. 
Although Bindley has what may be the 


lowest operating expenses in the wholesale 
drug industry, the company is trying to be- 
come even more efficient. He says the goal 


is to trim expenses to 1 percent of sales from 
the current 1.1 to 1.2 percent.

NIFEDIPINE CAPSULES, USP 


Brief Summary 


INDICATIONS AND USAGE: 
i. Vasospastic Angina: Nifedipine is indicated for the management of va- 
saspastic angina confirmed by any of the following criteria: 1) classical pat- 
tem of angina at rest accompanied by ST segment elevation, 2) angina or 
coronary artery spasm provoked by ergonovine, or 3) angiographically demon- 
strated coronary artery spasm. In those patients who have had angiography, 
the presence of significant fixed obstructive disease is not incompatible with 
the diagnosis of vasospastic angina, provided that the above criteria are sat- 
isfied. Nifedipine may also be used where the clinical presentation suggests a 
possible vasospastic component but where vasospasm has not been con- 
firmed, e.g., where pain has a variable threshold on exertion or in unstable angina 
where electrocardiographic findings are compatible with intermittent vasospasm. 
ov when angina is refractory to nitrates and/or adequate doses of beta block- 
ers. 
li. Chronic Stable Angina (Classical Effort-Associated Angina): 
Nifedipine is indicated for the management of chronic stable angina (effort-as- 
sociated angina) without evidence of vasospasm in patients who remain symp- 
omatic despite adequate doses of beta blockers and/or organic nitrates or who 
cannot tolerate those agents . 

nm chronic stable angina (effort-associated angina) nifedipine has been 
effective in controlled trials of up to eight weeks duration in reducing angina 
frequency and increasing exercise tolerance, but confirmation of sustained ef- 
fectiveness and evaluation of long term safety in these patients are incomplete. 

Controlled studies in small numbers of patients suggest concomitant use of 
nifedipine and beta blocking agents may be beneficial in patients with chronic 
stabie angina, but available information is not sufficient to predict with confi- 
dence the effects of concurrent treatment. especially in patients with compro- 
mised left ventricular function or cardiac conduction abnormalities. When 
introducing such concomitant therapy, care must be taken to monitor blood pres- 
sure closely since severe hypotension can occur from the combined effects of 
the drugs. (See WARNINGS } 


CONTRAINDICATIONS: 
Known hypersensitivity reaction to nifedipine 


~WARNINGS: 
Excessive Hypotension: Although in most patients, the hypotensive ef- 
fect of nifedipine is modest and well tolerated, occasional patients have had 
excessive and poorly toleratec r ypotension. These responses have usually oc- 
curred during initial titration or at the time of subsequent upward dosage ad- 
justment, and may be more likely in patients on concomitant beta blockers. 
Severe hypotension and/or increased fluid volume requirements have been re- 
ported in patients receiving nifedipine together with a beta blocking agent who 
underwent coronary artery bypass surgery using high dose fentanyl anesthesia. 
The interaction with high dose fentanyl appears to be due to the combination of 
nifedipine and a beta blocker, but the possibility that it may occur with nifedip- 
ine alone, with low doses of fentanyl, in other surgical procedures, or with other 
narcotic analgesics cannot be ruled out. In nifedipine treated patients where 
surgery using high dose-fentany! anesthesia is contemplated, the physician 
should be aware of these potential problems and, if the patient's condition per- 
mits, sufficient time (at least 36 hours) should be allowed for nifedipine to be 
washed out of the body prior to surgery 
increased Angina and/or Myocardial infarction: Rarely, patients, par- 
licusarly those whe have severe obstructive coronary artery disease, have de- 
veloped weli dscumented increased frequency, duration and/or severity of 
angina or acute myocardial infarction on starting nifedipine or at the time of 
dosage increase. The mechanism of this effect is not established. 
Beta Biocke: Withdrawal: Patients recently withdrawn from beta blockers 
may deveiop a withdrawal syndrome with increased angina, probably related to 
creased sensitivity to catecholamines. Initiation of nifedipine treatment will not 
prevent this occurrence and might be expected to exacerbate it by provoking re- 
iicx Catecholamine release. There have been occasional reports of increased 
engina in a setting of beta blocker withdrawal and nifedipine initiation. It is im- 
portant io taper beta biockers if possible, rather than stopping them abruptly be- 
{cre beginning nifedipine. 
Congestive Heart Failure: Rarely, patients. usually receiving a beta 
uiccker, have developed heart failure after beginning nifedipine. Patients with 
tight aortic stenosis may be at greater risk for such an event, as the unloading 
effeci cf nifedipine would be expected to be of less benefit to these patients, 
owing io their fixed impedance to flow across the aortic valve 


PRECAUTIONS: 
Generali: Hypotension: Because nifedipine decreases peripheral vascu- 
lar resistance, careful monitoring of blood pressure during the initial adminis- 
tration and titration of nifedipine is suggested Close observation is especially 
recommended for patients already taking medications that are known to lower 
bicod pressure. (See WARNINGS ) 
Peripheral Edema: Mild to moderate peripheral edema, typically associ- 
ated with arteria! vasodilation and not due to left ventricular dysfunction, oc- 
curs in about one in ten patients treated with nifedipine. This edema occurs 
primarily in the iower extremities and usually responds to diuretic therapy 
With patients whose angina is complicated by congestive heart failure, care 
shouid be taken to differentiate this peripheral edema from the effects of in- 
creasing ‘eft ventricular dysfunction. 
Laboratory fests: Rare, usually transient, but occasionally significant el- 
evations of enzymes such as alkaline phosphatase, CPK, LDH, SGOT and SGPT 
have been noted. The relationship to nifedipine therapy is uncertain in most 
Cases, but probable in some. These ‘avoratory abnormalities have rarely been 
associated with clinical symptoms, however, cholestasis with or without jaun- 
dice has been reported. Rare instances of allergic hepatitis have been reported. 

Nifedipine, like other calcium channel blockers, decreases platelet aggrega- 
tion in vitro. Limited clinical studies have demonstrated a moderate but statis- 
ically significant decrease in platelet aggregation and increase in bleeding 
time in sume nifedipine patients. This is thought to be a function of inhibition 
of caicium transport across the platelet membrane. No clinical significance for 
these findings has been demonstrated 

Positive direct Coombs test with/without hemolytic anemia has been reported. 

Although nifedipine has been used safely in patients with rena! dysfunction 
and has been reported to exert a beneficial effect in certain cases, rare, reversible 
elevations in BUN and serum creatinine have been reported in patients with pre- 
existing chronic renal insufficiency. The relationship to nifedipine therapy is un- 
certain in most cases but probable in some. 
Drug interactions: Beta-adrenergic blocking agents: (See INDICATIONS 
and WARNINGS.) Experience in over 1400 patients in a non-comparative clin- 
ical trial has shown that concomitant administration of nifedipine and beta-block- 
ing agents is usualty well tolerated, but there have been occasional literature 
reports suggesting that the combination may increase the likelihood of con- 
gestive heart failure, severe hypotension or exacerbation of angina. 
Long acting nitrates: Nifedipine may be safely co-administered with nitrates. 
bui there have been no controlled studies to evaluate the antianginal effective- 
fess Of this Combination. 
Digitalis: Administ ation of nifedipine with digoxin increased digoxin levels in 
nine cf tweive norma! volunteers. The average increase was 45%. Another in 
vestigator found no increase in digoxin levels in thirteen patients with coronary 
artery disease. In an uncontroiled study of over two hundred patients with cori- 


gestive heart failure during which digoxin blood levels were not measured, dig- 
italis toxicity was not observed. Since there have been isolated reports of pa- 
tients with elevated digoxin levels, it is recommended that digoxin levels be 
monitored when initiating, adjusting, and discontinuing nifedipine to avoid pos- 
sible over- or under-digitalization. 

Coumarin anticoagulants: There have been rare reports of increased pro- 
thrombin time in patients taking coumarin anticoagulants to whom nifedipine 
was administered. However, the relationship to nifedipine therapy is uncertain. 
Cimetidine: A study in six healthy volunteers has shown a significant increase 
in peak nifedipine plasma levels (80%) and area-under-the-curve (74%) after 
a one week course of cimetidine at 1000 mg per day and nifedipine at 40 mg 
per day. Ranitidine produced smaller, non-significant increases. The effect may 
be mediated by the known inhibition of cimetidine on hepatic cytochrome P- 
450, the enzyme system probably responsible for the first-pass metabolism of 
nifedipine. If nifedipine therapy is initiated in a patient currently receiving cime- 
tidine, cautious titration is advised. 

Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, impairment of Fertility: Nifedipine 
was administered orally to rats for two years and was not shown to be car- 
cinogenic. When given to rats prior to mating, nifedipine caused reduced fer- 
tility at a dose approximately 30 times the maximum recommended human dose. 
In vivo mutagenicity studies were negative. 

Pregnancy: Pregnancy Category C. Nifedipine has been shown to be terato- 
genic in rats when given in doses 30 times the maxirnum recommended human 
dose. Nifedipine was embryotoxic (increased fetal resorptions, decreased fetal 
weight, increased stunted forms, increased fetal deaths, decreased neonatal 
Survival) in rats, mice and rabbits at doses of from 3 to 10 times the maximum 
recommended human dose. In pregnant monkeys, doses 2/3 and twice the max- 
imum recommended human dose resulted in small placentas and underdevel- 
oped chorionic villi. In rats doses three times maximum human dose and higher 
caused prolongation of pregnancy. There are no adequate and well controlled 
studies in pregnant women. Nifedipine should be used during pregnancy only 
if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 


ADVERSE REACTIONS: 

in multiple-dose U.S. and foreign controlled studies in which adverse reactions 
were reported spontaneously, adverse effects were frequent but generally not 
serious and rarely required discontinuation of therapy or dosage adjustment. 
Most were expected consequences of the vasodilator effects of nifedipine.

Several of these side effects appear to be dose related. Peripheral edema oc- 
curred in about one in 25 patients at doses less than 60 mg per day and in 
about one patient in eight at 120 mg per day or more. Transient hypotension, 
generally of mild to moderate severity and seldom requiring discontinuation of 
therapy, occurred in one of 50 patients at less than 60 mg per day and in one 
of 20 patients at 120 mg per day or more. Very rarely, introduction of nifedip- 
ine therapy was associated with an increase in anginal pain, possibly due to 
associated hypotension. 

In addition, more serious adverse events were observed, not readily distin- 
guishable from the natural history of the disease in these patients. It remains 
possible, however, that some or many of these events were drug related. 
Myocardial infarction occurred in about 4% of patients and congestive heart 
failure or pulmonary edema in about 2%. Ventricular arrhythmias or conduc- 
tion disturbances each occurred in fewer than 0.5% of patients. - 

In a Subgroup of over 1000 patients receiving nifedipine with concomitant beta 
blocker therapy, the pattern and incidence of adverse experiences was not differ- 
ent from that of the entire group of nifedipine treated patients. (See PRECAUTIONS). 

In a subgroup of approximately 250 patients with a diagnosis of congestive 
heart failure as well as angina, dizziness or lightheadedness, peripheral edema, 
headache or flushing each occurred in one in eight patients. Hypotension oc- 
curred in about one in 20 patients. Syncope occurred in approximately one pa- 
tient in 250. Myocardial infarction or symptoms of congestive heart failure each 
occurred in about one patient in 15. Atrial or ventricular dysrhythmias each oc- 
curred in about one patient in 150.

Whitmire Distribution regards its ability 
to grow at over 30 percent a year for the past 
three to four years as a significant accom- 
plishment. 

Whitmire, formerly Amfac, does a lot of 
business with the hospital market, and as a 
consequence it has smaller facilities than 
the average high-volume wholesaler. 

The company has developed a strategic 
business plan geared to helping it react 
quickly to customer needs. 

“To a large extent,” says Mel Whitmire, 
“our business is based on the degree of ser- 
vice we can provide. 

“When you re dealing with an acute care 
hospital, you can't provide deliveries two 
times a week. They may need Saturday de- 
liveries or even daily deliveries. We pro- 
vide that service.” 

Whitmire has been able to grow its busi- 


‘ness “all across the board. Every segment is 


up—hospitals, chains and independents.” 

However, its largest increases are with 
managed care facilities, including HMOs. 

Whitmire’s work with both acute and 
managed care has helped its rapid expan- 
sion into high-ticket bio-tech pharmaceuti- 
cals. Sales of the drugs are up dramatically, 
and the company is responding by making 
adjustments to its facilities, including the 
construction of refrigerated vaults to ac- 
commodate the drugs as well as larger 
vaults for narcotics. 

Management now owns 20 percent of 
Whitmire Distribution’s stock, and its 
newest investor, Chemical Equity, has said it

just purchased and distribute it to manage-

years, the company continues to prosper. 

Whitmire Distribution is also courting 
the independent and chain drug market 
more aggressively than ever, and seeing 
larger sales increases in these segments as a

Sales of mouthwash aren't 
booming the way they were 
three years ago. In fact, Plax 24-

were the only SKUs in the seg-

share in 1990.
